    Environment & Ecology

    Environment and Sustainable Development · पर्यावरण एवं सतत विकास

    Environment (पर्यावरण)

    Everything surrounding an organism; its biotic (जैविक) and abiotic (अजैविक) parts interact with each other.

    • Definition: sum total of biotic and abiotic components that surround and influence an organism.
    • Word from French Environ = encircle / surround (घेरना).
    • Broad concept: totality of social, biological, physical, chemical elements, individually and collectively, composing nature and human-made surroundings.
    • Total of conditions surrounding man at a given point in space and time; social, cultural, physical conditions affecting survival, growth, development of people, animals, plants.
    • Environment (Protection) Act (पर्यावरण (संरक्षण) अधिनियम), 1986: includes water, air, land and the inter-relationship among and between them and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms, property. Book's short form: physical/abiotic + biotic components and their interaction (p. 7).
    • Composite of biotic factors (all living things) and abiotic factors (temperature, light intensity, amount of available water, etc.).
    • COMMON TRAP Three categories only: physical, biological, cultural. "Operational environment" is not one.UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    ComponentIncludes
    Physical / abioticSoil, air, water; landforms, water bodies, climate, soils, rocks, minerals
    Biological / bioticPlant, human, animal, microorganisms
    CulturalMan-made features: economical, social, political elements
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Name the three broad components of environment, with one example of each.

      Physical (soil), biological (microorganisms), cultural (political elements). p. 7

    2. Correct this: "Operational environment is one of the general categories of environment."

      False. The categories are physical, cultural and biological. p. 8

    3. Fill the labels: the Hydrosphere box in the book's figure branches into which four?

      Glacier, lake, river, ocean. p. 8

    Sustainable Development (सतत विकास)

    Development that meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs; a balance of economic development and environmental conservation.

    • Definition (Brundtland): meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; also phrased as saving energy and other resources for the future without sacrificing people's comfort in the present.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×3PCS Pre ’12, ’18, ’19
    • Important for the well-being of human society; the definition is the reason why.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Inter-generational sensibility in respect of use of natural resources (प्राकृतिक संसाधन).
    • Main objective: conservation, proper management and just, prudent use of natural resources.
    • Discussion began after Our Common Future = Brundtland Report, WCED (World Commission on Environment and Development), 1987. Book: this report coined the term (p. 8).UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    • Gro Brundtland: Norwegian politician, three terms as prime minister of Norway, chair of WCED. Key figures of the concept: Gro Brundtland, Maurice Strong, WCED.
    • Emphasised by UNCED; fully supported in Agenda-21 at Earth Summit (पृथ्वी शिखर सम्मेलन) 1992; prominent issue / main point of discussion at Johannesburg Summit 2002.
    • Important for SD: conservation of biological diversity, prevention and control of pollution, decreasing poverty (all three). Book: SD includes poverty mitigation (p. 8).UPPSCLower Sub ’04
    • Three-part concept: economic, environmental and social development together; banner Venn on p. 7: Environmental Protection and Enhancement, Social Progress, Economic Development.
    • Unsustainable development: pursuing immediate rewards without thinking of harm to others or the planet. Where development is sustainable, everyone has access to decent work, quality health care, education.
    • Now an alternative approach to the theories of development. Understand nature first (its beauty, boundaries), then prepare the road map of development.
    • Compelling terms for SD rest on availability of information: Remote sensing technology, Statistical method, Geographical Information System (GIS), Environment information system. Policy needs information on environment and ecology.
    Added concept

    Circular economy (चक्रीय अर्थव्यवस्था) (UPSC 2025, reported official key; not in the book): reduces raw-material inputs and wastage in production, and both of these explain its lower greenhouse-gas emissions.UPSC 2025

    EventDate

    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Which report and which body, in which year, started the SD discussion?

      Our Common Future (Brundtland Report), WCED, 1987. p. 9

    2. Put in order: Rio Earth Summit, Limits to Growth, Montreal enforcement, Brundtland Report.

      Limits to Growth 1972, Brundtland 1987, Montreal enforcement January 1989, Rio June 1992. p. 9

    3. In one sentence, how is SD "inter-generational"?

      It concerns how natural resources are used so that one generation's use leaves the next able to meet its needs. p. 9

    4. Name two sources of the information on which SD road maps are based.

      Any two: remote sensing, statistical method, GIS, environment information system. p. 8

    Water & Carbon Cycle (कार्बन चक्र) in Nature

    Biotic and abiotic factors interact in cycles; energy and matter flow between them.

    Carbon cycle
    • CORE CONCEPT Add CO₂: respiration (श्वसन), decay of organic matter, volcanic action / eruptions, burning of fossil fuels.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’11, ’14 · 3 papers
    • Photosynthesis (प्रकाश संश्लेषण) does not add CO₂: plants consume CO₂ and release oxygen.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’11, ’14 · 3 papers
    • Most autotrophs (plants) use CO₂ and water, in presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, to produce carbohydrates.
    • Elemental carbon: three crystalline allotropes: graphite, fullerene, diamond. Compound forms: CO₂, carbonates, hydrogen carbonates.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’11, ’14 · 3 papers
    • Carbon is recycled by different physical and biological processes.
    Water cycle (जल चक्र) and humidity
    • Solar radiation plays the most important role in the water cycle: it initiates and drives the cycle by evaporating water from oceans, lakes, rivers.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’00; Lower Sub (Spl) ’04
    • Vapour forms water droplets and clouds; droplets gain enough mass and fall to earth.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Essentially a closed system: volume of water in the hydrosphere today = amount always present in the earth system.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Humidity: a measure of water-vapour content of air (or other gas); measured using a hygrometer or psychrometer.
    • Amount of rain depends on humidity in the atmosphere: higher humidity, more vapour, more chance of cloud and rain if temperature drops.UPPSCPCS Pre ’17
    Root hairs and transplanted seedlings
    • Many transplanted seedlings do not grow because most root hairs are lost during transplantation.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Root hairs collect water and mineral nutrients from soil and take the solution up through the roots to the rest of the plant.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Made up of cellulose and nominal Pectin, which helps as a gelling agent with soil.
    • Another reason: fertilizers raise soil concentration, making it difficult to absorb water; causes desiccation of plant cells and leaves turn brown.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Of respiration, photosynthesis, decay, volcanic action, which one does not add CO₂ and why?

      Photosynthesis, since plants consume CO₂ and release oxygen. p. 11

    2. Why does the book call the water cycle essentially closed?

      Water in the hydrosphere today equals the amount always present in the earth system. p. 11

    3. Link root-hair loss to seedling failure in one sentence.

      Root hairs absorb water and minerals, so losing them during transplantation stops uptake. p. 12

    4. Fill the label: water moves by imbibition from soil solution of ___ concentration to root-hair vacuole of ___ concentration.

      Less; high. p. 11

    Atmosphere

    The thin layer of gases surrounding the earth; air is a mixture of gases.

    • Thin layer of gases around earth = atmosphere; mainly Nitrogen, Oxygen, Carbon dioxide, etc.
    • Air is a mixture; by volume about 78% nitrogen, about 21% oxygen; CO₂, argon, methane, ozone, water vapour in very small quantities.
    • Nitrogen: most abundant gas (78.08% in dry air).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Noble gas keyed as not present in air: Radon (not in the permanent-gas table, p. 12). Naturally occurring radioactive gas, product of the Uranium decay chain; odourless, colourless, tasteless, inert. Moves through voids in rocks and soils; book adds it enters homes with soil gases via cracks and openings in building foundations (p. 13), so read the key as "not a listed constituent".
    • Smart Radon Monitor (SRM): advanced real-time, portable radon monitor for multiple applications in radon studies.
    Permanent gas (NCERT, book's table)%
    Nitrogen (N₂)78.08
    Oxygen (O₂)20.95

    Carbon dioxide (CO₂)0.036
    Neon (Ne)0.002

    Plants, trees and oxygen
    • Photosynthesis takes in CO₂ and releases oxygen: if all plants and trees vanished, oxygen would decrease. Book's figure: balance of O₂ and CO₂ between Plants and Animals.
    • Tree functions: providing oxygen, improving air quality, climate amelioration, conserving water, preserving soil, supporting wildlife; clean the environment; roadside trees reduce sound pollution.
    • Book: Amazon forest is estimated to produce about 20% of total oxygen in the atmosphere, hence named 'Lungs of the Earth'; contains nearly a third of all tropical rainforests left on Earth (Raj. PCS 2023 key).
    Source check Book says Amazon produces about 20% of atmospheric oxygen (p. 13). FactCheck.org calls this false: estimates are closer to 6–9%, and the Amazon consumes nearly all it produces. Keep 20% only as that paper's keyed answer; for the ocean's share see → Ch 2. source
    Environmental degradation (पर्यावरण अवनयन) and related terms
    • Degradation: deterioration through depletion of resources (air, water, soil), destruction of ecosystems, extinction of wildlife; includes adverse change by human activity, overall lowering of quality, ecological imbalance.UPPSCPCS Pre ’06
    • Weathering (अपक्षय): natural process breaking rocks at the Earth's surface into sediments, clays, soils, dissolved substances. Typically begins when crust is uplifted by tectonic forces; loosened fragments then carried away by erosion.
    • Major environmental issues: climate change, pollution, environmental degradation, resource depletion.
    • Poverty alleviation = efforts to reduce or eliminate poverty, improve well-being, give access to resources for a dignified life; government policies to grassroots programs, symptoms and root causes.
    Source check U.P. UDA/LDA 2013 key (p. 14) says poverty alleviation is not related to environmental protection, yet the book lists poverty mitigation within SD (p. 8) and poverty eradication among Agenda 21's key elements (p. 19). Treat as that paper's key only.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Give the book's percentages for the first four gases in dry air.

      N₂ 78.08, O₂ 20.95, Ar 0.93, CO₂ 0.036. p. 12

    2. What kind of substance is air: compound, element or mixture?

      Mixture of gases. p. 12

    3. Correct this: "The Amazon is reliably shown to supply 20% of atmospheric oxygen."

      That is the book's keyed figure; FactCheck.org puts it nearer 6–9% and notes the Amazon consumes nearly all of it. p. 13

    4. What carries away the fragments loosened by weathering?

      Erosion. p. 14

    Sustainable Development Goals (सतत विकास लक्ष्य)

    Seventeen interlinked goals adopted by the UN in 2015, to be realised by 2030.

    • Global Goals: collection of 17 interlinked objectives adopted by UN in 2015 as a "shared blueprint for peace and prosperity for people and the planet, now and into the future". Space research is not a goal.UPPSCPCS Pre ’23
    • COMMON TRAP SDGs were proposed in 2012 at Rio+20, not in 1972 by the Club of Rome.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Officially 'Transforming our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'; 17 aspirational goals with 169 targets; to be achieved by 2030.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Nodal institution for coordination and implementation in India: NITI (National Institution for Transforming India) Aayog.UPPSCPCS Pre ’19
    #GoalAim (compressed)
    1No PovertyEnd poverty in all forms everywhere
    2Zero HungerEnd hunger; food security, improved nutrition, sustainable agriculture
    3Good Health and Well-beingHealthy lives, well-being for all at all ages
    4Quality EducationInclusive, equitable education; lifelong learning
    5Gender EqualityEmpower all women and girls
    6Clean Water and SanitationAvailability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all
    7Affordable and Clean EnergyAffordable, reliable, sustainable, modern energy
    8Decent Work and Economic GrowthSustained, inclusive growth; full, productive employment
    9Industry, Innovation and InfrastructureResilient infrastructure, sustainable industrialization, innovation
    10Reduced InequalitiesWithin and among countries
    11Sustainable Cities and CommunitiesInclusive, safe, resilient, sustainable settlements
    12Responsible Consumption and ProductionSustainable patterns
    13Climate ActionUrgent action on climate change and its impacts
    14Life Below WaterConserve, sustainably use oceans, seas, marine resources
    15Life on LandCombat desertification, manage forests sustainably, halt and reverse land degradation, halt biodiversity loss
    16Peace and Justice Strong InstitutionsPeaceful, inclusive societies; access to justice
    17Partnerships for the GoalsGlobal Partnerships for Sustainable Development
    • SDG-6 context (book): approx. 2.2 billion people lack safely managed drinking water; more than 4.2 billion lack safely managed sanitation.

    Sustainable agriculture
    • Production of food, fibre, other plant or animal products by techniques protecting environment, public health, human communities, animal welfare; in short, using land so that its quality remains intact.UPPSCPCS Pre ’01
    • Chemical fertilizers and pesticides have adversely affected soil health; response: National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA), for agricultural productivity, water use efficiency, nutrient management, livelihood diversification; part of National Action Plan on Climate Change.
    • Best environment-friendly strategy for Indian agriculture: mixed cropping, organic manures, nitrogen-fixing plants, pest-resistant crop varieties.UPSC PYQUPSC ’93
    • UN declared 2022 the International Year of Basic Sciences for Sustainable Development.
    • Conservation Agriculture (संरक्षण कृषि) (FAO): resource-saving crop production seeking acceptable profits with high, sustained production while conserving the environment.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • Principles: minimum tillage and soil disturbance; permanent soil cover with crop residues and live mulches; crop rotation and inter-cropping. Avoiding plantation crops and avoiding monoculture were outside the keyed set (IAS 2018).UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • GACSA (Global Alliance for Climate-Smart Agriculture): set up 2014, not an outcome of Paris 2015; concept developed by FAO in 2010 paper "Climate Smart Agriculture: Policies, Practices and Financing for food security, Adaptation and Mitigation". Membership creates no binding obligations; book: India just a signatory.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    Club of Rome
    • Born April 1968 when 30 people (scientists, educators, economists, humanists, industrialists, government officials) met at Academia dei Lincei, Rome; informal organization. Propounded 'Limits to Growth'.UPPSCPCS Pre ’19
    • Association of economists, civil servants, scientists promoting understanding of global challenges. Five priority areas: emerging New Civilisations; Planetary Emergency; Reframing Economics; Rethinking Finance; Youth Leadership and Intergenerational Dialogues.

    Earth Summit (RIO Summit)

    UNCED, Rio de Janeiro, 3–14 June 1992: a blueprint for international action on environment and development.

    • UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) = 'Earth Summit', Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, 3–14 June 1992; 20th anniversary of first Human Environment Conference, Stockholm, Sweden, 1972.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Primary objective: broad agenda and new blueprint for international action on environment and development issues.
    • More than 100 heads of states met. Leaders signed convention on climate change and convention on Biodiversity, endorsed the Rio Declaration and the Forest Principles, adopted Agenda 21.UPPSC ×4PCS Pre ’13, ’23, ’25; RO/ARO ’14
    • Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD) created to monitor and report on implementation of the Earth Summit agreement.
    • Earth Summit +5: special session of UN General Assembly, New York, 23–27 June 1997; five-year review of how countries, international organizations and civil society responded.UPPSCPCS Mains ’16
    • Rio+10 = World Summit on Sustainable Development (WSSD), Johannesburg, South Africa, 2002 (26 August to 4 September); biggest UN event of its kind to date; major objective: strategies for greater and more effective implementation of Agenda 21.
    • Rio+20 held in Rio de Janeiro, 2012.
    • Book's keyed name for the 1992 Rio meeting: "United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development" (see check below).
    Source check Book's answers name the 1992 Rio meeting "United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development" (pp. 18–19), but its notes call 1992 UNCED and reserve that name for Rio+20, 2012 (pp. 17, 19). Remember: 1992 = UNCED; 2012 = UNCSD.
    Global Environment Facility (GEF)
    • Established on the eve of the 1992 Rio Earth Summit to tackle the planet's most pressing environmental problems.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • CORE CONCEPT Financial mechanism for five conventions: Minamata (Mercury), Stockholm (Persistent Organic Pollutants), UN CBD, UNCCD (Combat Desertification), UNFCCC.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • International partnership of 186 countries and 18 implementing agencies; supports multi-stakeholder alliance to preserve threatened ecosystems on land and oceans, build green cities, boost food security for a prosperous, climate-resilient world.
    • Not a research body and not an OECD agency (IAS 2014 distractors, rejected by the key).
    • UNDP, UNEP and World Bank are associated with GEF. Book's position: Carlos Manuel Rodriguez is Chief Executive Officer and Chairperson.
    • Provides the Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF): provision and coordination of National Adaptation Programmes of Action (NAPAs).
    • Special Climate Change Fund (SCCF): established by COP7 (Marrakesh, 29 October to 10 November 2001); helps developing countries in adaptation and technology transfer.
    Source check Book's text says GEF serves five conventions (p. 18), while its figure on the same page also lists the Montreal Protocol under Conventions.

    1. Distinguish the 1992 and 2012 Rio conferences by full name.

      1992: UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED). 2012: UN Conference on Sustainable Development (Rio+20). p. 17, 19

    2. Where and when was Earth Summit +5?

      UN General Assembly special session, New York, 23–27 June 1997. p. 17

    3. Name the five conventions for which GEF is the financial mechanism.

      Minamata, Stockholm, CBD, UNCCD, UNFCCC. p. 18

    4. Correct this: "GEF is an OECD agency doing scientific research."

      It is a financial mechanism, an international partnership of countries and agencies. p. 18

    Agenda - 21

    A voluntary UN action plan for sustainable development, product of the 1992 Earth Summit.

    • Legally non-binding, voluntarily implemented action plan of the UN on Sustainable Development (a global action plan).UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • COMMON TRAP Originated at the Earth Summit, Rio 1992, not at Johannesburg 2002.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Related to sustainable development. Adopted with the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development and the Statement of Principles for the Sustainable Management of Forests by more than 178 Governments at UNCED, 3–14 June 1992.
    • Full implementation of Agenda 21, the Programme for Further Implementation and commitments to Rio principles strongly reaffirmed at WSSD, Johannesburg, 2002.
    • Key elements (figure): survey of biological diversity and protection of endangered species; poverty eradication and population control in developing countries; stress on generous capital transfer; food, clean water and social security to everyone.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Is Agenda 21 binding? Where did it originate?

      Non-binding and voluntary; Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro, 1992. p. 19

    2. State the four key elements in the book's figure.

      Biodiversity survey and species protection; poverty eradication and population control; capital transfer; food, clean water, social security. p. 19

    3. Fill the sequence: Stockholm 1972 → ___ 1992 → Agenda 21 → ___ 1997.

      Earth Summit; Earth Summit +5. p. 18

    RIO + 20 Conference

    UN Conference on Sustainable Development, Brazil, June 2012, marking 20 years since UNCED.

    • Rio+20 = United Nations Conference on Sustainable Development (UNCSD; also Rio 2012, Earth Summit 2012), Rio de Janeiro, June 2012: 20th anniversary of 1992 UNCED and 10th anniversary of 2002 WSSD, Johannesburg.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Outcome: non-binding document 'The Future We Want', a 49-page action plan. Book: third international conference on sustainable development.
    • Document called on governments, businesses and the UN to support countries in transition to a green economy; PAGE (Partnership for Action on Green Economy) created as the UN's direct response.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. What was the title of the Rio+20 outcome document?

      The Future We Want. p. 19, 20

    2. From which conference did PAGE emerge, and why?

      Rio+20, 2012, as the UN's direct response to its call on green-economy transition. p. 19

    3. Rio+20 marked which two anniversaries?

      20th of UNCED 1992; 10th of WSSD 2002. p. 19

    Organizations & Institutions

    National and international bodies established for environmental conservation and protection.

    National bodies
    • NEERI (National Environmental Engineering Research Institute): Nagpur, Maharashtra; established 1958 as Central Public Health Engineering Research Institute (CPHERI).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS6 papersUPPSC ×6PCS Pre ’12, ’14; PCS Mains ’05, ’11, ’17; Lower Sub ’04
    • CPHERI focus: water supply, sewage disposal and related diseases, to some extent industrial pollution. Pioneering laboratory in environmental science and engineering; part of Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS6 papers
    • Five zonal laboratories: Chennai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai. Under Ministry of Science & Technology, Government of India.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS6 papers
    • National Environment Appellate Authority (NEAA, "better known as NEA"): set up by Ministry of Environment and Forest under NEAA Act 1997 to hear appeals on restriction of areas in which industries, operations or processes may or may not be carried out, subject to safeguards under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
    • NEAA stands dissolved on establishment of NGT (18 October 2010); role taken over by NGT.
    • NITI Aayog: nodal for SDGs ↗.
    Source check Book keys the N.E.A. question "(*)" (p. 21), giving no listed option as correct; it only explains NEAA. Do not treat "National Environment Authority" as the expansion.
    International bodies and agencies
    BodyFacts (book's position where a post-holder is named)
    WMO (World Meteorological Organization)HQ Geneva, Switzerland. Framework for international cooperation in meteorology and operational hydrology. 193 Member States and Territories. Originated from International Meteorological Organization (IMO), founded 1873 for exchange of weather information across borders; became WMO 17 March 1951. Secretary-General: Prof. Celeste Saulo
    UNEPEstablished 1972; HQ Nairobi, Kenya. Executive Director: Inger Andersen of DenmarkREPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers

    • UNEA-4: Nairobi, Kenya, 11–15 March 2019; theme "Innovative solutions for Environmental Challenges and Sustainable Consumption and Production".
    • UNEA-5: (virtually) Nairobi, February 2021; theme "Strengthening Actions for Nature to Achieve the Sustainable Development Goals".
    • UNEA-7 (book, as scheduled): 8–12 December 2025, UNEP headquarters, Nairobi.

    Acts - Related to Environment Conservation

    The 1986 Act is India's umbrella statute; the NGT is the specialised forum for disputes.

    Constitutional basis
    • 42nd Amendment Act, 1976: added provisions in Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties.
    • Article 48A (DPSP): State to "protect and improve the environment and to safeguard the forests and wildlife of country".
    • Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty): every citizen to "protect and improve the natural environment including forest, lakes, rivers and wildlife and to have compassion for living creatures".
    Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
    • Enacted in 1986; extends to the whole of India; objective: protection and improvement of the environment.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS7 papersUPPSC ×6PCS Pre ’14, ’21, ’22; PCS Mains ’17; UDA/LDA ’13; BEO ’19
    • Known as Umbrella Legislation: framework for Central Government coordination of central and state authorities under previous laws such as the Water Act and the Air Act.
    • Enacted after the Bhopal Gas Tragedy under Article 253 of the Constitution; implements decisions of UN Conference on the Human Environment, Stockholm 1972.
    • Empowers Central Government to establish authorities [section 3(3)] with mandate to prevent pollution in all forms and tackle problems peculiar to different parts of the country. Book's dated statement: last amended in 1991 (pp. 23–24).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS7 papers
    • Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC): constituted under this Act; renamed from Genetic Engineering Approval Committee on 22 July 2010; apex body in Ministry of Environment and Forest under 'Rules for manufacture, use, import, export and storage of hazardous microorganism/genetically engineered organism or cells 1989'.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA): constituted under section 3(3); regulates and controls development and management of ground water.UPSC PYQUPSC ’22
    • CGWA powers: (i) section 5 directions on matters in section 3(2); (ii) penal provisions, sections 15 to 21; (iii) regulate and control ground water, issue regulatory directions; (iv) section 4 appointment of officers.UPSC PYQUPSC ’22
    • Protection of ecological balance: directly Forest Policy and Environment (Protection) Act; Industrial Policy and Educational Policy also include environmental approach (key: all four).UPPSCPCS Mains (Spl) ’04
    National Green Tribunal (राष्ट्रीय हरित अधिकरण) (NGT)
    • National Green Tribunal established on 18 October 2010 under NGT Act, 2010: effective, expeditious disposal of cases on environmental protection and conservation of forests and other natural resources, including enforcement of legal rights relating to environment.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Mains ’17
    • Enacted in consonance with Article 21: right to healthy environment construed as part of Right to Life. Not Article 275(1) or Article 243(A) (IAS 2012 key).UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Provides compensation to victims for property damage; helps reduce trials pending in high courts.
    • First chairman: Justice Lokeshwar Singh Panta (18 October 2010). Book's position: present chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    Source check Book says the Tribunal must solve applications and petitions within one month of filing (p. 23). NGT's own site says it is mandated to endeavour for final disposal within 6 months of filing. source
    India's climate instruments (as cited)
    • Clean Development Mechanism (CDM): Article 12 of Kyoto Protocol of UNFCCC; lets Annex-B Party with an emission commitment implement emission-reduction project in developing countries; projects earn saleable certified emission reduction (CER) credits, each = one tonne of CO₂, counted towards Kyoto targets.
    • National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC): established August 2015 to meet the adaptation cost of States and Union Territories particularly vulnerable to climate change.
    Source check On "not true" for India's climate steps (J.P.P.C.S. 2016, p. 25), the book keys "not attended the 19th BASIC meeting, Sun City" only because it has "no relation" to climate impact; it does not say whether India attended.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Why is the 1986 Act called umbrella legislation, and under which Article was it enacted?

      It frames Central coordination of authorities under earlier laws; Article 253. p. 24

    2. Explain the NGT–CPCB distinction on origin.

      NGT under the NGT Act 2010; CPCB is also statutory, under the Water Act 1974, so it is not a creation of executive order. p. 26

    3. Which constitutional Articles did the 42nd Amendment add on environment?

      Article 48A and Article 51A(g). p. 24

    4. Correct this: "NGT must decide every case within one month."

      The book says one month, but NGT's own site says it endeavours for disposal within 6 months of filing. p. 23

    5. Name one body each constituted under section 3(3) and under the 1989 Rules of the EP Act.

      CGWA; GEAC. p. 24

    Environment - Some Important Facts For Exams

    Standalone facts on books, labels, days, programmes and places.

    Authors and pioneers
    • 'Silent Spring' (1962): Rachel Carson, American marine biologist and ecologist; set the tone for the world environmental movement.UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    • 'Green Development: Environment and Sustainability in the Third World': W.M. Adams (William M. Adams); first edition 1990.UPPSCPCS Pre ’11
    • Masanobu Fukuoka: Japanese farmer and philosopher, discoverer of Natural Farming, re-vegetation of desertified lands; book "The One-Straw Revolution" (1975): farming in harmony with nature, minimal intervention, rejecting chemicals, tilling, excessive manipulation of land.
    World Environment Day
    • Celebrated on 5 June; decided at Stockholm Summit 1972 (1st World Summit on Environment); first celebrated 1973. 2022 marked 50 years since Stockholm.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papersUPPSC ×4PCS Pre ’12; PCS Mains ’04, ’11, ’14
    YearHostTheme
    2018IndiaBeat Plastic Pollution
    2019ChinaAir Pollution
    2020Colombia in partnership with GermanyBiodiversity
    2021PakistanEcosystem Restoration
    2022Only One Earth: living sustainably in harmony with nature
    2024Land restoration, desertification and drought resilience; slogan 'Our Land. Our Future. We are #GenerationRestoration'
    Labels, greenwashing and consumer indices
    • Eco-Mark (Ecomark, 'ECOMARC'): eco-labelling scheme started 1991 for environment-friendly products; certification mark issued and administered by Bureau of Indian Standards, for products ensuring least impact on the ecosystem.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSC ×3PCS Pre ’12, ’21; PCS Mains (Spl) ’04
    • Covers: soaps and detergents, food items, lubricating oils, packing/packaging materials, architectural paints and powder coatings, batteries, electric and electronic goods, food additives, wood substitutes, cosmetics, aerosols and propellants, plastic products, textiles, fire-extinguisher, leather, coir and coir products.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    • Environment-friendly product: made, used or disposed of in a way that significantly reduces the harm it would otherwise cause.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    • COMMON TRAP Greenwashing: an unsubstantiated or misleading claim of environmental benefit, conveying a false impression that a company's products are eco-friendly and environmentally sound.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’22 · 2 papers
    • Greendex: National Geographic Society with GlobeScan; first survey January 2008, 14 countries; measures environmentally sustainable consumer behaviour. India ranked first in 2009, retained 2014.UPSC PYQUPSC ’10
    Programmes and cases
    • Australia's Green Army: six-month programme for 17–24-year-olds; restoring native vegetation, heritage restoration, protecting animal habitats, regenerating wetlands in urban, rural, remote areas. Closed 30 June 2018.
    • Plachimada: village in Palakkad district, Kerala; Chittur block's Perumatty Panchayat. 2000: licence to Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages Private Limited (HCCBPL) for Coca-Cola (Coke), Fanta, Limca, Thums Up, Sprite, Kinley.UPPSCLower Sub (Spl) ’09
    • Groundwater contaminated by the company's chemical waste; local protest, supported by Panchayat; became an icon of such movements worldwide against a multinational company (MNC).
    • Greenhouse farming launched in Punjab: agreement between Markfed of Punjab and Sayag Group of Israel, April 2001.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’01, ’03
    Urbanisation, capital and climate index
    • Excess urbanization (नगरीकरण) and industrialization harm balanced development, environment and ecology, and biodiversity.UPPSCPCS Mains ’02
    • Negative aspects of development discussed in mid-80s: degradation of natural resources, environment pollution, displacement and rehabilitation of masses. Politics and Development was not among them (book's key).UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    • India is not over-urbanised (Assertion false), but most large cities lack adequate infrastructure (Reason true): Drinking Water, Transport, Sanitation, Electricity, etc.UPPSCPCS Mains ’17
    • Natural capital: all renewable (नवीकरणीय) and non-renewable (अनवीकरणीय) environmental resources (air, water, land, minerals, forests) created by nature without human interference. Roads excluded.UPPSCPCS Pre ’12
    • Natural vegetation is the true index of climate; water-loving / aquatic plants occur in moist climate, mostly muddy land and near ponds; reduced moisture leads to their erosion; increased atmospheric CO₂ also affects vegetation.UPPSCPCS Pre ’09
    • Smart City Mission: drive economic growth, improve (not merely stabilise) quality of life through local development and technology for smart outcomes.UPPSCPCS Mains ’17
    • Core elements: adequate water supply; assured electricity; sanitation incl. solid waste management; efficient urban mobility and public transport; affordable housing, especially for the poor; robust IT connectivity and digitalization; good governance, especially e-Governance and people's participation; sustainable environment; safety and security of citizens, particularly women, children, elderly; health and education.
    Source check Citing the census of 2011, book says "121 crore people (68.9%)" live in rural areas (p. 31), which clashes with its own 37.7 crore (31.1%) urban: 37.7 crore at 31.1% implies a total near 121 crore, so 121 crore is the country total, not the rural count.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Who wrote Silent Spring, Green Development and The One-Straw Revolution?

      Rachel Carson; W.M. Adams; Masanobu Fukuoka. p. 28

    2. State the date of World Environment Day, the first year it was observed, and the 2018 host.

      5 June; 1973; India. p. 26

    3. Which body administers Ecomark, and what is greenwashing?

      Bureau of Indian Standards; a misleading claim of environmental benefit. p. 27, 29

    4. Identify the false term: Natural capital includes forests, water, roads, minerals.

      Roads: only resources created by nature count. p. 31

    5. Fill the labels: which of petrol, forest, solar energy is exhaustible and non-renewable?

      Petrol. p. 31

    Ecology · पारिस्थितिकी

    Ecology (पारिस्थितिकी)

    Ecology studies organisms in relation to their environment; the ecosystem (पारिस्थितिकी तंत्र) is its functional unit.

    • Ecology: branch of biology on the relationship between organism and environment, including interaction with abiotic components.
    • Term ('Oekologie') coined by German zoologist Ernst Haeckel (1834–1919; book also prints "Hackle"), 1860s, to describe the 'economics' of living forms. Greek Oikos (house / living space) + logos (science / study).
    • Haeckel: study of relation of the animal to its organic and inorganic environment. Eugene Odum: study of structure and function of nature.
    • Now broader: plants, animals, climate, and also human beings, society and physical surroundings.
    • Book's figure (p. 32): Climate, Vegetation, Animal and Soil all interact in both directions.
    Ecosystem
    • Term proposed by A.G. Tansley, 1935: category of physical systems of organisms and inorganic components in relatively stable equilibrium, open and of various sizes and kinds.UPPSCUDA/LDA ’02
    • Other names for the idea: Karl Mobius, Biocoenosis; Forbes, Microcosm.
    • Community (समुदाय) of living organisms (plants, animals, microbes) with non-living components (air, water, mineral soil), interacting as a system through nutrient cycles and energy flows (ऊर्जा प्रवाह).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Size varies: a water droplet / drop in a pond (micro ecosystem) to an ocean; Earth itself is a large ecosystem.
    • COMMON TRAP Ecosystem is an open system, not closed: continuous but variable influx and loss of materials and energy.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Mains ’14
    • Functional unit of nature; integrates the whole mosaic of interacting organisms and environment; capable of energy transformation, circulation and accumulation; has its own productivity (उत्पादकता); occupies a definite area in the Biosphere (जैवमंडल).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Four basic components: abiotic materials, producers (उत्पादक), consumers (उपभोक्ता), decomposers (अपघटक) or reducers (last three = biotic).
    • Best description: a community of organisms together with the environment in which they live.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Components are interdependent: if the population of one organism rises or falls the rest is affected (foxes killed, rabbits increase). Human activities impact the environment through overpopulation, pollution, burning fossil fuels, deforestation (वनोन्मूलन), triggering climate change, soil erosion, poor air quality, undrinkable water.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’21; RO/ARO Mains ’16
    Source check Book says an ecosystem "covers a definite area" (p. 32) yet in an answer calls it a unit "with no limits of boundaries" (p. 33).
    Biosphere
    • Largest ecosystem of the earth = Biosphere; sum total of all ecosystems on the Earth; part of earth where life exists.UPPSCRO/ARO ’17
    • Integrated zone of atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water), lithosphere (land); thin layer of soil, rock, water, air; narrow layer around the surface.
    • Absent at extremes of the North and South Poles, the highest mountains and the deepest oceans.
    • Book's key (UP RO/ARO 2017): Biosphere is an example of an open system (true); the Reason denying reinvestment of new substances is false, since input and output of substances occur.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Who coined Oekologie and who proposed the term ecosystem, with years?

      Ernst Haeckel, 1860s; A.G. Tansley, 1935. p. 32

    2. Correct this: "An ecosystem is a closed system."

      It is an open system, with continuous but variable influx and loss of materials and energy. p. 33

    3. Name the four basic components of an ecosystem.

      Abiotic materials, producers, consumers, decomposers. p. 33

    4. Where is the biosphere absent?

      Extremes of the North and South Poles, highest mountains, deepest oceans. p. 34

    Components of Ecosystem

    All organisms and abiotic components of a place form its ecosystem; levels of organisation and ecosystem types build on this.

    • All components in mutual interaction in the biosphere form an ecosystem; living organisms form biosphere by different biological associations.
    • Biotic components: living things shaping an ecosystem. Producers (plants), Consumers (animals, humans), Decomposers (fungi, bacteria).
    • Autotrophs (स्वपोषी) produce their own food. Consumers are heterotrophs, getting energy by consuming other organisms, not by photosynthesis.
    • Decomposers break organic matter of dead bodies into inorganic material (not inorganic to organic).
    • Air is abiotic; plants, bacteria, animals are biotic.
    • Habitat (पर्यावास): actual location where an organism lives; provides food, water, air, shelter. Biome (बायोम (जीवोम)): plant and animal community covering a large geographical area; major biomes: forest, grassland, desert, tundra.
    Levels of biological organisation
    • Order, organism to biosphere: Population, Community, Ecosystem, Landscape.UPPSCPCS Pre ’17
    • Population: individuals of the same species, same area, capable of reproducing with one another.
    • Community: populations of two or more species in the same area and time period.
    • Ecosystem: community plus abiotic components. One or more ecosystems in a fixed terrain form a Landscape of a particular region.
    • Biome: large ecological area of similar climate, can hold multiple ecosystems. Biosphere: all living organisms with the spheres they interact with (lithosphere, hydrosphere, etc.).
    Types of ecosystem
    • Artificial: fulfils criteria of a natural ecosystem but made and controlled by humans: orchards, farmlands, field, rice field, gardens, human-made reservoirs. Forests, ponds, lakes are natural.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’16, ’18
    • Agriculture under man-made ecosystem has been instrumental to the existence of society and development.
    • Non-terrestrial: aquatic, marine, wetlands. Five major terrestrial ecosystems: desert, forest, grassland, taiga, tundra. Further classified by geographical region and dominant plant type. Marine is not a sub-category of terrestrial.UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’21
    • Aquatic: living and non-living parts of a water body and their interactions; marine + freshwater. Marine is the biggest type: about 71% of earth's surface, about 97% of planet's water.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’14; Lower Sub (Spl) ’03
    • CORE CONCEPT Marine / ocean = most stable ecosystem: remains unchanged over a long period, irrespective of geological and anthropogenic processes.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’13, ’18
    • About 85% of dissolved materials in seawater are sodium and chlorine. Stratification is a feature of the marine ecosystem.
    • Oceans: cradle of life on Earth, highest level of biodiversity; no terrestrial ecosystem matches the biological richness of a coral reef, in variety and originality of survival strategies.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papers
    Remember Two "largest" answers: Biosphere = largest ecosystem overall; Marine / ocean = largest among the types listed.
    Source check The book's figure prints "Aphotic Zone" directly below Sea Level (p. 35), though aphotic means without light. Treat this as the figure as printed, and check zone order before using it.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Reconstruct the order from organism to biosphere asked in exam.

      Population, Community, Ecosystem, Landscape. p. 35

    2. Distinguish habitat from biome.

      Habitat is where an organism lives; a biome is a plant and animal community over a large geographical area. p. 35

    3. What share of the earth's surface and of its water do marine ecosystems hold?

      About 71% and about 97%. p. 35

    4. Fill the labels: three man-made ecosystems in the book's figure.

      Farmland, aquarium, space ship. p. 35

    5. Correct this: "Decomposers convert inorganic matter into organic matter."

      They break down organic matter of dead bodies into inorganic material. p. 36

    Ecological Imbalance (पारिस्थितिक असंतुलन)

    Disruption of an ecosystem's natural balance by natural or human-caused disturbances.

    • Wildlife conservation and prevention of environmental pollution help maintain balance. Cutting forest / deforestation adds to imbalance.
    • Deforestation: one of the main causes of ecological imbalance in India. Desertification, floods and famines, rainfall variations are other causes.
    • Lumbering disturbs the balance; social forestry (सामाजिक वानिकी), Vanamahotsav, afforestation (वनीकरण) do not.UPPSC ×2RO/ARO ’14; UDA/LDA ’13
    • Associated with balance: water management, afforestation, wildlife protection. Book's key: industrial management is not.UPPSCPCS Pre ’05
    • Causes of deforestation (figure): natural disasters; heavy demand of papers; conversion of forest into grazing land; conversion of forest land into agricultural land; urbanization; Jhum cultivation; wood cutting for commercial and industrial use; forest fire; lack of concept of sustainable development in policy making.
    Source check Book's note calls desertification, floods, famines and rainfall variations "secondary causes of deforestation" (p. 37), but its answer calls them "other causes of ecological imbalance" (p. 38). The answer's reading is used above.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Name one main cause of ecological imbalance in India.

      Deforestation. p. 38

    2. Which disturbs balance: lumbering, social forestry, Vanamahotsav?

      Lumbering. p. 38

    3. List three of the book's causes of deforestation.

      Any three: heavy demand of papers, Jhum cultivation, urbanization, forest fire, conversion to grazing or agricultural land, wood cutting, natural disasters. p. 37

    Carrying Capacity (वहन क्षमता)

    The largest population an environment can sustain indefinitely.

    • Maximum population size of a species the environment can sustain indefinitely, given food, habitat, water and other necessities; the number of organisms an environment can sustainably support.
    • Population above carrying capacity pressures the ecosystem; excessive growth can lead to failure of the ecosystem.
    • Biotic potential: maximum reproductive capacity under optimum environmental conditions, denoted r. Carrying capacity is the limit beyond which growth cannot be sustained (K in the figure).
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Define carrying capacity in one sentence.

      The maximum population size of a species that the environment can sustain indefinitely. p. 38

    2. Which letter denotes biotic potential?

      r. p. 38

    3. Fill the label: the dashed line in the S-curve is ___.

      K, the bearing (carrying) capacity. p. 38

    Food Web (खाद्य जाल) or Food Chain (खाद्य श्रृंखला)

    Energy passes from one living organism to another along a feeding sequence.

    • Food chain: order in which organisms feed on each other; usually only four to five links. Some animals feed on living organisms, some on dead organic matter (the latter = detritus food chain).UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • COMMON TRAP Food chains are not found within the population of a species; a chain also does not show the number eaten.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Food = any substance consumed for nutritional support. Plants are self-feeding; animals depend on plants. Flow of energy through a chain is unidirectional.UPPSCPCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15
    • Food chain: flow of carbon and energy within an area from the feeding sequence of a community.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Grass, goat, human: Grass (Autotroph), Goat (Herbivorous consumer), Humans (Omnivorous consumer).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Common marine chain: Diatom, Crustaceans, Herring.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    Producers, consumers, decomposers
    • Green plants = Primary Producers (प्राथमिक उत्पादक): autotrophs making complex organic compounds (carbohydrates, fats, proteins) generally using light; fundamental to the food chain of all ecosystems.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’13
    • Trophic level (पोषण स्तर)-I = autotrophs / green plants, which fix solar energy for heterotrophs.
    • Primary consumer = herbivores (शाकाहारी); secondary = small carnivores (मांसाहारी); tertiary = large carnivores. Man is both primary and secondary consumer (plant products and meat).UPPSCPCS Pre ’16
    • Primary consumers (book's key): Deer (herbivorous) and Ants (book: decomposer, primary consumer and scavenger; eats plants, gets energy from cellulose). Tiger is carnivorous, fox omnivorous.UPPSCPCS Mains ’06
    • Phytoplankton (पादप प्लवक) (micro-algae): main marine primary producers; contain chlorophyll, need sunlight; most are buoyant and float in the upper ocean where sunlight penetrates; need nitrates, phosphates, sulfur, converted into proteins, fats, carbohydrates.UPPSCPCS Mains ’05
    • Decomposers: nature's recyclers, breaking organic matter of dead bodies. Organic matter = matter from living organisms. Mainly bacteria and fungi (yeasts, moulds); release compounds usable by producers. Virus not keyed as a decomposer.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Pond ecosystem: fungi, bacteria and flagellates act as decomposers; consumers are zooplankton, free-swimming and bottom-dwelling forms.
    • Autotroph-level production = primary productivity; heterotroph-level production = secondary productivity (herbivores are secondary producers).UPPSCRO/ARO ’17
    • Huge fall in butterflies: pollination of some plants adversely affected; lower food-chain member, meal of spider, bird, snake, so wasp, spider and bird populations could fall. Rise in fungal infections not keyed as a consequence (IAS 2017).UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Book's "correct match": Green plants with Ecosystem (plants are living organisms, part of an ecosystem). Bacteria are biotic, not abiotic.
    Primary ProducerEcosystem
    PhytoplanktonOcean or deep water
    Rooted PlantsShallow water
    Grasses of different kind and forest plantsGrassland
    Crop PlantsCropland
    Added concept

    UPSC 2025 (reported official key; not in the book): marine phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria produce about 50% of the world's oxygen. Rain forests do not exceed the oceans, and well-oxygenated surface water does not hold several-fold more oxygen than air. See the Amazon check at → Ch 1.UPSC 2025

    Source check M.P.P.C.S. 2024 (p. 41): book gives (c), decomposers, for fungi, bacteria, flagellates, and reports that the Madhya Pradesh Public Service Commission's final key accepted both (b) consumers and (c).
    Source check R.O./A.R.O. 2017 (p. 42): keyed "(*)". Book says producers and decomposers both act as intermediaries between biotic and abiotic components, so no single option is keyed.
    • Those who link biotic and abiotic components (book): producers (photosynthesis) and decomposers (recycling), together.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Reconstruct the grassland chain with the role of each member.

      Grass (producer), grasshopper (primary), frog (secondary), snake (tertiary consumer). p. 39

    2. Why can't a food chain exist within one species' population?

      That would mean a species feeding on itself, as with human eating human. p. 40

    3. Name the main primary producers in the ocean.

      Phytoplankton. p. 41

    4. Primary productivity is production at which level?

      Autotroph level. p. 42

    5. Fill the table: primary producer in cropland and in shallow water.

      Crop plants; rooted plants. p. 39

    Flow of Energy

    Energy enters by photosynthesis, moves one way, and diminishes at every trophic level.

    • Solar energy = primary source and driving force of an ecosystem.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSC ×3PCS Mains ’15; RO/ARO (Re-exam) ’16; BEO ’19
    • Flow is unidirectional: enters plants through photosynthesis, passes along the chain, is lost as heat and does not return to plants; always lower (producer) to higher (herbivore, carnivore) level.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • 1st law of thermodynamics: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only changed in form.
    • 2nd law: in energy conversion part is always lost as heat; product has less energy than its constituents.
    • Energy magnitude always decreases from one trophic level to the next (unusable heat lost at each level).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Ten percent law (दस प्रतिशत का नियम): Raymond Lindeman, first half of 1940s. Only about 10% of energy in organic food is stored as flesh at the next level; the rest is lost in transfer, respiration or incomplete digestion.
    • At every level (first, second, third, top) the consumer converts only 10% of accumulated energy into body weight. Book: herbivores can assimilate only 10% of gross productivity.
    Trophic Levels
    • Trophic levels are formed by organisms linked in a food chain, each level showing transfer of energy and nutrients; producers convert sunlight into chemical energy.UPPSC ×3PCS Pre ’19, ’23; RO/ARO ’17
    • Book's four levels: First, Producer (autotrophs); Second, Primary consumers (herbivorous); Third, Secondary consumers (carnivorous); Fourth, Tertiary consumers (omnivorous). Decomposers feed on all levels.
    Source check Book's level table and key treat the highest level as omnivores (सर्वाहारी) (pp. 43, 45), but p. 42 puts "tertiary consumer (large carnivores)" at the fourth level and p. 39 calls tertiary consumers large carnivores. Keep "omnivores" only as the U.P. UDA/LDA 2002 key.
    Pyramids
    • Pyramid of energy (ऊर्जा का पिरामिड): always upright, never inverted, since some energy is lost as heat at each step. Each bar shows energy at a level in a given time or annually per unit area.
    • Pyramid of Biomass (जैवभार का पिरामिड): biomass per unit area at each trophic level. Grasslands and forests: decrease from producers to top carnivores, so upright.
    • Inverted in a pond (producers are small organisms, biomass least, increases towards the apex) and generally in marine ecosystem (biomass of fishes far exceeds phytoplankton).UPPSCGIC ’10
    • Generally more producers than primary consumers, and more primary consumers than secondary consumers.UPPSCPCS Pre ’19
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Why is energy flow unidirectional?

      Energy given out as heat is lost to the environment and does not return for plants to use. p. 43

    2. Who gave the Ten Percent Law and when?

      Raymond Lindeman, first half of 1940s. p. 43

    3. Which pyramid is always upright, and where is the biomass pyramid inverted?

      Energy pyramid; pond and marine ecosystems. p. 44, 45

    4. Fill the label: in the pond pyramid, plankton is ___ Kg and big fishes ___ Kg.

      5; 1000. p. 43

    Biological Magnification (Biomagnification (जैव आवर्धन))

    Concentration of a persistent toxin rises at successive trophic levels.

    • CORE CONCEPT Increase in concentration of toxic materials at successive trophic levels; substance is accumulated, cannot be metabolized or excreted, passes to next level. Well known for Mercury (Hg) and DDT.UPSC PYQUPSC ’97
    • DDT: insecticide, non-biodegradable, deposited in fatty tissues; concentration increases from producers through primary and secondary to tertiary consumers. Highest of grasshopper, toad, snake, cattle = snake (tertiary consumer).UPSC PYQUPSC ’97
    • Bionomics (Greek bio = life, nomos = law): comprehensive study of an organism and its relation to its environment; synonymous with Ecology; stresses value of natural systems which influence human systems; not related to the management of life.UPPSCUDA/LDA ’01
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Why does DDT build up along a food chain?

      It cannot be degraded biologically, metabolized or excreted, so each level receives what the one before stored. p. 45, 46

    2. Correct this: "Bionomics means management of life."

      It is the study of an organism and its relation to its environment, synonymous with ecology. p. 46

    3. Name two substances the book links with biomagnification.

      Mercury and DDT. p. 45

    Biogeochemical Cycle (जैव-भू-रासायनिक चक्र)

    Chemical substances move through biotic and abiotic parts of Earth; communities themselves change in sequence.

    • Biogeochemical (nutritional) cycle: pathway by which a chemical substance moves through biotic and abiotic components of Earth; e.g. nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’20, ’21
    • Weathering of rocks is the main release route in the Phosphorus cycle: phosphate ion (PO₄³⁻) in water, soil, sediments; much is tied up in rock and sedimentary deposits, released by weathering, leaching, mining.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • Passes through freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems via plants, grazers, predators, parasites; returned by death and decay. Much deposited in the sea, in shallow sediments or ocean deeps; back to land through fish harvests and guano deposited by seabirds.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    Ecological succession (पारिस्थितिक अनुक्रमण)
    • Gradual process by which ecosystems change and develop over time.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Grassland: trees do not replace grasses because of water limits and fire. Past fires cleared trees and changed the ground composition; water washes away most soil, underlying ground becomes pioneer population replaced by grass; grass absorbs most water before it reaches shrub roots.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • F.E. Clements (book also prints F. Clement) studied wetland communities; gave a generally agreed definition in 1916: succession as development of the climax. E. Odum described biotic succession as a sequenced process.
    • Monoclimax theory: Clements (1936): every region has one climax community (चरम समुदाय) toward which all communities develop; climax is solely a function of climate.UPPSCRO/ARO ’21
    • Entire sequence of communities that successively change in an area = Sere.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    • Book notes biotic succession as displacement of one community by another in an area.
    • Order: Nudation, Migration, Ecesis, Reaction, Stabilization (U.P.P.C.S. 2024 asked it without Nudation).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’24; PCS Mains ’16
    • Invasive species (book): non-native, spread widely in a community; high reproductive rates and better dispersal mechanisms (sentence is cut at the page break, p. 47–48).
    • Ecesis: early colonizers proliferate by germination, growth, reproduction; pioneer species survive the dispersal mechanisms; book: due to allogenic mechanisms alone.
    • Climax community: mature, self-sustaining, stable, final stage; best adapted to the region; structure likely continues until another disturbance. Physical and chemical conditions are altered and stabilized to support the entire community.
    • Ecological Transition: first used by John W. Bennett, The Ecological Transition: Cultural Anthropology and Human Adaptation. Development of an anthropocentric orientation to nature emerging in the Western Renaissance; growing incorporation of Nature into Culture and breakdown of local self-sufficiency (ability of a local group to satisfy needs with existing resources in a particular geographical range).UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. For which cycle is weathering of rocks the main nutrient entry route?

      Phosphorus cycle. p. 47

    2. Sequence the five stages of biotic succession.

      Nudation, Migration, Ecesis, Reaction, Stabilization. p. 46

    3. What is a sere?

      The entire sequence of communities that successively change in an area. p. 48

    4. Explain why trees do not replace grasses in grassland.

      Water limits and fire: past fires cleared trees and grass takes water before shrub roots reach it. p. 47

    Environmental Movements

    Local struggles over forests and rivers shaped India's modern environmental movement.

    • Chipko: forest (plant) conservation movement started 1973. On 26 March 1974 Gaura Devi gathered women of her village in Garhwal Himalayas and stopped loggers by sticking to the trees; illiterate tribal and village women reclaiming traditional forest rights; non-violent; gave birth to the modern Indian environmental movement.UPPSC ×3PCS Pre ’12, ’15; PCS Mains ’03
    • Slogan of Chipko: "Ecology is permanent economy".UPPSCPCS Mains ’07
    • Narmada Bachao Andolan: against construction of a multi-modal dam (book's words) on the Narmada river.
    • Appiko Movement: started in Karnataka for environmental protection.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Whose slogan was "Ecology is permanent economy"?

      Chipko Movement. p. 49

    2. Give the year Chipko started and the date of Gaura Devi's action.

      1973; 26 March 1974. p. 48

    3. Match Appiko to its State.

      Karnataka. p. 48

    Ecological Footprint (पारिस्थितिक पदचिह्न) and Millennium Ecosystem Assessment

    Ways of measuring what people demand from ecosystems and what ecosystems provide.

    • Ecological footprint: measure of human demand on Earth's ecosystems, contrasted with the planet's ecological capacity to regenerate; biologically productive area needed to provide everything people need to sustain life (minimum land area for a person's life).UPPSCPCS Pre ’12
    • Includes fruits, vegetables, wood, fibres, fossil fuel use, release of carbon dioxide. Unit: Global hectares. Book's figure: emission from Motor vehicle, Sewage, Electric energy, Water-use.
    • Social Cost of Carbon: monetary value of long-term damage done by a tonne of CO₂ emission in a given year; EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) and other US agencies use it to evaluate climate impacts of rule making.UPSC PYQUPSC ’20
    • According to World Development Report 2010, Millennium Ecosystem Assessment describes five groups of ecosystem services. Nutrient recycling and crop pollination are examples.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Supporting services: necessary for production of all others; impacts on people indirect or over a very long time; e.g. soil formation and retention, nutrient cycling, crop pollination, water cycling.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. In what unit is ecological footprint measured?

      Global hectares. p. 49

    2. What does Social Cost of Carbon measure?

      In monetary value, long-term damage from a tonne of CO₂ emitted in a given year. p. 49

    3. Match: production of food and water; maintenance of diversity; control of climate and disease.

      Provisioning; preserving; regulating. p. 50

    Ecosystem: Some Facts for Exam

    High-frequency terms, laws, and marine facts collected at the end of the chapter.

    Niche (निकेत) and ecotone (इकोटोन (संक्रमिका))
    • Ecological niche: position of a species in an ecosystem, comprising habitat requirements and functional role. Term by Joseph Grinnell, 1917, who called it Micro-Habitats; "the ultimate distributional unit of species and subspecies".UPSC PYQUPSC ’13UPPSCPCS Pre ’05
    • Range of conditions tolerated, resources used, functional role; each species has a distinct niche; subsumes all interactions with biotic and abiotic environment.UPPSCPCS Pre ’22
    • If resources are abundant more species can coexist; species are fewer when resources are insufficient, since competition for food, space and other essentials restricts them.
    • Ecotone: region of transition between two biological communities; steep transition along an environmental or other gradient. Recognition of a transition zone by Clements could be called the beginning of ecotone research.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’12
    Aquatic facts
    • Lentic: static water habitats: ponds, lakes, swamps, marshes, ditches; ponds may be temporary, lakes large.
    • Lotic: flowing waters: rivers, streams, brooks, springs; higher oxygen level from continually moving current; clearer water.UPPSCPCS Pre ’23
    • Decreasing productivity: Mangrove (मैंग्रोव (कच्छ वनस्पति)), Grasslands, Lake, Ocean. Book: more diversity, more productivity.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’13 · 2 papers
    • Pycnocline: density gradient. Halocline: salt gradient. Thermocline: change in temperature with depth.UPPSCPCS Mains ’16
    • Oceanic upwelling: winds push surface water away; colder, nutrient-rich water rises to replace it (book p. 51 "Oceanic outflow": warm, nutrient-less surface water replaced by cold, nutrient-rich water by air flow). Brings nutrients to the surface and raises productivity, hence good fishing grounds.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Corals: invertebrate animals; reefs are built by hard corals secreting a skeleton (Australia's 'Great Barrier Reef').UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • Most reefs lie in tropical oceans near the equator; more than one-third are in the territories of Australia, Indonesia, Philippines.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • Occupy less than 1% of ocean floor, yet host more than 25% of known marine fish species; 32 of 34 recognized animal phyla on coral reefs versus 9 in tropical rainforests.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    Added concept

    UPSC 2026 asked why mangroves matter for climate resilience. Coaching-consensus answer, not an official key: they withstand tidal surges and offer biomass, acting as natural bio-shields and livelihood bases. Claims of freshwater storage for paddy and of salt-sensitive roots filtering seawater were rejected. Not in the book.UPSC 2026

    Eucalyptus, biomes and economics
    • Eucalyptus: 'Environmental evil' / 'enemy of the environment'. Consumes more ground water than other trees; water level goes down around plantation.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papersUPPSC ×4PCS Pre ’05, ’22; PCS Mains ’11; UDA/LDA Mains ’10
    • Mostly found in Australia; cultivated widely in Europe, Africa, Indian sub-continent. Recommended for poor soils with deficient moisture where little else grows.
    • Human-made biome: crop land.
    • Chhattisgarh: India's first State linking forest ecosystem services (clean air, water conservation, biodiversity) with Green GDP.
    • Green GDP: concept coined in late 1980s; from Net Domestic Product (GDP minus depreciation of produced assets such as machines and buildings), deduct cost of depletion of natural resources and degradation of ecosystems.
    • 'Deep ecology': Arne Naess, Norwegian philosopher, early 1970s.UPPSCPCS Mains ’14
    Acts and Eco-Sensitive Zones (पारिस्थितिक संवेदनशील क्षेत्र)
    ActYear
    Wild Life (Protection) Act1972
    Forest (Conservation) Act1980
    Environment (Protection) Act1986
    Scheduled Tribes and other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act2006
    Source check R.A.S./R.T.S. 2013 (pp. 53–54): keyed "(*)". Book gives the correct years and says none of the option codes is correctly matched.
    Verified update (checked Nov 2026) Book's dated name: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (p. 51). Section 3 of the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 (No. 15 of 2023, assent 4 August 2023) substitutes the short title "Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam". source
    • Eco-sensitive zones are mentioned under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, not the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • COMMON TRAP Purpose is not to prohibit all activity except agriculture: some activities are prohibited, some regulated, some permitted. Vehicles for commercial activities are regulated, not prohibited.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    ClassActivities in the book
    ProhibitedTourism activities like flying over protected areas in aircraft or hot air balloon; discharge of effluents and solid waste in natural water bodies or terrestrial areas
    RegulatedFelling of trees; hotels and resorts; commercial use of natural water; electrical cables; drastic change of agriculture system (heavy technology, pesticides etc.); widening of roads
    PermittedOngoing agriculture and horticulture by local communities; rainwater harvesting; organic farming; green technology; renewable energy sources
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Give the decreasing-productivity order of mangrove, ocean, lake, grassland.

      Mangrove, grasslands, lake, ocean. p. 51

    2. Distinguish pycnocline, halocline and thermocline.

      Density, salt and temperature-with-depth gradients. p. 51

    3. Under which Act are eco-sensitive zones mentioned, and is rainwater harvesting allowed there?

      Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; yes, it is a permitted activity. p. 55

    4. Correct this: "More species can coexist in a niche when resources are insufficient."

      Species are fewer when resources are insufficient; abundance allows more to coexist. p. 53

    5. How many of the 34 recognized animal phyla are found on coral reefs, and in tropical rainforests?

      32 and 9. p. 55

    Biodiversity · जैव विविधता

    Biodiversity (जैव विविधता): Meaning and Levels

    Variety of living organisms in an ecosystem, measured at three spatial scales and organised at three levels.

    • Biodiversity = diverse range of organisms (plants & animals) in an ecosystem; species organised into communities found in a particular ecosystem.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’14; RO/ARO Mains ’14
    • CORE CONCEPT Most significant aspect = maintenance of the ecosystem. Functions at levels of species, communities, ecosystems.UPPSCPCS Pre ’15
    • α, β, γ classification described by Whittaker, 1960.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Species richness = measure of species found in a community.
    Origin of the term
    • "Biological diversity": Raymond F. Dasmann, book A Different Kind of Country, 1968.
    • COMMON TRAP "Biodiversity" (contraction of "biological diversity"): first coined 1985 by Walter G. Rosen, National Research Council, as title word for a seminar on biological diversity.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Mains ’13
    Days, decade and targets
    • International Day for Biological Diversity (IDB) = 22 May (UN); to increase understanding and awareness of biodiversity issues.UPPSCPCS Pre ’18
    • History: late 1993, Second Committee of UNGA first designated 29 December (date CBD entered into force, 29 Dec 1993). December 2000: UNGA adopted 22 May, marking adoption of CBD text on 22 May 1992 by the Nairobi Final Act. Partly because many holidays around 29 Dec made celebrations hard to plan. Book: many countries still celebrate 29 Dec.
    • UN Decade on Biodiversity = 2011–20 (UN General Assembly Resolution 65/161, 22 December 2010). Goal: mainstream biodiversity at different levels; governments encouraged to develop, implement and report national strategies under the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Mains ’12
    • India's Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) target: 2030. LDN balances expected loss of productive land with recovery of degraded areas; a paradigm shift in land management.UPPSCPCS Pre ’19
    • India's first National Centre for Marine Biodiversity (NCMB): Jamnagar, Gujarat; goal: safeguard biodiversity of coastal areas.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’18, ’23
    Source check Q0341 (R.A.S. 2012): options included 29 December but not 22 May; book marks the answer "(*)" (p. 90) and gives 22 May as the current date. Do not treat 29 Dec as the current IDB.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. A student counts bird species along transects in a wood and in a field, then compares the two counts. Which diversity index does each step give?

      Each count = alpha; the comparison = beta. Gamma would need the whole region. p. 56

    2. Separate the contributions of Dasmann and Rosen.

      Dasmann used "biological diversity" (1968). Rosen coined the contraction "biodiversity" (1985). p. 56

    3. Why did the UN move the biodiversity day away from 29 December?

      Holiday clashes made it hard to plan events, so in 2000 UNGA chose 22 May, the date the CBD text was adopted in 1992. p. 90

    4. Fill the three levels of biodiversity and what each describes.

      Genetic (gene variation), species (among different species), community & ecosystem (found in a region). p. 56

    Biodiversity Gradient

    Biodiversity is uneven: it rises towards the equator and towards lower altitudes.

    • Not uniform on Earth; depends on climate, soil, temperature, rainfall, humidity, and on precipitation, altitude, geography and presence of other species.
    • Maximum biodiversity: tropical rain forest (book: 23.5°N–23.5°S, near the equator). Heavy rain + high temperature all year, so also called the optimum biome.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’94 · 5 papersUPPSC ×6PCS Pre ’12, ’16, ’18; PCS Mains ’13, ’14; RO/ARO ’17
    • Biodiversity increases towards the equator; varies greatly across the globe and within regions.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • CORE CONCEPT Latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG): species number increases from poles to Equator; recognised for over a century, reasons long a mystery. New study: higher equatorial diversity may come from higher speciation rates, driven by changes in precipitation across space and time.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’19
    • Left standing by the key: tropics harbour more species than temperate areas; greatest biodiversity in Amazonian rain forest; diversity falls from temperate areas towards poles. False statement was the reverse gradient (rising towards poles).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Normally greater at lower latitudes than higher, and at lower altitudes than higher along mountain gradients (valleys richer than high mountains).UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Book's figures: on Earth, low biodiversity at the poles, high at the equator (p. 58). On a mountain, high at the base, low at the top, with temperature falling 6.5°C per km of height (p. 59).
    • Himalaya rich in species mainly because it is a confluence of different biogeographical zones.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    Source check

    U.P.P.C.S. 2018 (higher species diversity (प्रजातीय विविधता)): book records key "(b & c)". Tropical rain forest on land and coral reefs (प्रवाल भित्तियाँ) in the sea are both among the most diverse systems, and UPPSC accepted both (p. 59).

    1. Correct this: "Species diversity rises from the equator towards the poles."

      Reverse it. Species number rises from the poles to the Equator (LDG). p. 60

    2. Why is the tropical rain forest called the optimum biome?

      Heavy rain and high temperature all year suit growth of flora and fauna. p. 58

    3. Give the most appropriate reason the Himalaya is species-rich.
