    Biodiversity Hotspots (हॉटस्पॉट (तप्त स्थल))

    Regions that are both exceptionally rich in endemics (स्थानिक) and severely threatened. Concept: Norman Myers.

    • Hotspot: biogeographical region, extremely biologically diverse and under severe threat (habitat loss, climate change, extensive species loss). Rich in endemic, rare, threatened species in relatively small areas; protection there might prevent extinction (विलोपन) of more species than in similar-sized areas elsewhere.
    • CORE CONCEPT To qualify (Conservation International): at least 1,500 vascular plant species as endemics and at least 70% of original habitat lost. Criteria behind Western Ghats–Sri Lanka and Indo-Burma recognition: species richness, endemism, threat perception.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Globally 36 hotspots (Conservation International): just 2.5% of land surface, but over 50% of endemic plant species and nearly 43% of bird, mammal, reptile, amphibian species as endemics.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papers
    • February 2016: CEPF declared North American Coastal Plains the 36th hotspot.
    • India: nearly 7.6% of mammals, 12.6% birds, 6.2% reptiles, 4.4% amphibians (book: of those found in 17 mega-diverse countries). Western Ghats = "biodiversity saturated" area among Q's options.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    • Hotspots are not confined to tropics: temperate examples California Floristic Province, Japan.UPSC PYQUPSC ’10
    • Mediterranean Basin (not "Eastern Mediterranean"): Portugal to Jordan, northern Italy to Morocco; second-largest hotspot; many unique reptiles, key for endemic plants. Southwest Australia (not "North-western").UPSC PYQUPSC ’09
    • Sikkim: full-fledged State by 36th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1975. "Botanist's paradise" as it lies under E. Himalaya hotspot. People mainly Lepchas, Bhotias, Nepalis.
    Source check Book prints "1,500 species of vascular plants (70.5% of the world's total)" (p. 64). This is a misprint: 1,500 species cannot be 70.5% of the world's plants. Usually quoted as 0.5%; CEPF's page could not be opened to confirm, so verify before quoting a percentage.
    Common trap

    Not among India's four: Western Himalaya, Eastern Ghats, Vindhyas, Aravalli Hills, Gangetic and Indo-Gangetic plains, Sundarbans, Thar Desert, Central India, Deccan Plateau, Naro Hills. "Andaman and Nicobar" is not one hotspot: the groups fall in two.

    Source check Q0238 (I.A.S. 1996, 'ecological hot spot'): book records key "(b & c)", i.e. Eastern Himalayas and Western Ghats both (p. 64).
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. State the two numerical thresholds for hotspot status.

      At least 1,500 endemic vascular plants; at least 70% of original habitat lost. p. 64

    2. Which Indian island group belongs to which hotspot?

      Andaman: Indo-Burma. Nicobar: Sundaland. p. 63

    3. Correct this: "Hotspots occur only in the tropics."

      False. Temperate hotspots include California Floristic Province and Japan. p. 62

    4. Name the three criteria the book links to the recognition of the Western Ghats–Sri Lanka and Indo-Burma hotspots.

      Species richness, endemism, threat perception. p. 65

    Causes of Biodiversity Loss

    Human influence on ecosystems is the root cause; habitat destruction (पर्यावास विनाश) leads every list.

    • CORE CONCEPT Main cause: destruction of natural habitat. Transforming natural areas loses plant species and the animal species tied to them. Forests, swamps, plains, lakes cleared for agriculture, housing, roads, pipelines.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papers
    • Habitat destruction = degradation or complete elimination of natural environment. Loss of vegetation (deforestation, conversion for agriculture or urban use) removes food, shelter, breeding grounds, leading to decline or extinction.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papersUPPSC ×5PCS Pre ’10, ’15, ’16, ’17, ’23
    • Habitat examples: cutting forests for fields, filling wetlands (आर्द्रभूमि) for houses, dams changing river flow.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papers
    • Influence of humans is the main driver. Threats summarised: alteration and loss of habitats; introduction of exotic species and GMOs; pollution; climate change; overexploitation.
    • Five main threats commonly recognised: invasive alien species (आक्रामक विदेशी प्रजातियाँ), climate change, nutrient loading and pollution, habitat change, overexploitation.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Book's figure of threats (p. 65): habitat loss and degradation; "rehabilitation of exotic species"; climate change and pollution; extinction of species, which may be natural, mass or human-induced.
    • Book's six main threats: human activities and habitat loss; deforestation; desertification; marine pollution; increasing wildlife trade; climate change.
    • Jhum / shifting cultivation (eastern and north-eastern India): extravagant, unscientific land use; devastating, far-reaching degradation.
    • Global warming, habitat fragmentation, alien species invasion = threats. Promotion of vegetarianism is not.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’12 · 2 papers
    • India's birds declining: habitat reduction; pesticides, chemical fertilizers, mosquito repellents. DDT enters food chain, shells crack prematurely, population falls.
    • Uttarakhand loss factors: expansion of roads, urbanization, extension of agriculture. Afforestation of barren land is not a cause.
    • COMMON TRAP Fewer trophic levels indicates abundance of one type of organism, so biodiversity falls. Productivity, intermediate-disturbance and ecosystem age add richness.UPPSCPCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15
    • Genetic assimilation (a wrong option, not a threat cited): a phenotypic character at first produced only in response to an environmental influence is, by selection, taken over by the genotype, so it forms even without that influence.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papers
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Explain why habitat destruction removes animals as well as plants.

      Animals lose the plants that give food, shelter and breeding grounds, so their species decline too. pp. 65, 67

    2. Relate DDT to falling bird numbers in one sentence.

      DDT passes up the food chain and shells crack prematurely, so fewer birds hatch. p. 65

    3. Which of productivity, ecosystem age, intermediate disturbance or fewer trophic levels does not add richness?

      Fewer trophic levels. p. 67

    Conservation of Biodiversity

    In-situ (स्व-स्थाने) keeps species in their natural home; ex-situ (बाह्य-स्थाने) moves them out. Biosphere reserves are the flagship in-situ strategy.

    Types of conservation
    • In-situ: conserving animals and plants in natural habitats. Examples: National Parks, Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves, Reserved Forest, Protected Forest, Nature Reserves. Genetic diversity (आनुवंशिक विविधता) in NPs and sanctuaries is maintained in-situ.UPPSCLower Sub (Spl) ’04
    • Ex-situ ('off site'): conserving outside areas of natural occurrence, moving target species from native habitat. Examples: seed banks (बीज बैंक), botanical gardens (वानस्पतिक उद्यान), zoological parks. COMMON TRAP Botanical garden is not in-situ; biosphere reserve, NP, sanctuary and sacred grove are in-situ.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’11 · 2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’18
    • Two ex-situ methods. (1) Primary facilities holding collections: aquaria, botanical gardens, zoos.
    • (2) Storage of seeds, pollen, tissue, embryos in liquid nitrogen (cryo-bank): virtually indefinite storage without deterioration over a much longer period.
    • In-situ and ex-situ techniques are both adopted for conservation.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    Source check Book's Q0258 explanation (p. 69) says ex-situ means "restricting them to natural habitat". This contradicts the book's own definition on p. 67 (outside the areas where they naturally occur). Use p. 67.
    Biosphere reserves
    • CORE CONCEPT Biosphere reserves = most important strategy for conserving biodiversity together with traditional human life (cultural diversity). Areas of terrestrial and coastal ecosystems reconciling conservation with sustainable use; an integral part of the human system; multifaceted ecosystem development given prominence.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’14 · 2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’13
    • Ecosystem with plants and animals of unusual scientific and natural interest; helps protect genetic variations of organisms and plants.
    • Objectives: (a) conserve landscapes, ecosystems, species, genetic variations; (b) foster socio-culturally and ecologically sustainable economic and human development; (c) support research, monitoring, education, information exchange on local, national, global issues.
    • India: 18 Biosphere Reserves, protecting larger areas of natural habitat. 12 of 18 in the World Network (UNESCO MAB Programme list): Nilgiri, Gulf of Mannar, Sundarbans, Nanda Devi, Nokrek, Pachmarhi, Simlipal, Great Nicobar, Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Agasthyamala, Khangchendzonga, Panna.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’14 · 2 papers
    • Gulf of Mannar BR: world's richest region from a marine biodiversity perspective; 21 islands with estuaries, beaches, nearshore forests, marine component with algal communities, sea grasses, coral reefs, salt marshes, mangroves. → Ch 7REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    Source check The 18 and 12 are the book's undated counts (pp. 68, 69). A November 2026 search suggested a later UNESCO addition, but no page could be opened to confirm it. Check the current World Network list before quoting.
    Coral reefs
    • Four major regions: Lakshadweep, Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Sundarbans is known for mangrove forest, not reefs.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Book's two dated areas: about 5,790 km² (2008); about 2,384 km² (2019). Keep each with its year. Reefs deteriorating worldwide, India no exception.
    • Fringing reefs common: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Andaman & Nicobar. Atoll reefs: Lakshadweep.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Coral bleaching (प्रवाल विरंजन): warmer water makes corals expel the algae (zooxanthellae) in their tissues, so coral turns completely white. Most effective factor: rise in sea-water temperature / global warming.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×3PCS Pre ’12, ’24; PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15
    • Book's p. 68 list of bleaching causes: increase in temperature and acidity of sea, global warming, atmospheric pressure.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Sort as in-situ or ex-situ: sacred grove, botanical garden, cryo-bank, national park.

      In-situ: sacred grove, national park. Ex-situ: botanical garden, cryo-bank. pp. 67–69

    2. Why are biosphere reserves preferred when traditional human life must also continue?

      They reconcile conservation with sustainable use and treat people as an integral part of the system. pp. 68–69

    3. Explain coral bleaching in one sentence.

      Overheated corals expel zooxanthellae and turn white. p. 70

    4. Which reef type is characteristic of Lakshadweep?

      Atoll reefs. p. 68

    Uses of Biodiversity

    Biodiversity underpins human existence directly and through ecosystem services.

    • Basis for human existence: soil formation, prevention of soil erosion, recycling of waste, pollination of crops. Also listed for medicinal purposes.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. List four ways biodiversity underpins human existence as stated in the book.

      Soil formation, prevention of soil erosion, recycling of waste, pollination of crops. p. 71

    2. Name the drugs and plant product listed under pharmaceuticals in the figure.

      Quinine, Taxol, Botanochemical, Morphine. p. 70

    3. Under which branch does "climate control by forests and seas" fall?

      Ecosystem services. p. 70

    IUCN

    A membership union, not a UN organ, whose Red List tracks extinction risk.

    • COMMON TRAP IUCN (created 1948) is a membership union of public, private and non-governmental organisations; not part of the UN. Runs a large portfolio of conservation field projects worldwide.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Works for nature conservation and sustainable use of natural resources. The only international observer in UNGA with expertise on environment, specifically biodiversity, nature conservation and sustainable resource use.
    • CITES: legally binding on States that join it, but does not take the place of national laws (statement left correct by key).UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Red Data Books (रेड डाटा बुक) (IUCN) list threatened plant and animal species. Endangered (संकटग्रस्त) species are listed there. They are not lists of endemics of hotspots or of protected sites.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’11 · 5 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’13; PCS Mains ’02
    • IUCN Red List: established 1964; world's most comprehensive source on global extinction risk status of animal, fungus and plant species.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papers
    • Called the Barometer of Life: as a barometer measures atmospheric pressure, the List measures pressure on species, guiding action to prevent extinctions.
    • Benefits of the Red List (figure, p. 71): raises awareness of endangered species; identifies and records them; gives in-situ direction to conservation work; forms a written list of loss of biodiversity.
    • Great Indian Bustard: highly endangered among Q's options.UPPSCPCS Mains ’05
    • Book's IUCN definition: species not seen during last 50 years is considered extinct (विलुप्त).UPPSCPCS Pre ’05
    Source check The 50-year test (p. 73) is the book's answer. IUCN's own page was blocked, so it could not be checked; current Red List wording is generally described as "no reasonable doubt that the last individual has died", without a fixed period. Treat 50 years as the exam key only.
    Source check Q0276 (I.A.S. 2012): key (a) groups Great Indian Bustard, Musk Deer, Red Panda and Asiatic Wild Ass as Endangered "at the time of the question" (p. 72). The book's 2015 statuses differ (table above). Keep the two apart.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Correct this: "IUCN is an organ of the United Nations."

      False. It is a membership union, not part of the UN. p. 71

    2. Why is the Red List called the Barometer of Life?

      It measures pressure on species as a barometer measures atmospheric pressure. p. 72

    3. State the book's status for Musk Deer and Wild Ass on the June 2015 list.

      Musk Deer: Vulnerable. Wild Ass: Near Threatened. p. 71

    Biodiversity and Endangered Species

    Case studies and range facts: know each species' place and threat.

    Vultures (गिद्ध) and diclofenac
    • Cause of vulture decline: Diclofenac Sodium given to diseased cattle. May 2003: Peregrine Fund scientist's paper. January 2004: joint study with Ornithological Society of Pakistan confirmed it as primary reason.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’12 · 5 papersUPPSC ×3PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Pre ’18; PCS Mains (Spl) ’08
    Species case notes
    • Dodo: giant bird, short stumpy legs, large hooked beak, on Mauritius; vanished by end of 17th century. Helped propagate seed of Tambalacoque (Dodo plant); seed eaten, dispersed via faecal matter. Without Dodo the tree failed to reproduce.UPSC PYQUPSC ’98
    • Indian flying fox (Pteropus giganteus) = bat, greater Indian fruit bat, family Pteropodidae. Bangladesh, China, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka.UPSC PYQUPSC ’09
    • Dugong ('Sea Cow'): herbivorous marine mammal, vulnerable (सुभेद्य); feeds on seagrass in sheltered waters, lagoons, bays. Eastern Africa, South & Southeast Asia, Australia. Schedule I, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. India: Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay/Strait; also Saurashtra coast of Gulf of Kachchh, Andaman & Nicobar. Not along the entire coast.UPSC PYQUPSC ’09, ’15
    • Indian wild ass: Rann of Kachchh (sandy, saline). No predators there; threatened by habitat destruction.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Prosopis juliflora: exotic plant; wipes out most native plants and animals around it; reduces biodiversity where it grows.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • Lion-tailed macaque: endangered; Western Ghats, mostly Kerala, Karnataka, border region of Tamil Nadu. Not Andhra Pradesh.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • COMMON TRAP Cheetah declared extinct in India 1952, so not "naturally found" at question time (2012). Book adds: Supreme Court earlier withheld the rehabilitation plan; government later introduced it in Madhya Pradesh from Namibia.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Snow leopard: habitat 3000–4500 m; surveys in Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh confirm presence. Black-necked crane: book gives as State bird of J&K.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Flying squirrel: India, Russia, Japan, China, Europe, Africa, North America. South Asia high diversity: about 17 species, 7 genera. In India most in eastern Himalaya and north-east, at Himalayan and Indo-Malayan confluence. Arunachal Pradesh study: 14 species; red giant most common, then particoloured (Hylopetes alboniger).UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Ceylon frogmouth (Batrachostomus moniliger), Coppersmith barbet (Megalaima haemacephala), Grey-chinned minivet (Pericrocotus solaris), White-throated redstart (Phoenicurus schisticeps): all birds.UPSC PYQUPSC ’20
    • Andaman & Nicobar: saltwater crocodile, whales, dolphins, dugong, marine turtles, sea snake, fish, prawns, lobsters, corals, seashells including rare, endangered Trochus. Key: shrew and tapir are not of Western Ghats' Malabar region (book places them in Himalayan ranges).UPSC PYQUPSC ’08
    • Red Panda (Ailurus fulgens): territorial; temperate deciduous and coniferous forests with bamboo understory and hollow trees; key species, indicator of forest health. Himalaya: Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar; India: Sikkim, West Bengal, Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh. Most world population in China; most Indian ones in Arunachal Pradesh. Not western Himalaya only.UPSC PYQUPSC ’07
    • Slow Loris: dense forests of NE India (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura); also Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Myanmar (incl. Mergui Archipelago), Thailand, Vietnam except south.UPSC PYQUPSC ’07
    • Mahseer, dolphin, cat: Blue-finned Mahseer: Cauvery River. Irrawaddy Dolphin: sea coasts, estuaries, rivers of Bay of Bengal and SE Asia, and Chilika Lake; not Chambal (Gangetic Dolphin there). Rusty-spotted Cat: Eastern Ghats.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • Indri (Indri indri, babakoto): among largest living lemurs, endemic to Madagascar (NE coast rainforests), diurnal, CR. Elk (Cervus canadensis, wapiti): second largest of deer family Cervidae; North America, Central and East Asia; not Indonesia. Bonobo (Pan paniscus, pygmy chimpanzee): endangered great ape, Congo Basin (Democratic Republic of the Congo). None was correctly matched to Brazil/Indonesia/Madagascar in the Q.UPSC PYQUPSC ’24
    Added concept Recent papers, not in the book. Coaching keys are not official.
    • Peacock (Gooty) tarantula, Prelims 2025, reported official key II and III: natural habitat in India limited to some forest areas; arboreal in its natural habitat. "Omnivorous crustacean" was not accepted.UPSC 2025
    • Western Hoolock Gibbon, Prelims 2026, asked: Endangered listing and a North-east Indian sanctuary home; brachiation; whether heavily built like gorillas. Coaching-consensus key 1 and 2, no official key. Book lists Hoolock Gibbon as Endangered (ENVIS, p. 74).UPSC 2026

      Treated cattle die → vultures eat carcasses → kidney poisoning → population crash → DCGI bans veterinary use. pp. 73–75

    Ramsar Convention

    Convention on Wetlands, signed 2 February 1971 at Ramsar, Iran. Wise use, not exclusion.

    • Associated with conservation and sustainable use of wetlands; also called the Convention on Wetlands.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • World Wetlands Day = 2 February: date of adoption in 1971 at Ramsar, on the shores of the Caspian Sea. Raises awareness of the vital role of wetlands for people and planet. Themes: 2020 'Wetlands and Biodiversity'; 2023 'Wetlands Restoration'; 2024 'Wetlands and Human Wellbeing'; 2025 'Protecting Wetlands for Our Common Future' (need for immediate action, for all people and future generations).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’23; PCS Mains ’08
    • Ramsar Site (रामसर स्थल) = wetland designated of international importance, protected under strict Ramsar guidelines.
    • CORE CONCEPT India, a party, must conserve Ramsar sites through an ecosystem approach and allow their simultaneous sustainable use.UPSC PYQUPSC ’10
    • Montreux Record: register of Ramsar-listed sites where changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring or are likely to occur from technological developments, pollution or other human interference. Maintained as part of the Ramsar list.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • India: 89 sites as of January 2025 (book). Four then added: Sakkarakottai and Therthangal Bird Sanctuaries (Tamil Nadu), Khachoedpalri Wetland (Sikkim), Udhwa Lake (Jharkhand).

    Karnataka: Aghanashini Estuary / Ankasamudra Bird CR / Magadi Kere CR4801 / 98 / 5431 Jan 2024
    • Bihar's first Ramsar site: Kabartal Wetland (Kanwar Lake), Begusarai; 26.20 sq km; declared 21 July 2020.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’22
    • Largest inland saline wetland of India: Sambhar Lake, Rajasthan.UPSC PYQUPSC ’09
    • Point Calimere WL & BS (Tamil Nadu), site no. 1210, 19 August 2002: along Palk Strait, covering Nagapattinam, Tiruvarur, Thanjavur; 38,500 ha. Only one among Q's options in a State (Hokera, Wular: J&K; Tso Moriri: Ladakh, both UTs).
    • Parvati Arga BS (Gonda district, UP; Tarabganj Tehsil, about 40 km from Gonda on Mankapur-Nawabganj Road): permanent freshwater, two oxbow lakes; over 100,000 birds in annual counts; refuge for white-rumped vulture (Gyps bengalensis) and Indian vulture (Gyps indicus), both CR, and Egyptian vulture (Neophron percnopterus), EN.
    Source check Q0309 (U.P.P.C.S. Mains 2015): book records key "(c & d)" since Sundarbans (West Bengal) and Bhoj Wetland (Madhya Pradesh) are both Ramsar sites (p. 80).
    Wetland functions and Indian rules
    • Wetlands hold water like a sponge, prevent flooding, keep river levels normal, filter and purify surface water; take water in floods, release slowly at low levels; release vegetative matter that feeds fish; rejuvenate rivers and surrounding ecosystems. Useful for nutrient recovery and cycling, heavy-metal uptake by plants, reducing river siltation by retaining sediments.
    • CORE CONCEPT Wetlands = Earth's kidneys: aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess nutrients. Plants like verticillata and water hyacinth remove heavy metals from waste water.UPSC PYQUPSC ’22
    • Ecosystem services: water storage, purification, flood mitigation, storm buffers, erosion control, aquifer recharge, microclimate regulation, aesthetic value, recreational, social, cultural activities. Vital parts of hydrological cycle; highly productive.UPSC PYQUPSC ’22
    • Hydrophytes thrive with fluctuating water thanks to aerenchyma: air channels in leaves, stems, roots give buoyancy and a low-resistance pathway for oxygen, carbon dioxide, ethylene between aerial and submerged tissues.
    • Q0315, I.A.S. 2012: key (a) "at the time when question was asked": Gujarat has largest wetland share. Now: inland 69.23%, coastal 27.13%, small wetlands (<2.25 ha) 3.64%. Gujarat 17.6%, West Bengal second. Coastal does not exceed inland.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Not mandatory under Ramsar for GoI to protect all wetlands in India. Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2010: framed on recommendation of an Expert Panel under National Environment Policy 2006, not on Ramsar recommendations; cover drainage area or catchment as determined by the authority.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • Wetlands (C&M) Rules, 2017 moved management focus from central authority to State bodies.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Give date and place of the Convention on Wetlands.

      2 February 1971, Ramsar, Iran. p. 78

    2. Relate the Montreux Record to the Ramsar List.

      It is part of the Ramsar list, registering sites whose ecological character has changed or is likely to, through human interference. p. 79

    3. Why are wetlands called the Earth's kidneys?

      Aquatic plants absorb heavy metals and excess nutrients. p. 81

    4. Correct this: "The 2010 Wetlands Rules were framed on Ramsar recommendations."

      False. They followed an Expert Panel under National Environment Policy 2006. p. 82

    5. Which tissue lets hydrophytes survive fluctuating water levels?

      Aerenchyma (air channels). p. 81

    Various Acts and Agreements

    India's biodiversity law flows from the CBD; other treaties and NGOs act alongside it.

    Biological Diversity Act (जैव विविधता अधिनियम) and NBA
    • Biological Diversity Act, 2002: passed by Parliament December 2002; President's assent February 2003. Preservation of biological diversity; equitable sharing of benefits from traditional biological resources and knowledge.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCUDA/LDA Mains ’10
    • Covers conservation, use of biological resources and associated knowledge; framework for access and benefit sharing; includes transfer of research results and application for Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) relating to Indian biological resources.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • NBA: established 2003, HQ Chennai; statutory autonomous body under MoEFCC. Checks biopiracy, protects indigenous and traditional genetic resources; IPR application on genetic/biological resources needs its approval.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • COMMON TRAP GM crop research is monitored by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC), under MoEFCC, not NBA.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • BMCs (Biodiversity Management Committees): constituted in local bodies under the Act and State rules. Key to realising the Nagoya Protocol (2010), under which benefits from genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge reach indigenous and local communities on mutually agreed terms. May levy collection fees for commercial access within jurisdiction.UPSC PYQUPSC ’23
    • The Act gives effect to India's commitments under CBD (1992); three goals: conservation of biological diversity; sustainable use of its components; fair and equitable sharing of benefits.UPSC PYQUPSC ’23
    • CEBPOL (Centre for Biodiversity Policy and Law): India with Norwegian Government, at NBA Chennai; builds professional expertise and capacity in biodiversity policies and laws.UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’17
    Treaties and NGOs
    • Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (to CBD): safe handling, transport, use of living modified organisms (LMO) from modern biotechnology; covers biodiversity and risks to human health. Adopted 29 January 2000; in force 11 September 2003.UPSC PYQUPSC ’05, ’09
    • India signed 23 January 2001 (ratified 2003); implemented by Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. MOP 1 (First Meeting of the Parties): 23–27 February 2004, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. USA is not a member.UPSC PYQUPSC ’05, ’09
    • IT PGRFA ('International Seed Treaty'): in harmony with CBD; food security through conservation, exchange, sustainable use of plant genetic resources. UN Convention to Combat Desertification and World Heritage Convention also bear on biodiversity.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • BirdLife International: world's largest global partnership of non-governmental conservation organisations; conserves birds, habitats, global biodiversity. Book: over 115 national partners; Friends of BirdLife raises funds for a partnership of 119 organisations in more than 100 countries. Identifies Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas: over 13,000 so far.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • COMMON TRAP Hotspot concept: British environmentalist Norman Myers, not BirdLife.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • TRAFFIC (Trade Records Analysis of Fauna and Flora in Commerce): NGO, established 1976, strategic alliance of WWF and IUCN; not a UNEP bureau. Mission: trade in wild plants and animals should not threaten nature conservation.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Ecuador's referendum rejected oil drilling in Yasuni National Park (Amazon); UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1989.

      GEAC. NBA handles access, benefit sharing and IPR approval. p. 84

    2. State the three objectives of the CBD.

      Conservation; sustainable use of components; fair and equitable benefit sharing. p. 83

    3. Who originated the hotspot concept?

      Norman Myers. p. 84

    4. Correct this: "TRAFFIC is a UNEP bureau."

    Biodiversity: United Nations and Other International Organizations

    CBD COPs by venue, with UN-REDD, TEEB and Wetlands International.

    • UN-REDD (2008): FAO, UNDP, UNEP; book also says under the aegis of UNFCCC member countries. Mitigates climate change by reducing net GHG emissions through enhanced forest management in developing countries. REDD+ focuses on conservation and sustainable management of forests.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Well-designed REDD+ can significantly help protect biodiversity, maintain resilience of forest ecosystems, and reduce poverty via technical and financial support.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity): "making nature's values visible". Mainstreams biodiversity and ecosystem service values into decision-making at all levels; helps decision makers recognize, demonstrate, capture value. Launched by Germany and EU, March 2007; led by Pavan Sukhdev 2007–2011.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Wetlands International: independent, not-for-profit global organisation, Government and NGO membership; not intergovernmental. Head office Netherlands. Leading scientific expert on peatlands and climate change, and on wetlands and waterbird migration.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Sustains and restores wetlands for people and biodiversity. Work: research, community-based field projects, advocacy with governments, corporates, international policy fora, conventions. Partnerships, specialist expert network, tens of thousands of volunteers.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    Added concept Recent papers, not in the book.
    • Nature Restoration Law, to tackle climate change and biodiversity loss: enacted by the European Union (Prelims 2025, reported official key).UPSC 2025
    • Mains 2026 GS-III asked: aim and goals of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework; India's commitments and initiatives, with examples. No key exists. The book gives only COP 15's dates and venues.UPSC 2026

    1. Sequence these CBD COP venues: Cali, Hyderabad, Nagoya, Cancun.

      Nagoya (10), Hyderabad (11), Cancun (13), Cali (16). pp. 85–86

    2. Which three UN bodies run UN-REDD?

      FAO, UNDP, UNEP. p. 86

    3. Correct this: "Wetlands International is formed by Ramsar signatory countries."

    Biodiversity: Miscellaneous

    Standalone facts the book collects at the end of the chapter.

    • Sea buckthorn: medicinal plant of Himalayan region; fruits grow in cold deserts of Ladakh, Lahaul-Spiti (HP), Uttarakhand, parts of Arunachal Pradesh. Bushy, dense branches check soil erosion, stabilise soil, help nitrogen fixation in cold desert areas; fruit gives nutritious juice. Well adapted to cold high altitude. Q stem: berries rich in vitamins and nutrients; Genghis Khan's troops; Russian cosmonauts' oil against radiation. Key rejects biodiesel and valuable timber.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12UPPSCPCS Mains ’04
    • Tallest known tree: Redwood (Sequoia), California (U.S.A.), up to 381 feet (116.1 m).
    • Niche: an organism's role in a community: physical and environmental conditions needed and interactions (predation, competition). Narrow niche = specialist (koalas, only eucalyptus leaves, Australia). Broad = generalist (coyotes, raccoons). Broad niche does not cause extinction; narrow niche, large body size, lack of genetic variability do, per key.UPPSCPCS Pre ’14
    • Hibernation (winter sleep): dormant inactivity to conserve energy in unfavourable weather; in cold- and warm-blooded animals. Squirrels, bears, some bats; metabolism slows, temperature plunges, breathing slows. Fat stored by eating in summer and autumn. Rodents: squirrels, muskrats, mice.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Bhitarkanika (protected area): Brahmani and Vaitarni merge before the sea. Brahmani known as South Koel in Jharkhand; formed by confluence of South Koel and Sankh near Rourkela. Vaitarni rises in Guptaganga hills, Keonjhar, Odisha.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Butterflies: climate regulates most insect life cycles; temperature drives flight, foraging, movement. They cannot tolerate low temperatures, so most species are tropical.
    • Psychrophiles (cold loving): grow best at 0–15°C; usually do not survive above 20°C; permanently cold habitats such as deep ocean waters. Extreme psychrophiles reported from Lake Whillans.
    • Limnetic zone: open, well-lit water of a freestanding freshwater body; primary habitat of plankton; highest phytoplankton density, so most photosynthetically active and main oxygen producer. Littoral zone is the shallow near-shore area, excluded. → Ch 2UPPSCPCS Pre ’22
    • Tomorrow's Biodiversity: Vandana Shiva.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Mains ’04, ’05
    • Biomass: all organic materials arising from plants (incl. algae, trees, crops); produced through photosynthesis; includes land and water vegetation and all organic wastes.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Place the biomes in descending annual biomass order: taiga, deep sea, prairie, deciduous forest.

      Deciduous forest, taiga, prairie, deep sea. p. 88

    2. Distinguish a specialist from a generalist with one example each.

      Specialist: narrow niche (koala). Generalist: broad niche (coyote, raccoon). p. 89

    3. Why is sea buckthorn valued in cold deserts?

      Dense bushy growth checks soil erosion, and its fruit is nutritious. p. 88

    4. Which two rivers merge at Bhitarkanika?

      Brahmani and Vaitarni. p. 88

    Greenhouse Effect and Climate Change · हरितगृह प्रभाव एवं जलवायु परिवर्तन

    Green House Effect

    Short-wave sunlight enters; Earth re-emits long-wave heat; greenhouse gases (हरितगृह गैसें) trap part of it and warm the surface and lower atmosphere.

    Mechanism
    • Solar energy reaches Earth as electromagnetic waves; very hot Sun → high-energy short wavelengths that penetrate the atmosphere.
    • Solar radiation = Ultraviolet (UV) + visible + infrared (अवरक्त). Harmful UV absorbed by ozone layer; visible and infrared reach Earth as thermal radiation.
    • Thermal radiation heats Earth by conduction, convection and radiation.
    • Heated Earth re-emits energy as long-wave radiation, because Earth is cooler than Sun.
    • GHGs absorb much of this long-wave energy, then re-emit it in all directions → warm surface and lower atmosphere. Short-wave passes in; long-wave cannot pass out freely.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papers
    • Like the glass of a greenhouse, which does not release warm air inside (hence "greenhouse effect (हरितगृह प्रभाव)").
    • CORE CONCEPT Greenhouse effect = natural phenomenon raising a planet's temperature. Global warming (वैश्विक तापन) = rise in average atmospheric temperature due to increase in GHGs.UPPSCPCS Pre ’18
    • Without greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature ≈ –18 °C.UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    • UPSC 2025 (reported official key: all three correct): without the atmosphere, temperature would be well below freezing everywhere on Earth's surface; heat absorbed and trapped by the atmosphere maintains average temperature; gases like CO₂ are particularly good at absorbing and trapping radiation.UPSC 2025
    • Concept given by Joseph Fourier (1820s).
    • IAS 2012 key: rising CO₂ warms the atmosphere because it absorbs the infrared part of radiation. Book: CO₂ molecules absorb and re-emit infrared; excess from human activity (mostly burning fossil fuels (जीवाश्म ईंधन)) is warming climate at a problematic rate.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    Source check Q explanation (p.95) says CO₂ absorbs "about 90%" of infrared "received from Sun"; the book's own mechanism (p.91) has GHGs absorbing long-wave energy emitted from Earth's surface. Learn the p.91 mechanism; treat the 90% figure as unverified.
    Greenhouse gases and their shares
    • Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (जलवायु परिवर्तन) (IPCC) meaning: a gas that absorbs and emits radiation within the thermal infrared range.
    • Present in Earth's atmosphere: CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), water vapour (जलवाष्प); ozone also listed. Main set: Carbon dioxide (कार्बन डाइऑक्साइड), Methane (मीथेन), Nitrous Oxide (नाइट्रस ऑक्साइड), Water vapour. Fluorinated gases are synthetic.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papers
    • Found naturally and most important: CO₂, methane, ozone, water vapour (Nitrogen oxide is not a naturally found GHG per UPPCS 2020 key — do not confuse with nitrous oxide).
    • Water vapour = most abundant GHG; NASA: responsible for about half of Earth's greenhouse effect.
    • Water-vapour feedback: warmer → more evaporation → more vapour → more heat trapped → warmer (positive feedback loop). Its concentration is linked to temperature; natural part of water cycle.
    • CO₂ = main GHG behind global warming (66% share in table) as its concentration is more than other GHGs.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papersUPPSC ×7PCS Pre ’06, ’13, ’15; PCS Mains ’04; PCS Mains (Spl) ’04, ’08; Lower Sub Mains ’13
    • Carbon dioxide + Methane = the pair chosen as main contributors. CF₄ and N₂O are relatively less responsible.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    • IPCC basket: directly related – CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, CFCs, SF₆, NF₃. Indirectly related – NOₓ, CO, NMVOC, SO₂. SO₂ also responsible for acid rain.
    Common trap Water vapour = largest share of the natural greenhouse effect (Q on "naturally occurring", p.93). CO₂ = main driver of global warming in the WMO table of long-lived gases. Read which one the stem asks.
    • Use the table above for share questions: UKPSC 2024 incorrect pair = CO₂ 40%. CGPSC 2020 order = CO₂ > CH₄ > CFCs > N₂O.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    Source check Book prints "NF6" among direct gases (p.91) but "NF3" on p.95. Use NF₃. Book says IPCC named 6 major gases; the list covers CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, CFCs, SF₆ and this fluoride.
    Gases that are not greenhouse gases
    • Argon (Ar): not a GHG, not responsible for global warming.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’22; PCS Mains ’16
    • Nitrogen: not a GHG.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    • Oxygen: not a GHG.
    • Hydrogen (H₂): not a GHG; diatomic gas; main component of outer layer of atmosphere.UPPSCPCS Mains ’12
    • Propane: UPPCS 2017 key = not a GHG. Substituting Propane for gasoline and fuel oil is an economical, viable step to cleaner air; cuts CO₂ and air pollutants (CO, nitrogen oxide).
    • Oxides of Sulphur and Nitrogen do not contribute to global warming directly.UPPSCPCS Pre ’13
    • NO₂ and O₂ are both named by the book as the non-GHG answer in a question it marks (*).
    Source check SO₂ (Q0370, CGPSC 2016, p.95): Chhattisgarh Public Service Commission's key was (e) "None of these" in this paper but (c) SO₂ in the earlier answer sheet. Book says SO₂ is not a GHG, and suggests (e) rests on direct vs indirect gases. Keep as disputed.
    Source check Q0404 (UPPCS 2016, p.103) is marked (*): book says both NO₂ and O₂ are the answer "(C & d)". Primary list there = CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, ozone.
    Source check Q0371 (UPPCS 2017, p.95) is marked (*): book rejects (a) rise in CO₂ as a result of the effect (no evidence found), rejects biological population as not atmospheric, and says both (b) humidity and (d) wind speed are correct. Its reasoning: more heat → more evaporation → more humidity; more temperature → more pressure → more air mobility (book's wording). Not resolved; do not treat a single option as settled.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Who first gave the concept of the greenhouse effect, and when?

      Joseph Fourier, 1820s. p. 91

    2. Why does the Earth re-emit energy as long-wave rather than short-wave radiation?

      Earth is much cooler than the Sun, so it radiates at long wavelengths, which GHGs can absorb. p. 91

    3. Name the four gases listed as indirectly related to the greenhouse effect.

      NOₓ, CO, NMVOC and SO₂. p. 95

    4. Correct this statement: "CO₂ is the most abundant greenhouse gas in the atmosphere."

      Water vapour is the most abundant. CO₂ is the main contributor to global warming in the WMO share table. pp. 91–93

    Cause of Greenhouse Effect

    Human activity adds CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O faster than sinks remove them, upsetting the balance of atmosphere, ocean and biosphere.

    Carbon dioxide
    • CO₂ is both useful and harmful: needed for photosynthesis (all life depends on it), but excess drives global warming. Plants take CO₂, release Oxygen.
    • CO₂ released by anthropogenic activities is absorbed by soil on land and by marine plants. A lot does not stay in the lower atmosphere because of photosynthesis by phytoplankton in oceans and plants on land (IAS 2011 key: only this reason; not escape to stratosphere or air trapped in polar ice caps).UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • World Meteorological Organization (WMO) GHG Bulletin 2024: global average CO₂ in 2023 = 420.0±0.1 ppm (Parts Per Million).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papers
    • Annual rise: 2.3 ppm (2022→2023), slightly above 2.2 ppm (2021→2022), slightly below past-decade average 2.4 ppm per year.
    • Pre-industrial level ≈ 278 ppm (278.3 ppm, p.98) ≈ 0.03%: a balance of fluxes among atmosphere, oceans and land biosphere. Now disturbed by combustion of fossil fuels, industries etc.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papers
    • UPPCS 2017 key: optimum CO₂ for natural balance = 0.03 percent by volume.UPPSCPCS Pre ’17
    • Book's graph (p.96; axis 300–440 ppm): CO₂ climbs every year 1959→2023, from a little above 310 ppm to about 420 ppm, steeper in later decades (read off the curve).
    • Carbon fertilization = more atmospheric CO₂ raises the rate of photosynthesis and plant growth. Varies with plant species, temperature, availability of water and nutrients. A quarter to half of Earth's vegetated lands showed significant greening over 35 years (1982–2015), largely due to rising CO₂.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    Verified update (checked Nov 2026) Book's figure: 420.0±0.1 ppm for 2023 (Bulletin 2024). WMO Bulletin No. 22 (published 27 Oct 2026): CO₂ reached 426.8±0.2 ppm in 2025. WMO
    Source check Book says CO₂ "is confined to troposphere only" (p.98). This absolute wording was not verified here, and p.99 only rejects stratospheric escape as the reason CO₂ leaves the lower atmosphere. Do not reproduce it as a rule.
    Methane and nitrous oxide
    • CH₄ = Marsh Gas. Sources: biogas, organic/bacterial decomposition and remnants, cud-chewing animals. It is both a GHG and an air pollutant.
    • Man-made: paddy (धान) (rice) fields, coal mines, reared cattle/domestic animals. Natural: wetlands, oceans, hydrates.UPSC PYQUPSC ’08
    • Wetlands emit the highest proportion: about 75–76% of methane from natural sources.UPSC PYQUPSC ’08
    • Natural detail: Wetlands are the largest source (bacteria decompose organic matter without oxygen); smaller – termites, oceans, sediments, volcanoes, wildfires.
    • Human detail: Agriculture – livestock such as cattle, paddy, manure stored in lagoons; globally the primary source. Industry – Methane is the primary component of natural gas. Waste – decomposition in landfills.
    • Paddy: anaerobic conditions emit methane.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’10 · 2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’19; PCS Mains ’17
    • Nitrogen-based fertilisers → N₂O emitted from cultivated soil.UPSC PYQUPSC ’10
    • Rice = most important anthropogenic crop source of both methane and nitrous oxide (IAS 2022).UPSC PYQUPSC ’22
    • Methane hydrate: crystalline solid, methane molecule surrounded by water molecules; usually exists as "ice". Large deposits in Arctic Tundra and under the seafloor. Global warming might trigger release.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • Atmospheric methane is relatively short-lived: oxidises to CO₂ after a decade or two.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    Primary drivers of climate change
    • Two groups: factors raising carbon emission (excess burning of fossil fuels, exploding numbers of oil-driven automobiles using petrol and diesel) and factors cutting carbon absorption (excessive deforestation).
    • COMMON TRAP Solar flares: NASA and other studies do not treat them as a major cause.
    • Burning crop/biomass residue (cheapest, easiest disposal, for land clearing and pest control) releases CO, SO₂, CH₄ and O₃ (IAS 2019 key; O₃ is strictly a secondary pollutant formed from precursors in the smoke).UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • Halocarbons, refrigerants, foam-blowing agents, CFCs, HCFCs, halons deplete the ozone layer; these are also constituents of GHGs. → Ch 5REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Key for "cause of climate change" (UPPCS, Jharkhand 2013) = all three: greenhouse gases, depletion of ozone layer, pollution. Anthropogenic environmental pollution may lead to climate change.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’13
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • UPSC 2025 (reported official key (b)): premise that cement accounts for more than 5% of global carbon emissions; silica-bearing clay is mixed with limestone, and limestone turns into lime in clinker production. Both are correct but only one explains the CO₂: conversion of limestone to lime (calcination releases CO₂).UPSC 2025
    Source check Causal wording conflicts: p.96 note says GHGs are directly responsible for climate change and some GHGs for ozone depletion; Q explanation (p.96) says GHGs and pollution are directly responsible for ozone depletion, with ozone depletion only indirectly responsible for climate change. Learn the p.96 note; the key is unaffected.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Define carbon fertilization and give two conditions on which it depends.

      Higher CO₂ raises photosynthesis. It varies with plant species, temperature, water and nutrients. p. 97

    2. Distinguish human and natural methane sources, naming the largest natural source.

      Human: paddy, coal mines, cattle, landfills. Natural: wetlands (largest, about 75–76% of natural), oceans, hydrates, termites. pp. 96, 98

    3. Explain in one sentence why rice cultivation is linked to both CH₄ and N₂O.

      Anaerobic conditions in rice cultivation emit methane, while nitrogen-based fertiliser releases nitrous oxide from soil. p. 99

    4. Correct this: "Solar flares are a primary cause of present climate change."

      NASA and other studies do not treat solar flares as a major cause. pp. 96–97

    Effects of Greenhouse Gases

    Warming melts ice, raises seas, shifts species and weather. IPCC thresholds at 2 °C and 3 °C are the most tested part.

    IPCC temperature thresholds
    • Scientific view: rise should not exceed 2 °C above pre-industrial level. IAS 2014 key rejects "all global wetlands permanently disappear" and "cereal cultivation impossible everywhere".UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    Sea level (समुद्र तल) and temperature estimates
    • Melting polar ice caps → rise in sea level, submerging coastal regions; book: many European countries have lost coastal regions.
    • IPCC estimate (book's dated figures): 1.4–5.8 °C rise and 0.33–0.45 m sea-level rise during 1990–2100; 142 out of 144 polar ice caps may melt. "One metre by 2070" statement was rejected.
    • Sea level up approx 390 feet since last ice age; now rising about 3 mm per year.
    • Temperature: book says about 1 °C in the past century (1.8 °F since 1900), over half of it since the mid-1970s. UPPCS 2012 key = 0.9 °C.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Evidence: reduced Arctic sea ice extent, increased ocean heat content, poleward shifts of temperature-sensitive fish, mammals, insects.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    Source check Book: Fiji's sea level rises 0.15 m (about 6 inches) per year, Fiji "likely submerged by 2044" (pp.100, 102), beside a global 3 mm per year on the same page: 50 times the global rate, so the figure looks garbled. Q0402 key (c) also accepts "all coral islands will be submerged", which the explanation does not support. Keep these as UKPSC 2002 key only, and the IPCC range as dated (1990–2100). No external source was opened for this.
    Observed and expected impacts
    • Impacts: rise in sea level, melting of glaciers (हिमनद), spread of diseases, bleaching of coral reefs, changes in weather conditions, rise in global temperature. Main gases named: water vapour, CO₂, CH₄, CFC.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’09 · 2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    • Species may go out of sync, e.g. plants bloom before pollinating insects are active (key accepted early flowering of mango).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    • Health risks: (i) direct-acting effects; (ii) effects via climate-related changes in ecological systems (crop fields, mosquito ecology, marine productivity).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papers
    • Arctic and Greenland Ice sheet = most fragile ecosystem, first affected; melt there affects the entire Earth.
    • Storms: ocean surface absorbs heat and releases it to atmosphere (creating wind and rain clouds); as surface temperature keeps rising, more heat released → stronger, more frequent storms like tropical cyclones and hurricanes.
    • Rising gases named here: CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, HCFCs, HFCs, ozone in lower atmosphere. Causes: burning fossil fuels, farming.
    • Measuring instruments show ocean surface water temperatures going up.
    • Corals: warming stresses them, they lose colour and die. A 2 °C rise in Indian Ocean temperature caused catastrophic bleaching and mass coral deaths in Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
    • Plankton is as important to sea ecosystems as grasses to terrestrial ones. Increased CO₂ uptake lowers plankton's nutritional quality → consequences for entire ocean food webs.
    • If an ocean's phytoplankton were destroyed: ocean as carbon sink and ocean food chains adversely affected; density of ocean water would not drastically decrease. Phytoplankton (microalgae) have chlorophyll, need sunlight.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • UPSC 2025 (reported official key: both correct), on a World Bank warning that India could be among the first places where wet-bulb temperatures routinely exceed 35 °C: peninsular India most likely to suffer flooding, tropical cyclones and droughts; survival of animals including humans affected as shedding body heat through perspiration becomes difficult.UPSC 2025
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Which effect separates a 3 °C rise from a 2 °C rise in the book's IPCC account?

      The terrestrial biosphere shifts towards a net carbon source. pp. 100–101

    2. Fill the gaps: at 2 °C, __ of ecosystems transform and __ of known species go extinct.

      1/6 and 1/4. p. 99

    3. Explain how warmer seas strengthen storms.

      A warmer surface releases more heat to the atmosphere, feeding stronger and more frequent cyclones and hurricanes. p. 101

    4. Correct this: "Destroying an ocean's phytoplankton would drastically lower seawater density."

      Density would not drastically decrease; the carbon sink and food chains would suffer. p. 102

    Climate Change

    Natural orbital cycles, the ice-core record, social stress, top emitters, net zero and ways of storing carbon.

    Astronomical theory and climate records
    • Change in Earth's position relative to Sun varies solar radiation received: astronomical principle = Milankovitch Hypothesis (Milutin Milankovitch, Serbian astronomer, climatologist, geophysicist; 1920s).
    • Three orbital factors: eccentricity of orbit, obliquity (axial tilt) of rotation axis, precession of equinoxes → cyclical variation in radiation = orbital forcing.
    • COMMON TRAP Solar irradiance is not part of this theory.UPPSCPCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15
    • Ice core = cylindrical sample drilled from a glacier or ice sheet (Antarctica, Greenland, high mountain glaciers); gives the cryogenic indicator of climate; most direct and detailed record of past climate and atmosphere.UPPSCPCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15
    • Annual snow layers: lower layers older than upper. Ice properties and inclusions, normally via isotopic analysis, reconstruct local temperature and atmospheric composition.
    Agriculture and social stress
    • Agriculture is the activity most affected. Rising temperature affects soil moisture and efficiency, raises soil salinity, cuts productivity; also changes water availability and needs.
    • Climate change raises pressure on resources (forest, grassland, agricultural land, river water, land water): conflict over them shows it as a factor in social tension.
    • Chain: extreme weather → food insecurity → unnecessary storing of food → social tension. UPPCS 2017: A and R both true, R explains A.
    Emitters, net zero and CCPI
    • Largest CO₂ emitter: China. Latest data in book (2023): China 34%, USA 12%, India about 7%, Russia 5%, Japan 2% of world total.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSC ×3PCS Pre ’10, ’18; Lower Sub ’15
    • Bhutan: world's top carbon-negative country; absorbs more than it emits.UPPSCLower Sub ’15
    • Net zero (= carbon neutrality) does not mean zero emissions: a country's emissions are compensated by absorption and removal of GHGs from the atmosphere.UPPSCPCS Pre ’21
    • Absorption via carbon sinks such as forests; removal via futuristic technology such as carbon capture and storage. Negative emissions possible if these exceed emissions.
    • Net-zero targets: India 2070, China 2060. International Energy Agency's roadmap "Net Zero by 2050" (2021) was the World's first comprehensive energy road map, ahead of the UN's November 2021 climate meeting.
    • Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI): published by Germanwatch, NewClimate Institute and Climate Action Network International. Measures 4 parameters: GHG Emissions, Renewable Energy, Energy Use, Climate Policy.
    • India's CCPI rank: 20th of 58 (2017), 14th (2018), 11th (2019), 10th (2022 edition), 8th (2023), 10th (2025).
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • UPSC 2025 (reported official key: II and III only): India ranks second in Asia-Pacific in CO₂ emissions from fuel combustion; electricity and heat producers are India's largest CO₂ source. The claim that India's emissions are under 0.5 t CO₂ per capita was rejected.UPSC 2025
    Source check Q0410 (UPPCS 2023, p.104) asks India's rank in world GHG emission in 2022; key (d) 10th, but the explanation gives only the CCPI rank, a performance index. Book's own p.103 puts India third in CO₂ emission. Do not read 10th as an emissions rank.
    Carbon sequestration (कार्बन प्रच्छादन) and farm practice
    • Carbon sequestration = capturing and long-term storing of atmospheric carbon in plants, geologic structures and sea.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Potential sites: abandoned and uneconomic coal seams, depleted oil and gas reservoirs, subterranean deep saline formations (IAS 2017: all three).UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • IAS 2023 key: all three discussed for capture and sequestration: finely ground basalt on farmlands, adding lime to raise ocean alkalinity, pumping captured CO₂ as carbonated water into abandoned mines.UPSC PYQUPSC ’23
    • Basalt: University of California, Davis and Cornell University field study: crushed volcanic rock stored carbon in soil even in an extreme California drought.UPSC PYQUPSC ’23
    • Captured CO₂: utilisation (urea manufacturing; methane, methanol, ethanol; aggregates) or permanent storage (depleted oil and gas reservoirs for enhanced oil production/EOR, deep saline aquifers, basaltic rock).UPSC PYQUPSC ’23
    • IAS 2012: all three aid soil carbon storage. Contour bunding: mechanical measure, minimises soil erosion in rainfed areas. Relay cropping: new crop sown before previous is harvested (nitrogen, shade, support, discourages pests). Zero tillage: least disturbance, retains water, nutrients, topsoil; stores soil organic matter.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Climate-Smart Village: part of a project led by CGIAR (Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research) Research Program on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS), built on Climate Smart Agriculture principles; technological, organisational and systemic support.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • CGIAR headquartered in France. ICRISAT (International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics, India) is a CGIAR centre: non-profit, non-political public international body, research for development in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa; awarded 2021 Africa Food Prize.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • Rural roads, to cut carbon footprint (कार्बन पदचिह्न): copper slag, cold mix asphalt technology, geotextiles preferred (IAS 2020).UPSC PYQUPSC ’20
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • UPSC 2025 (reported official key: all three correct): Direct Air Capture can serve carbon sequestration, plastic production and food processing, and supply carbon to combine with hydrogen for synthetic low-carbon aviation fuel.UPSC 2025
    • Mains 2025 asked what Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (CCUS) is and its potential role against climate change. Book's utilisation and storage routes above are the raw material; the paper has no official answer.UPSC 2025
    Source check Book's "Carbon overlay" (p.103) is defined exactly as carbon sequestration (p.106): merged here. Q0409's explanation does not discuss statement 2 (lime); the key (c) still counts it.
    Asia-Pacific Partnership (APP)
    • APP on Clean Development and Climate: international, voluntary, public-private partnership of Australia, Canada, India, Japan, People's Republic of China, South Korea, United States; announced July 2005.
    • Members account for over 45% of world GHG emissions, energy consumption, GDP and population. (UPPCS 2005 key also accepted 48% for energy and GHG.)
    • COMMON TRAP Not intended to directly support Kyoto. Unlike Kyoto's mandatory limits, it accelerates clean-energy technology with no mandatory enforcement, hence criticised by governments, climate scientists and environmental groups as worthless.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. List the three orbital variables in Milankovitch's theory.

      Eccentricity, axial tilt (obliquity) and precession. pp. 102, 105

    2. Correct this: "Net zero means a country will emit nothing by the target year."

      Emissions may continue if compensated by absorption and removal. p. 104

    3. Reconstruct the chain from extreme weather to social stress.

      Extreme weather → food insecurity → unnecessary food storage → social tension. pp. 103, 105

    4. Why are lower ice-core layers useful for old climate?

      Layers build up yearly, so deeper ice is older and preserves past conditions. p. 105

    Climate Change Conference

    UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; COPs meet under it; Paris (2015) set the temperature goal; the Green Climate Fund carries finance.

    UNFCCC and the COPs
    • UNFCCC: international environmental treaty adopted at UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED, the Earth Summit), Rio-de-Janeiro, 3–14 June 1992.UPSC PYQUPSC ’10
    • In force 21 March 1994, after support of more than 50 countries. Ratified by 198 countries (book's figure).UPPSCPCS Pre ’12
    • Deals with mitigation (शमन) of GHG emissions. Ultimate objective of all three agreements under it: stabilise GHG concentrations at a level preventing dangerous human interference with the climate system, in a time frame letting ecosystems adapt naturally and enabling sustainable development.
    • COP21: Paris, 30 November–12 December 2015; 21st yearly COP and 11th session of Meeting of the Parties to the 1997 Kyoto Protocol (क्योटो प्रोटोकॉल).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’18; Lower Sub ’15
    • COP25: 2–13 December 2019. COP16: 29 November–10 December 2010.
    • COP26: Glasgow, 31 October–12 November 2021. 120 world leaders, over 40,000 registered participants: 22,274 party delegates, 14,124 observers, 3,886 media representatives.
    • UN Climate Action Summit 2019: UN headquarters, New York City, 23 September 2019. Theme: "A Race We can Win. A Race We Must Win."UPPSCPCS Pre ’19
    • "Momentum for Change: Climate Neutral Now": launched by UNFCCC secretariat, to showcase successful climate action.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • Matched correctly: First World Climate Conference – 1979; First Earth Summit – Agenda-21; Earth Summit Plus 5 – 1997. Carbon Trading (कार्बन व्यापार) belongs to Kyoto, not Montreal.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Geo-engineering idea: Manchester University scientists suggested cloud brightening over the Pacific Ocean using sea water, for maximum reflection of sun rays.UPPSCPCS Mains ’09
    Paris Agreement (पेरिस समझौता)
    • Agreed by 194 nations (book’s figure; adoption is usually reported as 195 countries, 196 Parties with the EU) at Paris on 12 December 2015 (not "signed by all UN members").UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • CORE CONCEPT Aim: keep temperature rise this century well below 2 °C and drive efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Developed countries accepted responsibility; climate finance roadmap to USD 100 billion by 2020 (not 1000 billion).UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Book's count: 195 Parties (194 states + EU) out of 198 parties to the convention.
    • India at COP26 (per book): by 2030, 50% of energy requirement from renewable energy (not 60%), non-fossil capacity 500 GW, carbon emission cut by one billion tons. → Ch 8
    • UPSC 2025 (reported official key (a)): Article 6 of the Paris Agreement sets out principles of carbon markets and also promotes inter-country non-market strategies; both explain why it is so often discussed. Not in the book.UPSC 2025
    • IPCC: gradual or limited GHG cuts are insufficient for Paris goals; deep, rapid and sustained reductions are essential.UPPSCPCS Pre ’24
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • UPSC 2025 tested the COP28 Declaration on Climate and Health and India not signing it. Reported official key (c): only one of the two reasoning statements (binding and mandatory decarbonisation; risk to health-care resilience) is correct, and it explains India's stand.UPSC 2025
    Green Climate Fund (GCF)
    • Formally established at COP16, Cancun, 2010 (not Durban), within framework of UNFCCC. Based in Songdo Business district, Incheon, South Korea.UPPSCPCS Mains ’13
    • Purpose: assist developing countries in adaptation (अनुकूलन) and mitigation practices to counter climate change. Developed nations to provide 100 billion dollars per year by 2020.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Governed by GCF Board, 24 members; not founded under aegis of UNEP, OECD, ADB and World Bank.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    Earth Hour
    • Worldwide movement by World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), not UNEP/UNESCO; awareness on climate change and need to save the planet.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Non-essential lights off for one hour, 8:30–9:30 pm, usually last Saturday of March. Began as a lights-off event in Sydney, Australia, 2007.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Dates in book: 26 March 2022; 23 March 2024; 22 March 2025.

    1. When was the UNFCCC adopted, and when did it enter into force?

      June 1992 at Rio; in force 21 March 1994. pp. 107–108

    2. Name the COP and city where the Green Climate Fund was formally established.

      COP16, Cancun, 2010. pp. 107, 109

    3. Correct this: "Earth Hour is a joint UNEP and UNESCO programme."

    The Kyoto Protocol & Other Protocol

    Kyoto set binding cuts and created market tools (CDM, CER, carbon credits (कार्बन क्रेडिट)); a wider family of funds, metrics and alliances grew around it.

    Kyoto Protocol
    • International treaty extending the 1992 UNFCCC; relates to climate change; aims to reduce GHG concentration through internationally binding targets.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’19; PCS Mains ’17
    • Adopted Kyoto, Japan, 11 December 1997; in force 16 February 2005 after Russia's ratification.UPSC PYQUPSC ’05
    • Binding agreement: high-emitting countries to collectively cut GHGs by 5.2% during 2008–2012 (1990 baseline).
    • Deals with GHG reduction, not ozone depletion.UPSC PYQUPSC ’05
    • 192 Parties (book's figure). It operationalises the UNFCCC by committing industrialized countries and economies in transition to agreed individual targets; the Convention itself only asks them to adopt policies and report periodically.
    • Annex-I countries took part in the 1st Kyoto round; Annex-I countries and the EU agreed second-round targets.
    • Kyoto is unratified by the United States (book's wording: "currently").
    • GWP of CO₂ fixed at 1. Book: methane 81.2 (p.111) and about 86 times CO₂ (p.113); so methane is the more harmful gas per unit.UPSC PYQUPSC ’05
    Source check Book gives two methane values, 81.2 "in the last 20 years" (p.111) and about 86 (p.113), with no reconciliation; "last 20 years" reads like a 20-year time horizon. It also says GWP depends on "efficiency of the atoms" and "environmental life-cycle". Remember the qualitative point (methane far stronger than CO₂); not externally verified here.
    CDM, CER and carbon credits
    • CDM: Article 12 of Kyoto Protocol. Lets an Annex-B party (with an emission commitment) implement an emission-reduction project in developing countries.UPSC PYQUPSC ’08
    • Market-driven device under UNFCCC: developing countries get funds/incentives from developed countries for better technologies. It does not prohibit developed-country investment; it promotes it.UPSC PYQUPSC ’09
    • COMMON TRAP Projects are not limited to Annex-I: Annex-I (industrialized) countries fund them in Non-Annex-I (developing) countries.UPSC PYQUPSC ’08
    • Two aims: help Non-Annex-I achieve sustainable development and UNFCCC's objective; help Annex-I comply with quantified emission caps.UPSC PYQUPSC ’08
    • One of the Protocol's flexible, "project-based" Mechanisms.
    • CDM project types: afforestation, carbon sink, minimisation of carbon.
    • CER: tradable unit of CDM; 1 CER = 1 ton CO₂. Issued by CDM Executive Board for reductions verified by a DOE (Designated Operational Entity). Counted towards Kyoto targets.UPSC PYQUPSC ’08, ’16
    • Carbon credit concept originated from Kyoto. One credit permits emission of one ton of CO₂ (or other GHG). Carbon trading encouraged internationally; economic incentive to cut CO₂.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15; PCS Pre ’21
    • Credits awarded for cutting below quota; aim to limit rise in CO₂. Traded privately or on open market at current market value, not at a price fixed by UNEP.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Mechanics: caps set under Kyoto → national registries (validated and monitored by UNFCCC) → operators get allowances; those under quota sell, those over buy; so firms invest in cleaner practice or buy credits.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Emission Reduction Purchase Agreement, May 2011: for CERs, signed by Hubert Nove Josserand (World Bank deputy country director, for International Bank for Reconstruction and Development) and Sudripto Roy (Himachal Pradesh additional chief secretary): with Himachal Government, not Government of India. Book treats remaining options as correct: ten-year validity; Himachal Pradesh project; one ton CO₂ = one credit.UPPSCPCS Mains ’10
    Carbon metrics, tax and blue carbon
    • Carbon footprint: total GHGs produced, directly or indirectly, to support human activities.
    • GHG Protocol: most widely used international accounting tool for Government and business leaders to understand, quantify and manage GHG emissions. Partnership of World Resources Institute (WRI) and World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD); works with businesses, governments and environmental groups.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Common Carbon Metric (UNEP-supported): measures energy use and reports GHG from building operations; universal method for a building's carbon footprint; defines measurement, reporting, verification. Not a building rating tool; consistent with WBCSD and WRI GHG Protocol.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • Blue carbon: carbon captured by world's ocean and coastal ecosystems. Sea grasses, mangroves and salt marshes act as sinks; much smaller than forests but sequester at a much faster rate, and can continue for millions of years.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • Carbon tax: levied on energy resources releasing CO₂; a form of Pollution tax; makes fossil-fuel users pay for climate damage.
    • Singapore announced (February 2018) a carbon tax from 2019, under Paris commitments: facilities with 25,000 tons or more GHG per year.UPPSCRO/ARO ’17
    • New Zealand: book says it introduced a Carbon Tax for the first time in 2005 (IAS 2006 key).UPSC PYQUPSC ’06
    Source check Same explanation (p.116) says Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands and Norway had "already introduced" Carbon Tax, yet calls New Zealand first. The question asks who first proposed one for its people. Keep "New Zealand" as the question-time key only.
    Forest and climate funds
    • Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF): World Bank, June 2008. Global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society, indigenous people. Readiness Fund and Carbon Fund.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Helps developing countries in REDD+ (Reducing Emission from Deforestation and Forest Degradation: cut deforestation and forest degradation, conserve and enhance forest carbon stocks, sustainably manage forests) with financial and technical assistance. Does not fund universities, individuals or institutes.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • BioCarbon Fund ISFL (Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes): multilateral fund managed by World Bank; donors Norway up to $135 million, UK $120 million, USA $25 million. Promotes reduced land-sector GHG.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Global Climate Change Alliance (GCCA): European Union (EU) initiative, 2007 (operational 2008), with developing countries, in particular LDCs and SIDS. Coordinated by European Commission, not WRI/WBCSD.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Gives technical and financial support to integrate climate change in development policies and budgets. Started in 4 countries; budget more than £300 million (book); aim: a new treaty between EU and poor developing countries.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • UPSC 2026 asked which is India's first Plan Vivo certified REDD+ project. Coaching consensus, not an official key: Khasi Hills Community REDD+ project.UPSC 2026

    Observatories and coalitions
    • Deep Carbon Observatory: global community of more than 1000 scientists, a ten-year quest (2009–2019) on quantities, movements, forms and origins of carbon in Earth. Conducts field observation of deep microbial ecosystem.UPPSCPCS Pre ’19

    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. State the Kyoto adoption date, entry-into-force date and collective cut.

      11 December 1997; 16 February 2005; 5.2% during 2008–2012. p. 110

    2. In the CDM figure, what flows from Annex-I to Non-Annex-I and what flows back?

      Capital for CDM projects goes out; carbon credit comes back. p. 107

      They trade at market value, privately or on the open market. pp. 111, 115

    4. Distinguish the GHG Protocol from the Common Carbon Metric.

      GHG Protocol is a general accounting tool for governments and businesses; the Metric covers building operations. pp. 113–114

    5. Who manages the BioCarbon Fund ISFL, and which donor gives most?

      World Bank; Norway, up to $135 million. pp. 111, 116

    Action Plan of India in perspective of climate change

    NAPCC (2008) gives eight missions; INDCs set 2030 goals; Jharkhand is the book's state-level example.

    National Action Plan on Climate Change (जलवायु परिवर्तन पर राष्ट्रीय कार्य योजना)
    • India's first NAPCC: released by then PM Manmohan Singh, 30 June 2008; focuses on eight missions, to mitigate and adapt.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSC ×5PCS Pre ’16, ’18; PCS Mains ’16; RO/ARO Mains ’21; UDA/LDA Mains (Spl) ’10
    1. National Solar MissionREPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    2. National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency
    3. National Mission on Sustainable Habitat
    4. National Water Mission
    5. National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem
    6. National Mission for Green IndiaREPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    7. National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture
    8. National Mission on Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change
    Common trap Atomic/nuclear energy is not a mission (key in both 2010 and 2016 papers). The list also has no separately named waste-to-energy mission; afforestation sits under Green India.
    • Green India Mission (GIM): launched February 2014; protects, restores and enhances forest cover by combined adaptation and mitigation. Recognises forests' role in mitigation, water security, food security, biodiversity conservation and livelihood security of forest-dependent communities.
    • National Executive Council's second meeting (October 2015) approved annual plans of Mizoram, Manipur, Kerala and Jharkhand; Jharkhand PSC 2016 key = Jharkhand.
    India's INDC
    • Intended Nationally Determined Contributions (INDCs): post-2020 climate action countries publicly outlined under the Paris agreement at COP21 (December 2015); India's are for GHG reductions under UNFCCC.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Centre on clean, especially renewable, energy; energy efficiency; less carbon-intensive and resilient urban centres; waste to wealth; safe, smart, sustainable green transport; abatement of pollution; enhancing carbon sink through forest and tree cover.
    Source check Book's INDC box (33–35%, 40%; p.118) is the 2015 position, but later pages give different 2030 goals: 50% renewable energy (p.109), carbon intensity 45% and 500 GW (p.208). Compare → Ch 8 and state which commitment a question means. Later official figures could not be opened in this pass.
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • Mains 2025 asked for a review of India's Paris commitments, how COP26 strengthened them, and how the first NDC was updated in 2022. The book gives the INDC box and COP26 lines but not the 2022 text; the paper has no official answer.UPSC 2025
    • UPSC 2026 asked how three statements relate: LT-LEDS as a tool for net-zero by 2070; BUR-4 (December 2024) recording around 8% fall in GHG emissions in 2020 over 2019; and resilience depending on quick short-term cuts. Coaching consensus (b), not an official key: the first is supported by the second, and the third contradicts the first's approach.UPSC 2026
    Jharkhand climate action
    • State Climate Change Centre/Cell: Jharkhand with UNDP (May 2011); advises state government.
    • Functions: knowledge products for stakeholders (issue briefs, mitigation and adaptation options); outreach and network with other organisations; capacity development of government officers for mainstreaming climate concerns.
    • Jharkhand Action Plan on Climate Change: published 2013 and 2014 (see check below).
    • Most sensitive district (2014 report): Saraikela Kharsawan, score 0.78 on a scale of (–1) to (+1).
    Source check Q0467 (Jharkhand PCS 2016) is marked (*): the book says the State plan was published in 2013 & 2014, and both years are options. No single answer.
    Monitoring and institutions
    • Global Atmosphere Watch (GAW), a WMO programme: network of Global and Regional stations plus Contributing stations; about 30 global stations. Algeria, Brazil and Kenya listed; India had none as at UPPCS 2012; book adds Brazil is now out of the list.
    • SAFAR (System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting): state-of-the-art Air Quality and Weather Forecast System, unveiled by Dr Harsh Vardhan at Chandni Chowk, Delhi, 2018. Built indigenously by Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology, Pune; operationalised by India Meteorological Department (IMD).UPPSCPCS Pre ’18
    • True-colour LED display: real-time air quality index 24x7 with colour coding, plus 72-hour advance forecast. Monitors PM2.5, PM10, Sulfur Dioxide, Ozone, Nitrogen Oxides, Carbon Monoxide; also Benzene, Toluene, Xylene.
    • National Green Tribunal: set up 18-10-2010 under NGT Act 2010, for effective and expeditious disposal of environmental protection and forest conservation cases. Headquarters: New Delhi. → Ch 11
