    Ozone Layer · ओज़ोन परत

    Ozone and the Ozone Layer (ओज़ोन परत)

    Same gas, two roles: harmful near the ground, protective high up.

    • Ozone (O₃): three oxygen atoms; found in very small amount. Stratospheric ozone forms naturally from solar UV acting on O₂ molecules.
    • CORE CONCEPT At Earth's surface a pollutant, harmful to living organisms ("deadly poison"); at higher levels it shields Earth from UV, which is highly damaging and known to cause skin cancer (त्वचा कैंसर). O₂, by contrast, is essential for aerobic life.
    • Ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet (पराबैंगनी) radiation; protects life and the biosphere from it, preventing UV from reaching the Earth.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papersUPPSC ×7PCS Pre ’06, ’13, ’14, ’25; PCS Mains ’10; Lower Sub ’04; UDA/LDA Mains ’10
    • Found mainly in the stratosphere (समतापमंडल): lower portion, about 15–30 km (9–18 miles); thickness/density varies seasonally and geographically.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papers
    • So "around 20 km above the Earth" fits among Q's options.
    • About 90% of atmospheric ozone is in the stratosphere; about 10% in the troposphere (क्षोभमंडल) (book: "10% of the ozone layer").REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papersUPPSC ×5PCS Pre (Spl) ’08; PCS Pre ’18, ’23; PCS Mains ’12; UDA/LDA Mains (Spl) ’10
    • Key: Ozone layer–Troposphere is the mismatch. Left standing: Renneting–Cheese; Genetic Engineering–Plasmids; Golden rice–Vitamin A.
    • Ozone molecules are constantly formed and destroyed in the stratosphere; book adds that the total "has remained relatively stable during the decades that it has been measured" (p. 123), a statement about natural balance that sits beside the depletion pages.
    • Naturally regulated by Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂). Thickness highest in spring, lowest in the rainy season (book).UPPSCPCS Mains ’16
    • Unit: Dobson Unit (डॉबसन इकाई) (DU). 1 DU = 0.01 mm thickness of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm. Good indicator of total ozone concentration. Other options: decibel (sound level); ppb, parts per billion (pollutant concentration in air, volume ratio); ppm, parts per million (book: mass of contaminant per million units of total mass).
    • Total mass of ozone in atmosphere: about 3 billion metric tons.
    Homosphere and heterosphere
    • Order upward: troposphere (lowest), stratosphere, mesosphere (मध्यमंडल), thermosphere (तापमंडल), exosphere. Thickness differs slightly around the globe, varies with temperature and season. Troposphere is thickest at the equator.
    • Homosphere (uniform chemical composition): up to 56 mi (90 km); three thermal layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, each separated by a shallow transitional zone. COMMON TRAP Ionosphere (आयनमंडल) is not in the homosphere.
    • Heterosphere: heterogeneous, layered nitrogen, oxygen, helium, hydrogen, respectively. Book's graph places thermosphere, exosphere and ionosphere in the upper atmosphere, with curves for Active Sun and Average Sun.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Define one Dobson Unit.

      0.01 mm thickness of pure ozone at 0°C and 1 atm. p. 122

    2. Explain why ozone is called both a pollutant and a protector.

      Harmful at the surface; high in the atmosphere it shields Earth from UV. p. 122

    3. Name the three layers of the homosphere, from the ground up.

      Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere. p. 124

    4. Correct this: "The ozone layer lies in the troposphere."

      False. It lies mainly in the stratosphere, about 15–30 km up. p. 123

    Ozone Layer Depletion

    Man-made chlorine and bromine compounds, activated over the poles, destroy ozone faster than it forms.

    • British Antarctic Survey team first reported Antarctic ozone hole (ओज़ोन छिद्र): Joe Farman, Brian Gardiner, Jonathan Shanklin, journal Nature, May 1985.UPPSCPCS Mains ’13
    • Ozone hole: not literally a hole; a region of exceptionally depleted ozone in the stratosphere over Antarctica. Ozone forms very slowly over polar regions, so depletion effect is maximum over the poles.
    • CORE CONCEPT Chlorofluorocarbons (क्लोरोफ्लोरोकार्बन) are the main cause: released CFCs break ozone down through chemical reactions, cutting its UV-absorbing capacity.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papersUPPSC ×4PCS Pre ’16; RO/ARO ’14; RO/ARO Mains ’17; GIC ’09
    • CFCs: man-made compounds of carbon, chlorine, fluorine (book also says oxygen in one note); non-toxic, non-flammable, colourless, odourless, easily liquefied. Very stable, lasting 80 to 100 years. Book: one of the major causes of the greenhouse effect.
    • Uses: refrigerants in refrigerators, air conditioners; aerosol sprays (pressurizing agents), blowing agents for plastic foams and packing materials, solvents; trichlorofluoromethane dissolves grease and cleans electronic equipment. Tubeless tyres not a listed use.UPSC PYQUPSC ’12
    • Book: use rising since the 1960s with refrigerators, air conditioners, spray cases, solvents, foam constructions, pressed toiletries, micro-marine works in industries.
    • Green-house source pairs: key marks CFC–Automobile as the mismatch; left standing: CO₂–Thermal Power Stations, Nitrous Oxide–Waterlogged Paddy fields, Sulphur dioxide–Brick Kilns.
    • Refrigerator gas sold as Mafron, commonly a halonic hydrocarbon (book's key). Ammonia also used as coolant in big plants.
    • Chlorine and bromine atoms destroy stratospheric ozone. One chlorine atom can destroy over 100,000 ozone molecules before removal. ODS emitted at surface may take two to five years to reach the stratosphere.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papers
    • ODS releasing chlorine: CFCs, HCFCs, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform. Releasing bromine: halons, methyl bromide.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS8 papers
    • Book's list (pp. 125–126): CFC, Halon-1211,1301, Nitrous oxide, Trichloroethane etc. Uses named in Q: CFC-12 refrigerators, Halon-1211 fire fighting.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Antarctic hole: formed with a prominent polar front, polar stratospheric clouds and inflow of CFCs. Nitric acid in the clouds reacts with CFCs, giving chlorine that destroys ozone photochemically. Clouds help convert chlorine compounds into chlorine atoms.UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    Source check Book says the 1985 British team used a "total ozone mapping spectrometer" (pp. 125, 129). The British Antarctic Survey page could not be read to confirm this. Standard accounts credit ground-based Dobson spectrophotometer readings at Halley Bay, so avoid naming the instrument without checking.
    Source check Q0504 key (b) says methyl chloroform is not responsible for depletion (p. 126), but the book's own Q0503 note lists it as an ODS, and US EPA lists it too. Do not memorise it as harmless. Also, the book's list reads "Tricloroethlyn" (p. 125) and "Trichloroethane" (p. 126). source
    Source check

    U.P.P.C.S. 2008 keys carbon monoxide as not causing "ozone depletion (ओज़ोन क्षरण) in the troposphere", and its note lists water vapour, CO₂, methane, ozone, N₂O, CFCs (p. 126). That list is of greenhouse gases; the book locates depletion in the stratosphere elsewhere. Treat as a doubtful question.

    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Explain why depletion is most severe near the poles.

      Ozone forms very slowly over polar regions, and polar stratospheric clouds help release chlorine. p. 125

    2. Sort into chlorine and bromine sources: halons, HCFCs, methyl bromide, carbon tetrachloride.

      Chlorine: HCFCs, carbon tetrachloride. Bromine: halons, methyl bromide. p. 126

    3. How long may an ODS take to reach the stratosphere, and how many ozone molecules may one chlorine atom destroy?

      Two to five years; over 100,000. p. 126

    4. Name the journal and year in which the Antarctic ozone hole was announced.

      Nature, May 1985. p. 125

    Measures for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer

    The Montreal Protocol (मॉन्ट्रियल प्रोटोकॉल) phases out ozone-depleting substances; Kigali extends it to HFCs.

    • Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer: protocol to the Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer; phases out production and use of ODS.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’15 · 2 papers
    • Main ODS: chlorofluorocarbons, halons, carbon tetrachloride. Book: all banned after the Protocol.
    • Landmark multilateral agreement regulating production and consumption of nearly 100 man-made ODS chemicals. Parties meet once a year. COMMON TRAP Carbon Trade is not Montreal; it belongs to the Kyoto Protocol. → Ch 4
    • Other pairs left standing by key: First World Climate Conference–1979; First Earth Summit–Agenda 21; Earth Summit + 5–1997.
    • Tibetan Plateau ozone halo, 2005: team led by G.W. Kent Moore (University of Toronto, Canada). Ozone low over the centre, with a concentrated ring of excess ozone around the Plateau.UPPSCPCS Mains ’13
    • At high concentrations ozone can cause coughing, chest pain, lung damage. Book calls it highly volatile.
    • Day's themes: 2022 "Global cooperation protecting life on Earth"; 2024 "Montreal Protocol: Advancing Climate Action".REPEATED · ALL EXAMS6 papers
    Source check Book's note to Q0514 says the ozone layer is depleted "mainly by carbon dioxide and chlorofluorocarbons" (p. 128). CO₂ is on neither of the book's ODS lists (pp. 125–127). Keep only the CFC half.
    Source check Q0511 asks about the Tibetan "ozone halo", but the book calls it an "ozone hole" (p. 127). Its description (low centre, surrounding ring of excess ozone) fits a halo. Record the name as asked.
    Source check

    Uttarakhand Mains 2002: key (b) says Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, "not nitric acid", cause acid rain (p. 129). The book's pollution chapter names nitric acid as an acid in acid rain (p. 232, → Ch 9). The gases are precursors; the acid is what falls. Its other pairs: Ozone–CFC; Rocket fuel–highly refined kerosene; Greenhouse Effect–CO₂, second largest cause after water vapour.

    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Why is the ozone day fixed on 16 September?

      It marks the 1987 signing of the Montreal Protocol. p. 128

    2. Which substances does the Kigali Amendment phase down?

      Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). p. 129

    3. Correct this: "Carbon Trade comes under the Montreal Protocol."

      False. Montreal regulates ozone-depleting substances; carbon trading belongs to Kyoto. pp. 121, 128

    Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion

    Less ozone lets more biologically harmful UV reach the surface.

    • Harmful solar UV causes skin cancer. Long absorption by skin may cause genetic mutation in DNA, which can lead to skin cancer.UPPSCPCS Pre ’14
    • Assertion-Reason: ozone essential for biotic life because the layer protects the surface from high-energy radiation; R explains A. As a gas, ozone is poisonous to biotic life (direct, immediate harm to lungs and respiratory system).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Ozone layer absorbs 93–99% of the Sun's high-frequency UV light, potentially detrimental to life.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Without the ozone layer, UV would cause excessive damage to biological life.
    Source check P. 129 says the layer blocks "high wavelength" UV, while the Q0524 note says "high-frequency" UV on the same page. High frequency means short wavelength, so use the Q0524 wording.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Give the wavelength ranges of the three UV bands.

      UV-A 315–400 nm; UV-B 280–315 nm; UV-C 100–280 nm. p. 129

    2. Fill the missing labels: UV-B causes skin cancer, cataracts, sunburn and which plant effects?

      Hindrance in the growth of plants; harm to leaves. p. 129

    3. Why does UV-C not cause sunburn at the surface?

      Diatomic oxygen or ozone blocks it before it reaches the surface. p. 129

    Forest and Wildlife · वन एवं वन्यजीव

    Book's reference sites (p. 130): WII-ENVIS Centre on Wildlife (वन्यजीव) & Protected Areas; Wildlife Institute of India; State of Forest Report (FSI); World Wildlife Fund; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change; Environment, Forest and Climate Change Department, Uttar Pradesh; National Tiger Conservation Authority.

    Forest and their types

    Forest type tracks rainfall, altitude and the coast: evergreen (सदाबहार) above 200 cm, moist deciduous (पर्णपाती) at 100–200 cm, mangroves (मैंग्रोव) on tidal shores.

    Tropical evergreen and equatorial forests
    • Tropical evergreen: rainfall >200 cm; temp 15–30 °C; about 7% of Earth's land surface; more than half of world's plants and animals; mostly near equator.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • India: Western Ghats (western slope; Kerala, Karnataka); north-east (Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura, Jaintia & Khasi hills of Meghalaya); Andaman & Nicobar Islands.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • COMMON TRAPHimachal Pradesh: mainly Sub-Tropical Pine + Himalayan Moist Temperate forests, so not Tropical Wet Evergreen.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Maximum plant diversity: tropical evergreen forests. Greatest plant + animal diversity: tropical moist forests.
    • Tropical rainforest biome: 23.5°N–23.5°S; book: largest biome of world, about 8% of Earth's surface; >50% of world's biodiversity; rain all year; high heat + humidity make broad-leaved evergreen trees dominant.
    • Over 200 tree species per hectare; shade-tolerant shrubs, herbs, small trees, large woody vines climbing for sunlight; about 70–80% of known insect species.
    • Equatorial = tropical rain forests (उष्णकटिबंधीय वर्षा वन) (>200 cm). All three features correct (IAS 2013): tall closely-set trees with continuous canopy; co-existence of many species; numerous epiphytes on upper canopy.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Densest + highest biomass (जैवभार): equatorial forest biome; high rainfall and high temperature all year is the correct reason (book: warm, wet climate, much sunshine).UPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’17; RO/ARO ’23
    • Maximum plant biomass among ecosystems: tropical rain forest.
    • Amazon rain forest (Amazonia): moist broad-leaf forest over most of Amazon basin, South America; "Lungs of the Planet Earth" for absorbing CO₂ and releasing oxygen.
    Source check Book's rainforest figures are loose: about 7% of land (evergreen) and about 8% of surface (biome), both p. 130; biodiversity ">50%" and "about 80%" (p. 130; 80% also Q0527). Don't treat either as the only figure.
    Source check Book states the Amazon produces more than 20% of Earth's oxygen (pp. 130, 134). This popular figure is widely disputed; no source page was opened in this run, so no link is given. Verify before quoting.
    Tropical moist deciduous (monsoon) forests
    • Rainfall 100–200 cm; Teak (Sagaun) is the dominant tree.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Other commercially important species: Bamboo, Sal, Shisham, Sandalwood, Khair, Kusum, Arjun, Mulberry.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Broad leaves shed once a year; about 6–8 weeks in spring/early summer when moisture is short.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Also called monsoon forests; found in India, Myanmar, Thailand, areas of south-east Asia.
    • Maximum area under teak: Madhya Pradesh (book cites "IFSR 2023, % of RFA").
    • Tropical deciduous forests most extensive in Asia. Book's explanation describes deciduous forests broadly: warm, moist summers + mild winters; mainly Northern Hemisphere, Eastern North America, East Asia, Europe.UPPSCRO/ARO ’14
    Himalayan and southern mountain forests
    • Book labels temperate forests as "deciduous forests". Himalaya shows succession from tropical to tundra with altitude.
    • Southern mountain forests (Peninsular India): Western Ghats + Nilgiris. Closer to tropics, only 1,500 m high: temperate on higher regions, subtropical on lower regions, especially Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka.
    • Naturally seen in the Himalayas: Oak, Rhododendron. Not Sandalwood (tropical deciduous; mainly South India; negligible chance in Himalaya).UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Subtropical forests: North-West (except Kashmir), Khasi hills, Nagaland, Manipur. Pine main tree; broad-leaved Oak in highly humid areas; rhododendron shrubs.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    • Uttarakhand: Oak-Rhododendron are characteristic of temperate forests. Species: Banj Oak (Quercus leucotrichophora), Burans (Rhododendron arboreum), Kaphal (Myrica esculenta), Aynor (Lyonia ovalifolia), Ilex dipyrena, Kharsu oak (Quercus semecarpifolia).
    Notable tree species
    • Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus): endemic, southern Eastern Ghats, South India; tropical dry deciduous forests; Palkonda and Seshachalam hills. Not a tropical rainforest tree.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Red Sanders wood white, turning red through a red gummy juice; valued for rich red colour; mainly exported to China and Japan; used in traditional herbal medicine, toys, worship materials.
    • Taxus tree: naturally in Himalaya; listed in Red Data Book; source of anti-cancer drug Taxol (breast and lung cancer per book).UPSC PYQUPSC ’10
    Source check Book keys IAS 2010 as (d), accepting that Taxol is effective against Parkinson's disease (pp. 131, 135). NCI's list of FDA-approved paclitaxel uses covers Kaposi sarcoma, breast, non-small cell lung and ovarian cancer, with no mention of Parkinson's. Treat Parkinson's as the book's claim only. source
    Mangrove forests
    • "Mangrove" means two things: tidal swamp ecosystem (tropical deltas, estuaries, lagoons, islands) and its characteristic tree species.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Specialised ecosystems of tropical + subtropical tidal coasts in saline water. Stabilise shoreline, bulwark against the sea (IAS 1996: R correctly explains A).UPSC PYQUPSC ’96
    • Protect biodiversity; link between sea and coast; check coastal erosion and wave damage. Unique adaptations to harsh coastal conditions.
    • CORE CONCEPTSafety hedge after 2004 Tsunami: trees are not uprooted by storms and tides because of extensive roots (not because of canopy shelter).UPSC PYQUPSC ’11
    • Largest mangrove area: Sunderbans delta; Sundari tree popular.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Mains ’08
    • IAS 1995 quotation (monoculture, palm cultivation, mangrove destruction, drying freshwater pockets): book keys Sunderbans, saying only that the place "seems near" Sundarban.UPSC PYQUPSC ’95
    • Coringa: Godavari delta; among largest mangrove extensions; diverse mangrove trees and birds.UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’21
    • Protected mangrove region: Chorao Island, Goa.UPPSCPCS Mains ’16
    • Andaman & Nicobar has mangrove + evergreen + deciduous forests together; about 608.29 km² mangrove (ISFR 2023).UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    • Bhitarkanika: deltas of Brahmani and Baitarni, Kendrapada district, Odisha (not West Bengal; not Vansadhara/Subarnarekha); Ramsar site 2002. → Ch 3
    • Coastal Odisha: cyclones of Bay of Bengal hit more often than any other state; massive deforestation (वनोन्मूलन) in Mahanadi delta added to the risk.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    Source check Book keys Q0547 as (a), "R explains A" (p. 135), but its own text says only that Mahanadi delta deforestation "added the risks arising due to cyclones" (p. 135). Mangrove loss raises vulnerability; it isn't the cause of cyclone frequency.

    Eco-regions and forest matches
    • Book's incorrect pair: Tarai Duar – Broadleaf forests. Correctly matched: South-Western Ghats – Moist; Rann of Kachchh – Grasslands (घासभूमि); Eastern Deccan Plateau – Moist.
    • Western Himalayan region: Kashmir to Kumaon; temperate zone rich in Chir, Pine, broadleaf forests.

    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. State the rainfall band for tropical evergreen and for tropical moist deciduous forests.

      Above 200 cm; 100–200 cm. Teak dominates the second. p. 130

    2. Correct this: "Himachal Pradesh has Tropical Wet Evergreen forests like Mizoram."

      False. Himachal is mainly Sub-Tropical Pine and Himalayan Moist Temperate; Mizoram and Arunachal have Tropical Wet Evergreen. p. 131

    3. Fill in the missing band: foothills deciduous → 1,000–2,000 m ____ → 3,000–4,000 m alpine.

      Wet temperate (pines at 1,500–1,750 m; blue pine and spruce at 2,225–3,048 m lie between). p. 130

    4. In one sentence, why do mangroves act as a safety hedge?

      Their extensive roots keep them from being uprooted by storms and tides. p. 135

    5. Name Bhitarkanika's river deltas and district.

      Brahmani and Baitarni; Kendrapada, Odisha. p. 131

    Benefits and Uses of Forest

    Natural resources are graded by development stage; forests count as renewable because they can be reused after sustainable exploitation.

    • Resources by development stage: Potential, Actual, Reserve, Stock.
    • Potential: located in an area, usable in future. Actual: surveyed, quantity and quality determined, in use now.
    • Development of an actual resource depends on technology and cost of production (A and R both true; R does not explain A).
    • Forest is renewable because it can be reused after sustainable exploitation. It also enhances environment (absorbs CO₂, produces oxygen), but that is not why it is renewable.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Aluminium = "green metal" for eco-friendly sustainability. It can substitute wood, but saving forests is not the substantive reason (A true, R false).UPPSCPCS Mains ’09
    • Living root bridges (tree shaping): southern part of Meghalaya.UPSC PYQUPSC ’15
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Distinguish potential from actual resources.

      Potential exist and are usable in future; actual are surveyed, measured and in present use. p. 136

    2. Why is "forests enhance the environment" a wrong reason for "forests are renewable"?

      Renewability comes from reuse after sustainable exploitation; both claims are true but unconnected. p. 136

    3. Name the state with living root bridges.

      Meghalaya. p. 137

    Deforestation and Its Impacts

    Population pressure drives forest loss in developing countries; urbanization is a cause, not an effect.

    • Forest loss in India is directly linked to demographic transition; forest cover (वनावरण) negatively related to population growth (R explains A). Drivers: population growth, density, distribution, migration, urbanization; more food demand converts forest to farmland.UPPSCRO/ARO ’16
    • Generally negative link in developing countries; not implied for developed countries, where forest area rises through awareness and sensitivity.
    • Book's main cause of forest loss: industrialization. Urbanization also cuts forest; empty land goes to agriculture.UPPSCPCS Mains ’11
    • COMMON TRAPUrbanization is a cause, not an impact; towns and cities expanding shrink forest area.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Nagaland hills turning barren mainly through shifting cultivation (स्थानांतरित (झूम) कृषि).
    • Jharkhand: forest fire (वनाग्नि) is a major issue affecting climate; Hazaribagh, Jamshedpur, Palamu, Bokaro; problem of reserved and conserved forests.
    • Over 90% of forest fires anthropogenic: deliberate (personal gain, rivalry), negligence or accident. NTFP collectors ignite fires that may spread in extreme heat.
    • Main NTFP linked to fire in Jharkhand: Mahua flowers (Madhuca indica), boiled with Sal (Shorea robusta) seeds for a local beverage; pickers burn dry leaves to clear a small circle under a tree.
    • Valparai, Coimbatore district, Tamil Nadu: specialised in plantation (among options).UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’13
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Identify and correct: "Urbanization is an impact of deforestation."

      False. It is a cause; drying of water sources, biodiversity loss and soil erosion are impacts. p. 138

    2. Which forest product links to Jharkhand's fires, and how?

      Mahua flowers. Pickers burn dry leaves to clear the ground, and the fire spreads in hot weather. p. 138

    3. Explain the population-forest relationship in one sentence.

      Population growth raises food demand and converts forest to farmland, chiefly in developing countries. pp. 137–138

    National Forest Policy (राष्ट्रीय वन नीति) (1952)

    The policy sets the one-third forest target; 1952 classified forests while 1988 set programmes.

    • NFP 1952 classes: Protected/Conserved, National, Village, Tree Lands. National Parks are not a class.
    • CORE CONCEPTCurrent policy: one-third (33%) of total land under forest or tree cover (वृक्षावरण).REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’99 · 4 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’02, ’14
    • Mountain and hilly regions: two-thirds under such cover, to prevent erosion and land degradation and stabilise fragile ecosystems.
    • NFP 1988 includes: afforestation (वनीकरण) and wasteland development; reforestation and replantation in existing forests; wood substitutes and other fuels. Not included: wide use of insecticides and pesticides.UPSC PYQUPSC ’96
    • Draft National Forest Policy, 2018 cleared by various ministries at a meeting on November 21, 2019.
    • International Day of Forests: 21 March, proclaimed by United Nations General Assembly in 2012; 2018 theme "Forests and Sustainable Cities"; 2025 theme "Forests and Food" (p. 139: "The future of food begins in the forests"; book prints "beings"). ↗
    Basic objectives (NFP)
    1. Environmental stability: preserve and restore ecological balance disturbed by depletion of forests.
    2. Conserve natural heritage: remaining natural forests, flora and fauna, biological diversity, genetic resources.
    3. Check soil erosion (मृदा अपरदन) and denudation in catchments of rivers, lakes, reservoirs; mitigate floods and droughts; retard reservoir siltation.
    4. Check extension of sand-dunes in the desert areas of Rajasthan and along coastal tracts.
    5. Substantially increase forest/tree cover through massive afforestation and social forestry (सामाजिक वानिकी), especially on denuded, degraded, unproductive lands.
    6. Meet fuel-wood, fodder, minor forest produce and small timber needs of rural and tribal populations.
    7. Increase forest productivity for essential national needs.
    8. Efficient use of forest produce; maximum substitution of wood.
    9. Massive people's movement involving women, to minimise pressure on existing forests.
    Source check Book keys Q0569 as (c), statements 1 and 4 (UDA/LDA 2001), but the same book lists one-third forestation as a main objective (p. 139) and social forestry among objectives (p. 140), which the key leaves out.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Give the forest-cover targets for the country and for hill regions.

      One-third; two-thirds. p. 139

    2. Which item is excluded from NFP 1988: wood substitutes, or wide pesticide use?

      Wide pesticide use. p. 139

    3. Name the four forest classes of NFP 1952.

      Protected/Conserved, National, Village, Tree Lands. p. 138

    India State of Forest Report, 2023

    ISFR 2023 is the latest report in the book: forest cover 21.76% of geographical area; forest + tree cover 25.17%.

    Report and method
    • Biennial; released by MoEF&CC December 2024; 18th in series. Covers growing stock in forests and trees outside forests, bamboo, carbon stock and other parameters.
    • Book links Nagar Van Yojana to India's aim of additional 2.5–3 billion tonnes CO₂-equivalent carbon sink by 2030.
    • Forest cover: all patches with canopy density ≥10% and area ≥1 ha, irrespective of land use, ownership or species. Mapped at 1:50000.
    • Increase in forest cover is not uniform.
    • 33% target is from National Forest Policy, 1988; also a key target of Strategy for New India @ 75 (NITI Aayog, 2018).
    National figures
    • Forest cover 21.76% (7,15,342.61 km²) + tree cover 3.41% (1,12,014.34 km²) = 25.17% of geographical area (82.7 million ha).
    • Forest cover +156.41 km²; forest + tree cover +1445.81 km² vs 2021 assessment.
    • Book's dense forest: 12.37% of geographical area; very dense 3.12%, moderately dense 9.36%. see flagUPPSCPCS Mains ’08
    • Dense forest = 57.34% (4,10,175.48 km²) of forest cover, not about 40%. National Forestry Action Programme aims at one-third of India under tree/forest cover.UPSC PYQUPSC ’05
    • Increase observed in very dense forest. Top three by forest cover increase: Mizoram 241.73, Gujarat 180.07, Odisha 151.89 km².
    • Highest forest cover increase inside RFA/GW: Mizoram 192.92, Odisha 118.17, Karnataka 93.14, West Bengal 64.79 km². Reasons: plantation and agro-forestry.
    • Forest + tree cover improvement credited to afforestation, better forest management, community participation, decrease in forest fires; top states Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan.
    • Northeast: forest cover down 327.30 km²; forest + tree cover 174394.70 km² = 67% of these states' area.
    • Recorded Forest Area (अभिलिखित वन क्षेत्र) 23.59% of India; recorded forest = area recorded as forest in government records.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’91
    State rankings
    • Largest forest cover by area: Madhya Pradesh (77073.44), then Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Maharashtra; MP also has largest recorded forest area.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papersUPPSC ×3PCS Pre ’00; PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; PCS Mains ’12
    • CORE CONCEPTHighest % of geographical area (states): Mizoram 85.34%, then Arunachal 78.67, Meghalaya 75.65, Manipur 74.29, Nagaland 73.72. Not Nagaland, as one option claimed.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS7 papersUPPSC ×7PCS Mains ’02, ’12, ’17; RO/ARO ’16; Lower Sub (Spl) ’08; UDA/LDA ’10; GIC ’10
    • Top five States/UTs by %: Lakshadweep, Mizoram, A&N Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya (all >75%).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS7 papers
    • 33–75%: Manipur, Nagaland, Tripura, Goa, Kerala, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Chhattisgarh, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, Assam, Odisha, Jammu & Kashmir (12 states/UTs; 17 in all above 33%, stated for ISFR 2021 in Q0599 and repeated p. 140).UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’21
    • Largest very dense forest: Arunachal 20,985.32 km² (Maharashtra 9865.62, Odisha 7224.42, MP 7021.31).UPPSCPCS Pre ’11
    • Least forest cover (by area and %) among states: Haryana.
    • Descending % (2019 → 2023): Manipur 75.46 → 74.29; Odisha 33.15 → 33.67; Maharashtra 16.50 → 16.53; Haryana 3.62 → 3.65.
    • Ascending % (ISFR 2023): Maharashtra 16.53, MP 25.00, Odisha 33.67, Chhattisgarh 41.28.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • RFA highest in Himachal Pradesh (68.16%) among that question's options (forest cover remains Mizoram).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS7 papers
    Forest fires
    • Fire season 2023-24: 203544 forest fires. Fire season 2020-21: around 3,45,989.
    • Severe fires in many forest types, especially dry deciduous; evergreen, semi-evergreen, montane temperate less prone.
    • States: Uttarakhand 21033, Odisha 20,973, Chhattisgarh 18,950; Andhra Pradesh 4th.
    • Districts: Gadchiroli (Maharashtra) 7042; Alluri Sitharama Raju (AP) 6399; Bijapur (Chhattisgarh) 5018.
    • Maximum fire-affected area: AP 5286.76, Maharashtra 4095.04, Telangana 3983.28 km². Highest % RFA/GW affected: Telangana 14.82, AP 13.94, Bihar 10.71.
    Source check Book's heading reads "Increase in forest fires" (p. 141), but its numbers fall from 3,45,989 (2020-21) to 203544 (2023-24), and p. 141 credits "a decrease in forest fires".
    Other findings
    • Hill districts: forest cover 40.00% of their area; 2023 increase 234.14 km².
    • Tribal districts (2021 assessment): 37.53% of their area; −655 km² inside RFA/GW, +600 km² outside.
    • Mangrove cover 4991.68 km²; down 7.43 km² vs 2021. Max increase: AP 13.01, Maharashtra 12.39, Karnataka 2.54 km².
    • Bamboo-bearing area 154670 km²; +5227 km² vs ISFR 2021.
    • Growing stock 6429.64 million m³ (4478.89 inside forest, 1950.75 outside recorded forest); +262.32 million m³.
    • Forest carbon stock 7,285.5 Mt; +81.5 Mt vs 2021; annual increase 40.75 Mt.
    • Soil organic carbon: largest pool; 55.06% of forest carbon.
    • Carbon stock by state: Arunachal 1021.16 Mt, MP 608.42 Mt, Chhattisgarh 504.61 Mt.

    Second largest mangrove area: Gujarat (1164.06 km²). Mangroves: shrubs or small trees of coastal saline water.

    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Give ISFR 2023 forest, tree and combined cover as % of geographical area.

      21.76 + 3.41 = 25.17. p. 140

    2. Give the four canopy classes with their thresholds.

      Very dense ≥70%; moderately dense 40–70%; open 10–40%; scrub <10%. p. 140

    3. Distinguish forest cover from recorded forest area in one sentence.

      Forest cover is canopy-based, ≥10% and ≥1 ha irrespective of ownership; recorded forest is what government records list as forest. pp. 140, 151

      Gujarat, 1164.06 km². p. 151

    IUCN

    IUCN's Red List tracks threatened species; Indian fauna questions test status, habitat and scientific names.

    • IUCN: established 1948; headquarters Gland, Switzerland; works on nature conservation and sustainable use of natural resources; seeks practical solutions to environmental and developmental challenges.
    • Red list gives information on endangered plants and animals.
    • At question time (2003), Indian crocodile and Asian Elephant both listed endangered. At present: Mugger (Crocodylus palustris) vulnerable; Asian Elephant endangered.UPSC PYQUPSC ’03
    • Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus; fish-eating Crocodilia): Ganga tributaries; mostly India and Nepal; most numbers in Chambal and Girwa. Best place to see it: Chambal river. IUCN: critically endangered.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Gharial, Leatherback turtle, Swamp deer: all in book's "endangered/threatened" group (IAS 2013).UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Kharai camel (swimming camel): only in Kutch, Gujarat; swims up to three km into sea for mangroves, its primary food; lives in coastal and dry ecosystems. Statement that it stays wild and can't be domesticated is wrong.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Recognised by National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources as a separate breed, one of nine in India (book p. 152 says "species" and calls it endangered); merchant community's livelihood depends on it.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16UPPSCPCS Mains ’13
    • Whale shark: India's largest fish, one of largest in world; up to 50 feet. Habitat: coasts of Australia and South Africa; comes to Gujarat coast March–May for gestation; protection programme 2004.UPPSCPCS Pre (Spl) ’08
    • Naturally in India: Star Tortoise, Monitor lizard, Pygmy hog. Not Spider monkey: tropical forests of Central and South America, southern Mexico to Brazil.UPSC PYQUPSC ’13
    • Pugmark technique estimates populations of wild animals; identifies animals by footprints ("Pug" means foot in Hindi); each individual species has a distinct pugmark.UPPSCPCS Mains ’08
    AnimalScientific name
    Onager (Asiatic wild Ass)Equus hemionusUPSC PYQUPSC ’02
    Swamp deer (Barasingha)Rucervus duvaucelii (Cervus duvauceli in Q)UPSC PYQUPSC ’02
    ChinkaraGazella bennettiiUPSC PYQUPSC ’02
    NilgaiBoselaphus tragocamelusUPSC PYQUPSC ’02

    1. Name IUCN's founding year and headquarters.

      1948; Gland, Switzerland. p. 152

    2. Which listed animal is not naturally found in India: Pygmy hog or Spider monkey?

      Spider monkey (Central and South America). p. 153

    3. Correct: "Kharai camel lives only in the wild."

      False. It is a recognised breed used by graziers, feeding on mangroves. p. 153

    4. State the IUCN status of the Gharial given in the book.

      Critically endangered. p. 152

    Indian efforts related to Conservation of Forest Resources

    India's framework joins wildlife and forest statutes, specialised bodies, people's movements and state schemes.

    • India: 2.4% of world's land; about 8% of known biodiversity; about 7.28% of world's animal species ('Faunal Diversity of India', J.R.B. Alfred). Q0644 marked (*): 8% and 7.28% match no single option.
    Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972
    • First comprehensive wildlife law; passed by Parliament; assented by President 9 September 1972. Protects wild animals in India; aims to stop illegal hunting and trafficking.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’15, ’16
    • Book: 66 sections in 7 chapters, 6 schedules. see update
    • Covers wild animals, birds and plants, not wild animals only.
    • Tiger is in Schedule I; a tortoise declared protected under Schedule I gets the same level of protection as the tiger.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Schedule VI plant: cultivation prohibited except under licence from Chief Wild Life Warden or an officer authorised by the State Government.UPSC PYQUPSC ’20
    • Gharial, Indian Wild Ass and Wild Buffalo can't be hunted by anyone except under provisions in law.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Section 39(1): every wild animal is State Government property; if hunted in a sanctuary or National Park declared by Central Government, Central Government property. Hence "property of the government" held correct.UPSC PYQUPSC ’22
    • Equal protection inside and outside protected areas. Capture/killing only if animal has become a danger to human life or is diseased/disabled beyond recovery, by Chief Wildlife Warden; mere apprehension of danger is not enough.UPSC PYQUPSC ’22

    Community reserves fall under protected areas with marine protected areas, National Parks, sanctuaries and conservation reserves.

    Verified update (checked Nov 2026) Book's 6 schedules is the pre-2022 position (p. 154). Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Bill passed Lok Sabha 2 Aug 2022, Rajya Sabha 8 Dec 2022: total schedules cut to four, vermin schedule removed, new schedule for CITES specimens. The page does not state the plant schedule's new number; check current text before quoting "Schedule VI". source
    Forest and environment statutes
    • Chronology: WLPA 1972 → Project Tiger (बाघ परियोजना) 1973 → Project Elephant (हाथी परियोजना) 1992 → Biological Diversity Act 2002.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’19, ’20
    • Forest Conservation Act 1980; Environment Protection Act 1986; Air Act 1981; Water Act 1974.UPPSCRO/ARO ’21
    • Forest (Conservation) Act (वन (संरक्षण) अधिनियम) enacted 27 December 1980; book: implemented from 25 October 1980.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’17; Lower Sub ’13
    • EPA 1986: lays down standards for emission/discharge of pollutants. Doesn't empower Government to state public-participation requirements.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • Indian Forest Act, 1927, as amended in 2017: bamboo grown in non-forest areas removed from definition of trees; tribals and poor farmers can use it economically.
    • Felling/transport permitted for bamboo grown on non-forest areas (Indian Forest (Amendment) Ordinance, 2017); the claim that forest dwellers may fell bamboo grown on forest areas is wrong.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006: minor forest produce = all non-timber forest produce of plant origin, including bamboo; ownership of MFP to forest dwellers.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • "Critical wildlife habitat" defined only in FRA 2006; Baigas first in India to get Habitat Rights; Ministry of Tribal Affairs (not MoEFCC) decides Habitat Rights for Primitive and Vulnerable Tribal Groups.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • New Forest Inventory Design (2016): revisit time cut from 20 years to 5.UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’17
    Verified update (checked Nov 2026) Forest (Conservation) Amendment Bill, 2023 passed Lok Sabha 26 Jul and Rajya Sabha 2 Aug 2023. It limits the Act to certain land, excludes land converted to non-forest use before 12 Dec 1996, exempts some border-security projects and small roadside amenities, and allows zoos, safaris and eco-tourism. Book's 1980 dates remain the original enactment. source
    Institutions
    BodyKey facts
    Forest Research InstituteDehradun, Uttarakhand; under ICFRE; est. 1906 as Imperial Forest Research Institute; deemed university by UGC, 1991; trained forest officers and rangers.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papers
    Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE)Apex body of national forestry research; HQ Dehradun; MoU with TIFAC for forest-based communities.
    IIFMBhopal; autonomous; est. 1982 under Ministry of Agriculture, later under Environment and Forest Ministry.
    Survey of IndiaNational survey and mapping body, set up 1767; under Department of Science and Technology; not an environment body.
    National Bureau of Plant Genetic ResourcesNew Delhi; est./rechristened 1977; plant introduction, germplasm augmentation; ten regional stations: Shimla, Jodhpur, Thrissur, Akola, Shillong, Bhowali, Cuttack, Hyderabad, Ranchi, Srinagar.
    Animal Welfare Board of IndiaStatutory advisory body; est. 1962 under Section 4, Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (not EPA 1986).UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    National Tiger Conservation AuthorityStatutory body under MoEFCC.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    National Ganga River Basin AuthoritySet up 20 February 2009; chaired by Prime Minister; Union Ministers concerned and Chief Ministers of Ganga states as members. Later dissolved → Ch 10.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    National Research Centre for Agroforestry (कृषि वानिकी)Jhansi, UP; unit of ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research) est. 1988; renamed Central Agroforestry Research Institute (CAFRI) December 2014; about 10 km from Jhansi station; "KRISHIVANIKI".
    National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board (NAEB)Set up 1992.
    People's movements and tribal practice
    • Chipko (चिपको आंदोलन) (1970s): against large-scale forest cutting (deforestation).REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Raini village, Joshimath (Chamoli): Forest Department auctioned about 680 ha; Gaura Devi led hundreds of women who clung to trees.
    • Chandi Prasad Bhatt: protagonist; founded the organisation that became Chipko's base; Ramon Magsaysay Award 1982.
    • Sundarlal Bahuguna: leading role; book accepts him as a leader of Chipko (MPPCS 2014).
    • Maiti Movement: Kalyan Singh Rawat, teacher at Government Inter College, began 1995 at Gwaldam. Newly-wed bride plants a sapling on leaving home ("mait" = married woman's parental home); groom gives parents money for its care.
    • Post-Kargil: women of Ochati village + Border Security Force raised a Maiti forest dedicated to soldiers: Shaurya Van (Gallantry Forest).
    • Gond and Korku: plant fruit-bearing saplings during a month-long ecological festival every year.UPSC PYQUPSC ’14
    Added concept
    • UPSC Prelims 2026 asked whether the yearly arrival of Amur Falcons at Doyang Lake, Nagaland, from Mongolia reflects sustained local conservation (statement 1), advanced tracking technology (2) or permanent residency in India (3). Coaching-consensus key: 1 only; no official answer seen; not in the book.UPSC 2026
    Source check Q0646 (MPPCS 2016): MPPSC held (c) Sunderlal Bahuguna; the book holds (d) Chandi Prasad Bhatt and says the commission is wrong (p. 160). Know both names; expect either as "leader".
    Awards, schemes and programmes
    • Rajiv Gandhi Wildlife Conservation Award: annual; two awards of Rupees One Lakh; for education and research institutions, organisations, forest and wildlife officers/research scholars/scientists, wildlife conservationists.UPPSCPCS Pre ’98
    • Amrita Devi Smriti award: Forest Department, Government of Rajasthan; cash award to individuals/institutions for wildlife protection.
    • SAVE (Saving Asia's Vultures from Extinction): 10-year programme launched February 2011 by RSPB (British Royal Society for the Protection of Birds), Zoological Society of London and Nepal government; vultures poisoned by medication in carrion.UPPSCPCS Mains ’11
    • "Apna Van Apna Dhan": Himachal Pradesh; promotes afforestation.UPPSCPCS Pre ’12
    • Mukhyamantri Jan Van Yojana: Jharkhand, under CM Raghubar Das: greener area, less pressure on notified forests, groundwater conservation through plantation, income from trees.
    • Mukhyamantri Vriksharopan Protsahan Yojana (Chhattisgarh): began 1 June 2021 (not 1 July); Rs. 10,000 per acre incentive; open to all farmers, village and joint forest management committees; CAMPA fund usable for high-tech nursery.
    • Jharkhand Wildlife Management Plan: 10 years, for wildlife sanctuaries.
    • Jharkhand Reserve Forests: all activities prohibited unless permitted. Latitude 22° 00' N–24° 37' N; longitude 83° 15' E–87° 01' E; area 79,716 km² (2.42% of India); RFA 25118 km² (Reserve Forest 4500 + Protected 18922 + Unclassed 1696), about 31.51%.
    • Project Elephant: launched February 1992, centrally sponsored; protects elephants, habitats, corridors; tackles man-animal conflict; welfare of domesticated elephants too (wild and captive, not wild only).UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’17
    • Green India Mission: one of eight missions under National Action Plan on Climate Change; launched February 2014.
    • UPPCS 2020 keys population growth as "not a major cause" of wildlife extinction; book names loss of natural habitat, forest fire and illegal trade as major, adding that population growth raises competition for food and shelter.UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    Source check Q0658's key (p. 162) sits uneasily with p. 137, where population growth drives forest loss. Treat it as that exam's key, not a general rule.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Put in sequence: Project Elephant, WLPA, Biological Diversity Act, Project Tiger.

      WLPA 1972, Project Tiger 1973, Project Elephant 1992, Biological Diversity Act 2002. p. 156

    2. Who declares and who manages a Community Reserve?

      State Government declares (s. 36C); Community Reserve Management Committee manages (s. 36D). p. 157

    3. Correct: "Animal Welfare Board of India was established under the EPA, 1986."

      False. Under Section 4 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, in 1962. p. 161

    4. Who led the Raini village protest and how?

      Gaura Devi; hundreds of women clung to trees. p. 160

    5. Which ministry decides Habitat Rights for PVTGs?

      Ministry of Tribal Affairs. p. 162

    Global efforts of the Conservation of Forest

    Global action spans land-use treaties, forest declarations, country-level forest shares and observance days.

    Forest area by country (World Bank 2022 est.)

    • Among China, India, Indonesia, Japan: Japan highest (68.4%).
    • Among Japan, Indonesia, Suriname, Guyana: Suriname highest (94.5%).
    • Bhutan: constitutional provision (Q0667: "resolution") to keep forest on at least 60% of land; about 71.6% forested (WB 2022 est.).UPPSCPCS Mains ’16
    Conventions and declarations
    • United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (मरुस्थलीकरण) (UNCCD), established 1994: sole legally binding international agreement linking environment and development to sustainable land management; drives SDG 15 and Land Degradation Neutrality.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • UNCCD aims at effective action through innovative national programmes and supportive international partnerships; bottom-up approach, local participation. No special South Asia/North Africa focus or allocation of funds to them.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • New York Declaration on Forests: first endorsed at UN Secretary-General's Climate Summit, New York, 2014; voluntary, not legally binding; cut natural forest loss in half by 2020, strive to end by 2030.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • Also calls for restoring forests and croplands larger than India's area; meeting goals cuts 4.5–8.8 billion tons carbon pollution a year (about current US emissions).UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • Endorsed by over 200 entities: more than 50 governments, 50 big companies, 50 civil society and indigenous organisations. Not endorsed by India.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    WWF, observance days and tiger forum
    • WWF (World Wide Fund for Nature, founded 1961): symbol Giant Panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca), for all endangered species able to thrive in their natural range.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papersUPPSC ×4PCS Pre ’01; PCS Mains ’02; Lower Sub (Spl) ’02, ’03
    • Giant Panda habitat: temperate broad-leaf and mixed forests of Southeast China (book's wording); about 1864 in China.
    • World Wildlife Day 3 March: proposed at CITES CoP 16 (March 2013); United Nations General Assembly 68th session decided 20 December 2013; 2025 theme "Wildlife Conservation Finance: Investing in People and Planet". Q0662 marked (*): date not among options.
    • India's Wildlife Week: 2nd to 8th October. World Environment Day: June 5. World Forestry Day/International Day of Forests: March 21.
    • First International Tiger Forum (World Tiger Summit): 21–24 November 2010, Saint Petersburg, Russia.UPPSCPCS Pre ’11
    Other tested points
    • Miyawaki method: creates mini forests in urban areas; fast forest cover on degraded land, using native trees and natural regeneration principles.UPSC PYQUPSC ’22
    • Hyderabad: recognised twice as Tree City of the World (2020 and 2021) by Arbor Day Foundation and FAO, not UNCDF. Statement 2 correct (commitment to grow and maintain urban forests). Mumbai recognised 2021.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • Arbor Day Foundation: non-profit, founded 1972 in Nebraska, USA, by John Rosenow; largest membership organisation for tree planting.UPSC PYQUPSC ’21
    • WWF founded 1961. June–July 2000: tigers in Nandankanan zoo died of Trypanosomiasis (statement said "13 lions"). Eucalyptus called environmental enemy, not friend. Biggest aquarium in India: Kolkata.
    • Desert plants: hard waxy leaves, tiny leaves, thorns all limit water loss; wax cuts evaporation. → Ch 10UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    Source check Q0668 (UPPCS 2002) is keyed (*): the book says no option fits; its text has tigers, not the statement's 13 lions, and calls eucalyptus an environmental enemy (p. 165).
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Name the sole legally binding land-degradation treaty and its year.

      UNCCD, 1994. p. 164

    2. Is the New York Declaration binding, and did India endorse it?

      Not binding; India did not endorse. p. 164

    3. Which three days fall on March 21, March 3 and June 5?

      International Day of Forests; World Wildlife Day; World Environment Day. pp. 162–163

    4. Explain what the Miyawaki method does in one sentence.

      It builds quick mini forests on degraded land using native trees, following natural regeneration. p. 163

    Sanctuary/Biosphere Reserve · अभयारण्य एवं जैवमंडल आरक्षित क्षेत्र

    National Park (राष्ट्रीय उद्यान)

    Protected areas (संरक्षित क्षेत्र) are a principal method of conserving biodiversity. National Parks are the strictest category; sanctuaries allow limited activity.

    National Park vs Sanctuary vs Biosphere Reserve (जैवमंडल आरक्षित क्षेत्र)
    • NP eligibility: rich biodiversity, almost pristine habitat; of ecological, faunal, floral, geomorphological and hydrological importance; needs protection and conservation.
    • BR: representative parts of natural and cultural landscapes over a large area of terrestrial or coastal/marine ecosystems.UPSC PYQUPSC ’10
    Source check Book says Biosphere Reserves "entertain no human activity in their sphere" (p.167). Its own banner on that page allows settlements and crop cultivation in the transition zone (संक्रमण क्षेत्र), grazing and tourism in the buffer, and p.170 says each reserve reconciles conservation with sustainable use. Only the core is free of human activity.
    Jim Corbett National Park
    • CORE CONCEPT India's first and oldest NP: established 1936 as Hailey National Park; first NP in mainland Asia.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS7 papers
    • Renamed after James Edward Corbett, noted hunter turned conservationist.
    • Uttarakhand: NP in Nainital district. Corbett Tiger Reserve (बाघ आरक्षित क्षेत्र) spans Pauri, Nainital, Almora.
    • NP 521 km²; Tiger Reserve 1288.31 km² after additions.
    • Project Tiger launched here, 1973.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS7 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’02, ’18
    • Fauna: Royal Bengal Tiger, Asiatic Elephant, reptiles, birds.
    • Corbett and Rajaji use remote sensing and GIS for wildlife management; book's answer: small-scale aerial photographs suit this.

    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Who may alter a National Park's boundary, and how does this differ from a sanctuary's permitted activity?

      Only on a State Legislature resolution. A park allows no human activity except as the Chief Wildlife Warden permits; a sanctuary allows limited activity. p. 170

    2. Correct this: "Biosphere Reserves are declared to conserve a few specific species."

      False. They conserve in situ all forms of life with their support system. p. 170

    3. Reconstruct Rajaji's formation with years.

      Rajaji 1948, Motichur 1964, Chilla 1977 merged 1983; Tiger Reserve 2015. p. 168

    4. Name the rivers of Corbett and the park's original name.

      Ramganga and Kosi; Hailey National Park (1936). pp. 167–168

    Biosphere Reserve

    Biosphere reserves conserve genetic variation of species while reconciling conservation with sustainable use, through concentric zones.

    Concept and zones
    • "Biological diversity": first used by Raymond F. Dasmann, 1968, in A Different Kind of Country. Contracted form "biodiversity": coined by W.G. Rosen, 1985.
    • BR programme: effective method of conserving genetic variation of species. Reserves cover terrestrial, marine and coastal ecosystems.
    • Core area(s): strictly protected ecosystem conserving landscapes, ecosystems, species, genetic variation.
    • India: 18 BRs set up by MoEFCC, 12 within UNESCO-MAB (book's position).
    • Keyed pair (UPPCS 2013): Biosphere reserves – Edward Suess; the other three pairs were wrong as printed (see note).UPPSCPCS Pre ’13
    Source check "Biosphere reserve" first used by Edward Suess (p.183, the keyed answer). Not verified against an outside source here; treat as the exam key, and check before quoting. On "biodiversity", p.183 credits Dasmann alone, while p.182 separates Dasmann ("biological diversity") from Rosen (the contraction). On p.183 "Ecology" is credited to Reiter and Ernst Haeckel; Ecosystem to A.G. Tansley.
    UNESCO-MAB list
    Verified update (checked Nov 2026) Book: 12 of 18 in the World Network. PIB (3 Nov 2025): India has 18 notified BRs (about 91,425 km²), 13 recognised by UNESCO, after the Cold Desert BR was included in September 2025. PIB
    • IAS 2008 framed four reserves on the network (then Nilgiri, Gulf of Mannar, Sunderbans, Nanda Devi). Marked (*) because the list has since grown to include Khangchendzonga.UPSC PYQUPSC ’08
    • Rann of Kachchh: not in UNESCO's network.
    • Nanda Devi BR: around Nanda Devi peak, Uttarakhand; on the World Network.
    • COMMON TRAP Nanda Devi BR is a World Heritage Site (UNESCO, 1988; extended to Valley of Flowers 2005) as well as a MAB reserve (2004): two different lists.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’08; PCS Mains ’05
    • Agasthyamala BR contains Neyyar, Peppara and Shendurney WLS, and Kalakad Mundanthurai Tiger Reserve.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • Latest in RAS 2010: Cold Desert (added 2009), as at question time.

    Rhino, Manas and flagship claims
    • One-horned rhino: found in West Bengal and Assam.
    • Kaziranga: famous for one-horned rhino; hosts two-thirds of the world's Great One-horned rhinoceros. On the Brahmaputra bank, 889.51 km²; mainly Rhino and Elephant.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS3 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’12
    • Kanha, Ranthambhore, Bandhavgarh: part of Project Tiger. Kaziranga was not a Tiger Reserve in 1997 (hence *), but has been since 2007.
    • Manas (Assam): famous for Tigers and Rhinos; among the first reserves under Project Tiger (1973-74). Also Elephant Reserve and BR.UPPSCPCS Mains ’13
    • Manas: Natural World Heritage (UNESCO, 1985); World Heritage in danger 1992; removed from danger list 21 June 2011.
    • Periyar Game Sanctuary, Kerala: famous for wild elephants.UPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’11, ’14
    Source check Book says "Gir, Ranthambore and Corbett are famous for Tigers" (p.189). Gir is the Asiatic Lion's habitat on pp.168, 170 and 191; do not learn Gir as a tiger site.
    Uttarakhand sanctuaries

Established for endangered Himalayan musk deer (कस्तूरी मृग) (Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary). Snow leopards (हिम तेंदुआ), Indian leopards, jackals, Himalayan black bear, yellow-throated marten, red fox. Gauri Kund–Temple trek route
    Nanda DeviUpper Himalaya; Chamoli, Pithoragarh, Bageshwar. With Valley of Flowers on UNESCO WH list; unique transition between Zanskar range and Great Himalaya. Snow leopard, Himalayan musk deer, Asiatic black bear, Himalayan brown bear, bharal, Himalayan tahr, plants
    BinsarErstwhile summer capital of Chand Dynasty (ruled Kumaon, 7th to 18th century AD); 2,420 m
    Askot (Musk Deer Sanctuary)54 km (34 mi) from Pithoragarh; to conserve musk deer (Moschus leucogaster) and habitatUPSC PYQUPSC ’20

    Kuno and sites outside India
    • CORE CONCEPT Palpur-Kuno WLS, Sheopur, MP (near Palpur): selected for Asiatic Lion reintroduction; lions hunted to extinction there about 1873.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • March 2017: environment ministry expert committee approved translocating Asiatic Lions from Gir to Kuno Palpur as a second home. Contested by Gujarat (book's dated position). Kuno listed as NP (2018) in the MP table.REPEATED · ALL EXAMSUPSC ’17 · 2 papers
    • Suklaphanta/Shuklaphanta: south-west Nepal, Terai, 305 km²; Wildlife Reserve 1976; NP 2017.UPPSCPCS Mains ’16
    • Sakteng WLS: in Bhutan; China has claimed territory around it as "disputed".
    Source check Suklaphanta: "Kanchan district" (p.189) vs "Kanchanpur district" (p.193); hunting "prohibited in 1969" (p.189) vs "banned for hunting till 1969" (p.193). Book is inconsistent on both.

    Project Tiger

    India's pioneering tiger programme: a viable population in natural habitats, protected from extinction.

    Launch, aims and numbers
    • CORE CONCEPT Project Tiger launched 1 April 1973; tiger conservation programme to save the national animal from extinction.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’94
    • International Tiger Day: 29 July; decided at Saint Petersburg Tiger Summit, 2010.UPPSCPCS Mains ’14
    • India: 3682 tigers (tiger census 2022, MoEFCC), highest in the world.
    • Census 2018 detailed report (July 2020): India has 70% of world tigers; nearly 30% of India's tigers live outside tiger reserves.UPPSCPCS Pre ’20
    • Madhya Pradesh has the highest tiger population.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS4 papers
    • Natural range: Asiatic lion only in India (Gir). One-horned rhino in India and Nepal. Double-humped (Bactrian) camel native to Central Asia; in India, Nubra Valley.UPSC PYQUPSC ’19
    • International Biodiversity Day 22 May; theme 2022 "Building a shared future for all life"; 2024 "Be Part of the Plan". The statement calling it National biodiversity was keyed wrong.
    Source check Book puts the world tiger population at 3000–4000 (p.196) while India alone has 3682 and "70%" of world tigers (p.200). These cannot all stand together; use India's 3682 and treat the world range as the book's unreconciled figure.
    Source check (*) keys, launch and count: UPPCS 2018 options omit 1973; MPPSC 1994 (all four parks are listed, so no "not listed" option); BPSC 1995 (none of the options fits).
    M-STrIPES and drones
    • M-STrIPES: Monitoring system for Tigers – Intensive Protection and Ecological Status; software-based monitoring across tiger reserves; in the news in the context of their maintenance.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Two components: (a) field protocols for patrolling, law enforcement, recording wildlife crimes, ecological monitoring; (b) customised software for storage, retrieval, analysis, reporting.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Gives interpretable reports and maps for management and policy; managers assess intensity and spatial coverage of patrols in a GIS-based tool.
    • Cuts response time to poaching or habitat degradation.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Bandipur Tiger Reserve (Karnataka) monitored by drones/unmanned aerial vehicles; better than traditional on-land monitoring.

    Miscellaneous

    Project Elephant, UNESCO World Heritage sites, wetland and river links, and stray facts.

    Project Elephant and elephant biology
    • Launched 1992 by MoEF as a centrally sponsored scheme: long-term survival of elephants; protect elephants, habitats, migration corridors; address man-animal conflict; welfare of captive elephants. Financial and technical support to major elephant-bearing States. UPPCS 2007 options omit 1992 (*).
    • Census 2017: synchronised population about 29964.
    • Karnataka highest (6,049), then Assam (5,719), Kerala (5,706), census 2017.UPSC PYQUPSC ’20
    • Group leader: generally a female. Gestation 18–22 months, longest of all mammals. First birth at 16–17 years; can calve until 60 or more.UPSC PYQUPSC ’20
    • Order Proboscidea. African: Loxodonta africana. Asian/Indian: Elephas maximus.
    • Asian elephant passage (IAS 1999, dated): India has the largest population; about 20,000 to 25,000 in natural habitat; evergreen forests, dry thorn forest, swamps, grasslands; prime habitat moist deciduous forests. North-West (Dehradun, Nainital; Bijnor), Western Ghats (Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu), Central (Southern Bihar, Orissa), East (North Bengal, Assam).UPSC PYQUPSC ’99
    Verified update (checked Nov 2026) Book: 29964 (2017). DNA-based SAIEE 2021–25 estimates 22,446 (range 18,255–26,645); Karnataka 6,013, Assam 4,159. Scientists say this is not comparable with past estimates, so do not read it as a decline. Mongabay

    Non-Conventional Energy · गैर-परंपरागत ऊर्जा

    Energy and Energy Resources

    Energy is either renewable (non-conventional (गैर-परंपरागत)) or non-renewable (conventional). Fossil fuels (जीवाश्म ईंधन) are stored ancient solar energy (सौर ऊर्जा).

    • Two categories: Renewable = Non Conventional; Non Renewable = Conventional.UPPSCPCS Pre ’23
    • Renewable energy (नवीकरणीय ऊर्जा): from sources naturally replenishing over a relatively short period but flow-limited; virtually inexhaustible in duration, limited in energy available per unit time. Solar and wind electricity qualify; thermal-plant and coal electricity do not.
    • Renewables replenish faster than consumed. Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) take hundreds of millions of years to form; burning them emits GHGs such as CO₂.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Fossil fuels: from decomposition of buried plants or dead organisms over millions of years. Non-renewable; major energy source at present; once used, cannot be recovered. Examples: coal, natural gas, petroleum. COMMON TRAP Uranium is not a fossil fuel.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSCPCS Pre ’21
    • Ultimate source of energy stored in fossil fuels: Sun.UPPSCRO/ARO (Re-exam) ’16
    • Energy crisis: danger of exhaustion of fossil fuels such as crude oil, natural gas, coal, petrol.
    • Uranium: raw material for nuclear power. Nuclear energy (नाभिकीय ऊर्जा) comes from the nucleus of an atom through Nuclear Fusion or Nuclear Fission.
    • UPPCS 2022 key: nuclear energy is not a biomass (जैवभार) source; usually treated as non-renewable, most often using uranium.UPPSCPCS Pre ’22
    • Biomass feedstocks: dedicated energy crops, agricultural crop residues, forestry residues, algae, wood processing residues, municipal waste, wet waste (food waste, industrial wastes, sorted municipal solid waste [MSW], urban wood waste, purpose-grown grasses, woody energy crops).
    • UN General Assembly unanimously declared 2014–2024 the "Decade of Sustainable Energy for All"; the Sustainable Energy for All initiative supports it.UPPSCPCS Pre ’17
    • Sustainable energy is SDG 7 of the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals: affordable, reliable, sustainable, modern energy for all by 2030.
    • UPRO/ARO 2021 key: solar is the second most important source after fossil fuels for Indian energy need; book puts solar's share in total non-fossil fuel at about 12.5 per cent (no year given).UPPSCRO/ARO ’21
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Fill the figure: name the two non-renewable sources besides coal, petroleum and natural gas.

      Atomic energy and shale gas. p. 206

    2. Correct this: "Uranium is a fossil fuel."

      Uranium is a raw material for nuclear power, not a fossil fuel. pp. 206–207

    3. Why is the Sun the ultimate source of the energy in coal?

      Fossil fuels formed from dead organisms whose stored energy came from solar radiation. p. 207

    Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Resources

    India's renewable mix has flipped from wind-led (2014–15) to solar-led (2025); 2030 targets rest on non-fossil capacity.

    Source check Same five 2025 figures are dated 28.02.2025 in the chapter banner (p.206) and "April, 2025" in the text (p.208). Quote them as early 2025. Later official figures could not be opened in this pass.
    • Examples of renewable sources: solar, wind, tidal, hydroelectric.
    • Best electricity source for sustainable development, among coal, mineral oil, gas, atomic energy: hydroelectricity, as it uses water without depleting it (UPPCS 2012; comparison limited to those options).UPPSCPCS Pre ’12
    • Chhattisgarh's major power source: thermal.
    • 2030 goals per book: reduce carbon intensity, 50 percent cumulative electric power installed from renewables, net zero carbon emission by 2070, 500 GW of renewable energy capacity. → Ch 4
    Source check Wording drifts. p.208: carbon intensity "be less than 45%" and 500 GW "renewable"; p.109: 500 GW "non-fossil", 50% of "total energy requirement"; p.118 INDC frames intensity as a percentage reduction from 2005 level. Read 45% as a reduction, and check whether a question says energy or installed power capacity.
    Test Your Memory — Original Practice

    1. Which renewable led India in 2014–15, and with what share?

      Wind, 58.54%. p. 208

    2. Why did the book call hydro best for sustainable development?

      It generates electricity without depleting water, unlike finite coal, oil, gas and atomic fuel. p. 208

    3. Fill in: India's net-zero year is __; its renewable target is __ GW by 2030.

      2070; 500 GW. p. 208

    Alternative Energy/Solar Energy

    Sun is the largest alternative source. Exams focus on ISA facts, DCR and India's solar "firsts".

    Solar basics
    • Sun: most comprehensive, unlimited source; Solar Energy is a renewable resource from solar radiation and the largest source (storehouse) of alternative energy.
    • Most used in organic form: essential for Photosynthesis and survival of living organisms.UPPSCPCS Mains ’04
    • Technologies: solar heating, photovoltaics, solar thermal; broadly passive or active, by how energy is captured and distributed or converted.
    • Solar cell (सौर सेल) (photovoltaic cell): converts light directly into electricity by the photovoltaic effect; most eco-friendly of the given options.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×4PCS Pre ’15, ’18; PCS Mains ’06; Lower Sub ’04
    • No atmospheric pollution during conversion of solar to electrical energy; pollution-free source.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Solar power has the greatest renewable potential in India; panels called the fuel of the future.UPPSCPCS Mains ’11
    • Conveniently used for street lighting, minor irrigation, hot water to residential buildings, railway signal, solar cooker.UPSC PYQUPSC ’96
    • IAS 1996 position: electrifying clusters of villages and small towns was not cost-effective; a few pilot projects only (dated).UPSC PYQUPSC ’96
    • Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE): 50% subsidy on installation cost of a solar plant in North-Eastern States.
    International Solar Alliance (ISA)
    • Launched at UN Climate Change Conference, Paris, 30 November 2015, by PM Narendra Modi and then President of France Francois Hollande (then UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon present).UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Sun-rich countries lying fully or partially between Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. As at the IAS 2016 question it did not include all UN members.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Headquarters/Secretariat: Gurugram, Haryana.
    • Target: raise USD 1 trillion for solar energy by 2030.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • First ISA Summit: New Delhi, 11 March 2018. 2nd: New Delhi, 31 October 2019.
    • Sixth Assembly: New Delhi, 30 October–2 November 2023; Seventh: November 2024, Delhi.
    • Pact with Asian Development Bank (March 2018) to promote solar deployment in Asia and Pacific.
    Source check Membership differs inside the book: 122 (104 Members + 18 Signatories) on p.209; "about 116+" on p.210. p.209 says countries "located between" the Tropics; p.210 says "fully or partially". Later ISA pages could not be opened in this pass, so eligibility and current count need a fresh check.
    Missions, DCR and tariffs
    • National Solar Mission: part of NAPCC → Ch 4; aims to make India a global leader in solar; renamed Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM), January 2010.
    • Domestic Content Requirement (DCR): relates to developing solar production. Both solar photovoltaic (SPV) cells and modules must be made in India, to MNRE specifications and testing; for crystalline Silicon, all process steps at PV manufacturers' works in India.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Target (2018 question): 175 GW renewable by 2022 = 100 GW solar + 60 GW wind + 10 GW bio-power + 5 GW small hydro. Target date has passed; book gives no outcome.
    • IAS 2018 (both rejected; position as at 2018): India was not third in Silicon Wafers; panels were only assembled here with material from China, Europe etc. Solar tariffs are set by Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC), not Solar Energy Corporation of India.UPSC PYQUPSC ’18
    • Highest installed solar capacity as on March 2023 (MPPSC 2025 key): Rajasthan.
    Source check For Q0898 the book's support is generation in January 2025 (MU: Rajasthan 3854.00, Gujarat 1822.79, Karnataka 1455.99, Tamil Nadu 1223.51; Monthly Renewable Energy Generation Report), not installed capacity at March 2023. Key stands; the table does not prove it.
    Added concept Not in the book.
    • UPSC 2025 (reported official key: all three correct): PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana targets one crore solar rooftop panels in the residential sector; MNRE aims to train at grassroot levels on installation, operation, maintenance and repairs; aims at more than three lakhs skilled manpower through fresh skilling and up-skilling.UPSC 2025
    Solar firsts and largest
    • Cochin International Airport (Kochi), Kerala: first airport in the world powered entirely by solar; first Indian international airport developed under Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Model.UPPSCPCS Mains ’17
    • Surat, Gujarat: first district with 100% solar-powered Primary Health Centres (PHC): all 52, as on 26 March 2018.
    • Diu: first Union Territory to run 100 percent on solar; plants on more than 50 acres in 2018.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papersUPPSC ×2PCS Pre ’19; RO/ARO ’17
    • Diu Smart City: first Indian city on 100 percent renewable energy during daytime.
    • Bhadla Solar Park: world's largest (approx 14,000 acres), Phalodi tehsil, Jodhpur district, Rajasthan. So "Gujarat has India's largest" was rejected (UPPCS 2022).
    • India's largest floating solar: Ramagundam, Telangana, 100 megawatt (MW), by National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) through Bharat Heavy Electricals (BHEL) under Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC); not Goa (as at UPPCS 2022).
    Source check p.209 calls the Tamil Nadu plant at "Kameethi", Ramnathapuram, the "world's largest solar plant at a single location"; p.212 calls Bhadla the world's largest solar park. No dates given for the first. Treat "largest" claims as time-bound.

    1. Where and when was ISA launched, and where is its secretariat?

      Paris, 30 November 2015; Gurugram. p. 209

    2. Explain what DCR demands of solar projects.

      Both cells and modules must be made in India. p. 211

    3. Correct this: "The Solar Energy Corporation of India determines solar tariffs."

      Book credits the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission. p. 212

    4. Match: Surat, Diu, Bhadla, Ramagundam.
