    Miscellaneous · विविध

    Agenda 21 and other Conventions

    One UN plan, one disarmament body, Indian quality marks and two cooperation instruments.

    Agenda 21
    • Agenda 21 = legally non-binding, voluntarily implemented UN action plan on sustainable development.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Aim: conserve the world's environment in the 21st century.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Product of UNCED (United Nations Conference on Environment and Development, the Earth Summit), Rio-de-Janeiro, Brazil, 1992.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS2 papers
    • Structure: 40 chapters grouped into 4 sections.
    Source check Page count differs inside p. 263: note says 351, explanation says 350. Q on p. 263 asks how many "agreements" (key 4); explanation on p. 264 says "4 agreement in Agenda-2021". The 4 are the book's sections or groups, so read that key as "4 sections", not 4 treaties.
    OPCW
    • Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons: intergovernmental; implementing body of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC, in force 29 April 1997).
    • Headquarters: The Hague, Netherlands. Members: 193 countries (book's "currently"), 98% of global population and landmass.
    • Mission: world free of chemical weapons and the threat of their use.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Credible, transparent verification of destruction; prevents re-emergence, monitoring chemical industry, while protecting legitimate national security and proprietary interests.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Gives assistance and protection to States Parties against chemical weapons threats.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Also: peaceful uses of chemistry; universal membership through international cooperation and national capacity building.
    • Book: Hundred percent of declared stockpiles of possessor states verifiably destroyed.
    • 2013 Nobel Peace Prize for "extensive efforts to eliminate chemical weapons".
    • COMMON TRAP OPCW is not an organisation of the European Union working with NATO and WHO; that statement was false.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    Standards and quality marks
    Mark or lawFacts
    Indian Standards Institution (ISI)Set up January 1947; organised start of industrial development, consumer protection and standards formation.
    Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)National Standards Organization of India; BIS Act 1986, in force 1987; aim: standardization, symbolization of objects, quality certificate.
    ISI markMain BIS symbol; on processed food and daily-use goods such as electric equipment, cement, iron pipes.
    BIS standard mark on tyres and tubesMandatory for automotive tyres and tubes; pneumatic tyres for two and three-wheeled motor vehicles need ISI Certification before launch or import into India. Granted only to product manufacturers (Indian or foreign), not to traders, dealers or distributors.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    AGMARK ActAgricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937; grading and marking of agriculture and other produce; in force 1937.
    AGMARK markIssued by Directorate of Marketing and Inspection, Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (not FAO). Directorate set up 1935; categorises and symbolises food products.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    Eco-MarkGovernment of India eco-labelling scheme, 1991; easy identification of environment-friendly products. Drugs and Antibiotics are not in the list (soaps and detergents, paper and plastics, cosmetics and aerosols were the other options).

    Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011: every package carries (1) name of food, (2) List of Ingredients, (3) Nutritional information, (4) Energy value in Kcal, (5) protein, carbohydrate (specify sugar) and fat in gram or ml, (6) any nutrient with a nutrition or health claim, (7) vegetarian or non-vegetarian declaration, (8) food additives declaration. Key: ingredients including additives, nutrition, veg/non-veg are mandatory; a "medical profession recommendation on allergy" is not.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16

    UN-Habitat and Asian Rhinos
    • United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat): UN agency for human settlements and sustainable urban development; established 1978, Nairobi, capital of Kenya.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Mandated by UN General Assembly: socially and environmentally sustainable towns and cities, adequate shelter for all.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Contributes to UN objective of reducing poverty and promoting access to safe drinking water and basic sanitation.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • COMMON TRAP Partners are not only governments and local municipal authorities; also private and non-governmental partners.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • "New Delhi Declaration on Asian Rhinos 2019": five rhino range nations = India, Nepal, Malaysia, Indonesia, Bhutan.
    • Second Asian Rhino Range Countries meeting, 26–28 February 2019, New Delhi; organised by MoEFCC with IUCN Asian Rhino Specialist Group, WWF-India and Aaranyak.
    Added concept Not in the book; from the recent-paper file.
    • Nature Solutions Finance Hub for Asia and the Pacific: launched by the Asian Development Bank (ADB), as per the reported official key for UPSC Prelims 2025.UPSC 2025

    Disaster Management (आपदा प्रबंधन)

    Global decades, the Indian statutory ladder, phases of management, and hazard facts.

    Global decades and alliances
    • UN General Assembly designated 1990–99 as International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction (IDNDR).
    • Objective: cut loss of life, property destruction, social and economic disruption from earthquakes (भूकंप), tsunamis, floods, landslides (भूस्खलन), volcanic eruptions, droughts and other natural disasters.
    • 2021–2030: United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration.
    • International Drought Resilience Alliance (IDRA): launched by Spain with Senegal at UNFCCC COP27, November 2022; first announced by Spain at the 77th UN General Assembly, September 2022. (COP 28: Nov–Dec 2023, Dubai.)
    Source check IDNDR question (p. 277) is marked "Ans. (*)": none of its options (1991–2000 etc.) matches the book's 1990–99.
    Disaster Management Act and authorities
    • Disaster Management Act: passed 2005 (enacted 23 December 2005), for efficient management of disasters; book: came into force January 2006.
    • Act envisaged NDMA headed by the Prime Minister and SDMAs headed by Chief Ministers, for a holistic, integrated approach.
    • NDMA = apex body: lays down policies, plans and guidelines for timely and effective response.
    • DDMA: headed by District Magistrate or District Collector, as the case may be.
    • Section 14(1): book says it empowers the Governor to establish a State Disaster Management Authority, after notification under Section 3(1).
    • National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM): New Delhi; book dates founding to 1995 (named National Center for Disaster Management, NCDM, on p. 274).
    • Book: National Disaster Management Institute established under the Disaster Management Act, 2005.
    • SRIJAN (Development of Disaster Management Knowledge-cum-Demonstration Centre): creates such centres, spreads awareness, provides local need-based information.
    • Designed for disasters such as drought, flood, forest fire; a major centre for local information, communication and technology equipment.
    Source check NDMA "formed": key says 2005 (p. 277) but the explanation says it was notified on 27 September 2006 through the DM Act, 2005 (p. 278). Remember both: Act 2005, notification 2006, and read the year asked.
    Phases and vulnerability
    • Book's five main phases: prevention, preparedness, response, mitigation, recovery.
    • CORE CONCEPT Reconstruction is a post-disaster measure.
    • India is prone to many natural and man-made disasters: droughts, floods, earthquakes, cyclones (चक्रवात), avalanches.
    • Floods are the most common natural disaster in India; heavy southwest monsoon rain makes the Brahmaputra and other rivers extend their banks.
    • Bhopal gas tragedy was man-made; mangroves reduce cyclone impact; natural disasters cause maximum damage in developing countries.UPPSCPCS Pre ’18
    Added concept Mains prompts not treated in the book; they state what was asked, with no model answer.
    • GS-III 2026: managing the contradiction between rapid infrastructure development and disaster-risk reduction in ecologically-sensitive areas of India, with examples.UPSC 2026
    • GS-III 2026: "Community participation is the cornerstone of effective disaster management": analyse with Indian examples; challenges to participation and measures to strengthen it.UPSC 2026
    Source check Book prints key (c) for this set (p. 278) but also says the Hindi version made statement 3 read "India is a disaster-prone country", so UPPSC removed the question from evaluation. Treat it as deleted; India is not disaster-free.
    Tsunamis and hurricanes
    • Tsunami: series of large waves from abrupt ocean-floor movement.
    • Causes: earthquake, underwater landslide, volcanic eruption, very rarely a large meteorite strike; powerful undersea (submarine) earthquakes cause most.
    • Hurricane Sandy (2012) struck the north-east and east coast of the USA; Katrina, Wilma (book: Vilma) and Rita were 2005.UPPSCRO/ARO Mains ’14

    Biodiversity, Parks and Species

    Stray "Various Facts" on megadiversity, productivity, protected areas, fossils and particular plants and animals.

    Megadiverse countries
    • Megadiverse countries: world's top biodiversity-rich countries, where maximum species are found.
    • American non-profit Conservation International identified 17 in 1998.
    • The 17: U.S.A., Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, Brazil, Democratic Republic of Congo, South Africa, Madagascar, India, Malaysia, Indonesia, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, China, Australia.
    Primary productivity
    • Primary productivity: rate at which photosynthetic and chemosynthetic autotrophs convert energy to organic substances.
    • Total productivity in a region or system = gross primary productivity.
    • Lowest mean net primary productivity among the four biomes below: temperate grasslands.UPPSCPCS Pre (Re-exam) ’15
    Source check Book prints these as "gm per cm² per year" (pp. 274, 280). Grams per square centimetre would be implausibly high for any ecosystem, so read the values as relative magnitudes and confirm the area unit from a standard ecology text.

    • Anthropogenic biomes (anthromes, human biomes): terrestrial biosphere in its contemporary, human-altered form, as units defined by sustained direct human interaction.
    • Cropland is an anthropogenic biome; crop field, park, aquarium, garden are anthropogenic ecosystems.
    • Afforestation: increases greenery and atmospheric oxygen; reduces air pollution, global warming and soil erosion.UPSC PYQUPSC ’09
    Climate, soils and earth history
    • 'Vegetation is the true index of climate': Koppen Climate Classification, Wladimir Petrovich Koppen; first published 1900, revised 1918.UPPSCPCS Pre ’18
    • Koppen: Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are Cwg. Book: Aw covers south India; Dfc covers Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and parts of Assam.
    • Winterline: from mid October to January at sunset, the western horizon turns yellow, red, orange and mauve; book: unique to Mussoorie and a part of Switzerland.
    • Book's key: glaciation of peninsular India occurred in the Pleistocene Ice Age.UPPSCUDA/LDA Mains (Spl) ’10
    • Soil order: most general level of USDA (United States Department of Agriculture) Soil Taxonomy.
    • India, ICAR-USDA, decreasing area, per book's key: Entisols > Alfisols > Aridisols > Ultisols.
    • Explanation's shares are world, not India: Entisols about 16%, Alfisols about 12%, Aridisols about 10% of ice-free land.
    • Entisols occur on recently deposited parent materials, or where erosion or deposition outpaces soil development: dunes, steep slopes, flood plains.
    Source check Key on p. 285 says Pleistocene, with only a one-line explanation. A geology overview instead dates glacial deposits across central India to Permo-Carboniferous glaciations, which matches option (b), Carboniferous. Treat this key as doubtful. source
    Energy terms
    • Net metering: domestic or commercial users generating their own electricity through solar panels or photovoltaic systems export surplus energy to the grid.UPSC PYQUPSC ’16
    • Domestic Content Requirement (DCR): provided for developing solar power production in India.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • National Solar Policy (earlier Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission), January 2010; aim: India as global solar leader; solar utilities and batteries manufactured in India used for projects.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • First phase: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy gives 30% subsidy on decentralized solar devices such as lighting equipment, water heating equipment or solar coolers.UPSC PYQUPSC ’17
    • Natural gas: colourless, odourless, environment-friendly hydrocarbon mixture, primarily Methane.UPPSCPCS Pre ’18
    Instruments and techniques
    • SODAR (Sonic Detection and Ranging): meteorological instrument used as wind profiler, measuring scattering of sound waves by atmospheric turbulence and wind speed at various heights.
    • In India, SODAR is established at Kaiga, Kalpakkam, Tarapur and Trombay.
    • Helium: inert gas filled in balloons for weather science dispatch.
    • LANDSAT: data for an area adjacent to the west comes after a certain number of days at the same local time, due to the satellite's revolution around the earth.
    • DNA barcode: unique DNA sequence pattern, like a universal product code (UPC); non-experts can objectively identify species even from small, damaged or industrially processed material.
    • COMMON TRAP It distinguishes look-alike species and detects undesirable plant or animal material in processed foods; it does not assess the age of an organism.
    • Used for food authentication, especially fish and seafood, where species outnumber cattle, sheep, goat, horse; also exposed contaminants in roasted barley tea (Hordeum vulgare) exported from China and returned.
    Stray items
    • Uttar Pradesh's first biotech park: Lucknow; Department of Biotechnology (जैव प्रौद्योगिकी) (DBT) partnership since 2003.REPEATED · ALL EXAMS5 papersUPPSC ×5PCS Mains ’05, ’08, ’10, ’11; UDA/LDA Mains ’10
    • India's largest 'Charkha': made of waste plastic, inaugurated in Noida on the eve of Mahatma Gandhi's 150th birth anniversary.UPPSCPCS Pre ’19
    • Blue Flag Certification: eight Indian beaches across five states and two union territories, by a jury of UNEP, UNWTO (United Nations World Tourism Organization), FEE (Foundation for Environment Education) and IUCN.
    • The eight: Shivrajpur (Dwarka, Gujarat), Ghoghla (Diu), Kasarkod (book: Kararkod) and Padubidri (Karnataka), Kappad (Kerala), Rushikonda (Andhra Pradesh), Radhanagar (Andaman & Nicobar Islands), Golden beach (Puri, Odisha).
    • Book's 2023 count: 12 Blue Flag beaches in India; they give community pride and attract tourism.

Exam codes: UK = Uttarakhand, CG = Chhattisgarh, JPSC = Jharkhand, RAS = Rajasthan, UP-LS = Lower Subordinate, UP-RO = RO/ARO. Priority is revision guidance, not a prediction.

    Latest UPPSC Questions (2021–2025)

    The newest UPPSC questions in the book, newest first, shown as the fact each one tested. They show the current style. 2024 is the latest UPPSC paper the book covers; the 2025 list (PCS Pre 2025 and the RO/ARO re-exam held in July 2025) is not from the book and rests on UPPSC's provisional keys.

    2025 (36 questions)

    • Green plants capture about 1% of incident sunlight and only about 10% of organic matter (energy) passes to the next trophic level (ten per cent law). PCS Pre
    • Per ISFR 2023, Chandauli and Shravasti have forest cover above 20% of their area, while Bahraich does not. PCS Pre
    • Delhi's bio-decomposer, a fungal consortium solution, is sprayed free of cost to turn paddy stubble into manure instead of burning it. PCS Pre
    • Himalayan vegetation is altitudinally zoned because climate changes with height. PCS Pre
    • Carrying capacity requires resource extraction to stay at or below regeneration and waste generation to stay within the environment's absorption capacity. PCS Pre
    • Biogas consists mainly of methane and carbon dioxide. PCS Pre
    • UPPSC's provisional key treats both statements as correct: large Himalayan hydro potential, and eastern UP/Bihar unable to use it because the Himalayas to their north lie in Nepal. PCS Pre
    • The ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet radiation, protecting life on earth. PCS Pre UPPSC ×7
    • Agenda 21 of the 1992 Rio Summit relates to sustainable development. PCS Pre UPPSC ×4
    • Sarsai Nawar Jheel and Samaspur Bird Sanctuary are Ramsar sites in Uttar Pradesh; Rudrasagar Lake (Tripura) and Sultanpur National Park (Haryana) are not. PCS Pre
    • Lichens are bio-indicators of air pollution. PCS Pre UPPSC ×7
    • World Wildlife Day is 3 March (22 March is wrong); International Ozone Day is 16 September and World Environment Day is 5 June. PCS Pre
    • The Annual Groundwater Quality Report 2024 was prepared by the Central Ground Water Board. PCS Pre
    • By volume the world's water is held in oceans, then polar ice and glaciers, then ground water, then rivers. PCS Pre
    • Dachigam is in Jammu and Kashmir, Keoladeo in Rajasthan, Kanha in Madhya Pradesh and Periyar in Kerala. PCS Pre
    • MISHTI aims to restore mangrove forests; it was launched in 2023 (Budget 2023-24), not 2019. PCS Pre
    • Per the provisional key only statement 2 is correct: World Solar Bank and One Sun One World One Grid were initiated under the ISA, whose membership is far larger than 38 countries. PCS Pre
    • Uttar Pradesh's SDG National Indicator Framework progress report is prepared by the Department of Planning. PCS Pre
    • India's performance is decisive for the global SDGs because it holds about one-sixth of the world's population. PCS Pre
    • The Appiko forest-conservation movement is associated with Karnataka. PCS Pre

    Uttar Pradesh Environment

    Protected areas, Ramsar sites, State symbols, forest figures, policies and schemes of Uttar Pradesh. UPPSC regularly asks UP-specific facts, and the book covers few of them.

    UP protected areas: totals

    • Dudhwa in Lakhimpur Kheri district is Uttar Pradesh's only national park, notified in January 1977. Wikipedia ↗ Note: Only-national-park status is from Wikipedia's list of protected areas of Uttar Pradesh.
    • Uttar Pradesh has 26 wildlife sanctuaries covering 5,822.20 km², alongside one national park. as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Count includes bird sanctuaries and Pilibhit. Older lists show 24 or 25; official UP Forest Department total could not be opened.
    • Hastinapur Wildlife Sanctuary (1986), at 2,073 km², is the largest sanctuary in Uttar Pradesh. as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Chandra Prabha Wildlife Sanctuary in Chandauli, declared in 1957, is the oldest sanctuary in Uttar Pradesh's list. as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.

    Dudhwa National Park / Tiger Reserve

    • Dudhwa began as a wildlife sanctuary for swamp deer in 1958 and became Dudhwa Tiger Reserve in 1987. Wikipedia ↗ Note: NTCA's table lists Dudhwa's tiger reserve notification year as 2010 (statutory notification).
    • Dudhwa Tiger Reserve comprises Dudhwa National Park, Kishanpur Wildlife Sanctuary and Katarniaghat Wildlife Sanctuary. Wikipedia ↗
    • Rhinos were reintroduced in Dudhwa in 1984-85, when seven animals were brought from Assam and Nepal. ecotourism.up.gov.in ↗
    • Dudhwa National Park lies on an alluvial plain along the Mohana and Suheli rivers and has over 450 bird species. ecotourism.up.gov.in ↗
    • NTCA lists Dudhwa Tiger Reserve at 2,201.77 km²: core 1,093.79 km² and buffer 1,107.98 km². ntca.gov.in ↗

    UP wildlife sanctuaries

    • Kishanpur Wildlife Sanctuary, in Lakhimpur Kheri and Shahjahanpur districts, was declared in 1972 and covers 227 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Ranipur Wildlife Sanctuary, in Banda and Chitrakoot districts, was declared in 1977 and covers 230.31 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Mahavir Swami Wildlife Sanctuary in Lalitpur district was declared in 1977 and covers 5.41 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • National Chambal Sanctuary in Uttar Pradesh, covering Agra and Etawah districts, was declared in 1979 with 635 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Kaimoor (Kaimur) Wildlife Sanctuary, in Mirzapur and Sonbhadra districts, was declared in 1982 and covers 500.73 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Hastinapur Wildlife Sanctuary spans Meerut, Muzaffarnagar, Ghaziabad, Bijnor and Amroha (Jyotiba Phule Nagar) districts. as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Sohagi Barwa Wildlife Sanctuary in Maharajganj district was declared in 1987 and covers 428.2 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Suhelwa (Sohelwa) Wildlife Sanctuary, in Balrampur and Shravasti districts, was declared in 1988 and covers 452.47 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗
    • Kachhua (turtle) Sanctuary at Varanasi was declared in 1989 on a 7 km stretch of the Ganga. as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Bakhira Wildlife Sanctuary in Sant Kabir Nagar district was declared in 1990 and covers 28.94 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.
    • Vijai Sagar Sanctuary in Mahoba district was declared in 1990 and covers 2.62 km². as of March 2025 Wikipedia ↗ Note: Year, area and district as tabulated on Wikipedia (data to March 2025); UP Forest Department site was unreachable for cross-check.

    • Katarniaghat's Girwa river habitat holds gharial and Gangetic dolphin; the sanctuary forms part of Dudhwa Tiger Reserve's core. ecotourism.up.gov.in ↗

    UP tiger reserves

    • Uttar Pradesh is usually credited with four tiger reserves: Dudhwa, Pilibhit, Amangarh and Ranipur. as of October 2022 businesstoday.in ↗ Note: NTCA's list shows three UP reserves and treats Amangarh as a buffer of Corbett Tiger Reserve.
    • Pilibhit Tiger Reserve was notified in 2014 with 730.25 km²: core 602.79 km² and buffer 127.45 km². ntca.gov.in ↗
    • Ranipur Tiger Reserve was notified in 2022 with 529.36 km²: core 230.31 km² and buffer 299.05 km². ntca.gov.in ↗
    • Ranipur, announced on 31 October 2022, is Uttar Pradesh's fourth and newest tiger reserve and India's 53rd. as of October 2022 businesstoday.in ↗
    • Ranipur is the first tiger reserve in the Bundelkhand region; the State cabinet approved it on 28 September 2022. as of October 2022 businesstoday.in ↗
    • NTCA lists Amangarh (80.60 km², 2012) as a buffer of Corbett Tiger Reserve, not a separate reserve. ntca.gov.in ↗
    • Amangarh Tiger Reserve lies in Bijnor district and was originally part of Jim Corbett National Park. ecotourism.up.gov.in ↗ Note: The State eco-tourism page gives its area as 95 km²; NTCA gives 80.60 km².
    • Uttar Pradesh's tiger number rose from 173 in 2018 to 205 in the 2022 estimation. as of 2022 nationalheraldindia.com ↗
    • Dudhwa Tiger Reserve's tiger count rose from 82 in 2018 to 135 in 2022. as of 2022 nationalheraldindia.com ↗

    UP elephant reserves

    • The Centre approved the Terai Elephant Reserve in October 2022 over 3,049 km² in Lakhimpur Kheri and Pilibhit districts. as of October 2022 drishtiias.com ↗ Note: Wikipedia gives the notified area as 3,072 km².
    • Terai Elephant Reserve includes Dudhwa and Pilibhit tiger reserves, Kishanpur and Katarniaghat sanctuaries and parts of South Kheri forest division. as of October 2022 drishtiias.com ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh has two elephant reserves: one of 744 km² notified in 2009 and the Terai reserve notified in 2022. as of 2023 Wikipedia ↗ Note: The 2009 reserve is named variously as Uttar Pradesh/Shivalik Elephant Reserve (Saharanpur-Bijnor); name not confirmed on the opened page.

    Etawah Lion Safari

    • Etawah Lion Safari covers 350 hectares with an 8 km perimeter: 50 hectares of safari and 300 hectares of buffer. ecotourism.up.gov.in ↗
    • Etawah Safari Park offers lion, deer, antelope, bear and leopard safaris and has an Asiatic lion breeding centre. ecotourism.up.gov.in ↗

    Kukrail gharial centre / night safari

    • Kukrail Gharial Rehabilitation Centre in Lucknow, set up in 1975, is India's first gharial conservation centre. drishtiias.com ↗ Note: One Mongabay commentary gives 1978; 1975 is the more widely cited year.
    • The Supreme Court in July 2026 allowed Uttar Pradesh to build India's first night safari at Kukrail, Lucknow. as of July 2026 drishtiias.com ↗
    • The Kukrail night safari will be the world's fifth, after Singapore, Thailand, China and Indonesia. as of July 2026 drishtiias.com ↗
    • Kukrail Reserve Forest in Lucknow was notified in 1950 and spans about 4,500 acres. as of July 2026 drishtiias.com ↗

    Vulture conservation centre, Gorakhpur

    • The Jatayu Conservation and Breeding Centre is at Bharivaisi in Campierganj range, Gorakhpur Forest Division. as of November 2024 chronicleindia.in ↗
    • The Gorakhpur centre is described as the world's first dedicated breeding centre for the Asian king (red-headed) vulture. as of November 2024 chronicleindia.in ↗
    • The Gorakhpur vulture centre is run by the UP Forest Department with the Bombay Natural History Society. as of November 2024 chronicleindia.in ↗
    • Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath laid the vulture centre's foundation at Campierganj on 7 October 2020. downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's vulture count fell from 2,070 in 2012 to 1,350 in 2017, per State forest surveys. as of 2017 downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • UNCONFIRMED The Gorakhpur vulture centre was inaugurated on 6 September 2024. as of September 2024 chronicleindia.in ↗ Note: Date appeared only in search snippets; the opened page says 'recently' without a date.

    Dolphins in UP

    • Uttar Pradesh has 2,397 river dolphins, the highest of any State, out of India's 6,327. as of March 2025 downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath declared the Gangetic dolphin Uttar Pradesh's State aquatic animal in October 2023. as of October 2023 dtnext.in ↗
    • In Uttar Pradesh, Gangetic dolphins are found in the Ganga, Yamuna, Chambal, Ghaghra, Rapti and Gerua rivers. as of October 2023 dtnext.in ↗
    • India's second range-wide dolphin estimation was launched in January 2026 from Bijnor, Uttar Pradesh. as of January 2026 PIB ↗

    Sarus crane count

    • Uttar Pradesh's June 2024 census counted 19,918 sarus cranes, up from 19,522 in 2023 and 17,329 in 2021. as of June 2024 drishtiias.com ↗ Note: A March 2025 PTI report quoting the State gives 19,994 for 2024.
    • Etawah Forest Division had the most sarus cranes in the 2024 census, 3,289. as of June 2024 drishtiias.com ↗
    • UNCONFIRMED A later winter census reportedly counted 20,628 sarus cranes in Uttar Pradesh. as of 2026 ↗ Note: Figure seen only in search snippets; no page carrying it was opened, so no source URL is given.

    UP Ramsar sites

    • Uttar Pradesh has 14 Ramsar sites, second only to Tamil Nadu's 20. as of 25 October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Upper Ganga River (Brijghat to Narora), designated on 8 November 2005, was Uttar Pradesh's first Ramsar site. Wikipedia ↗ Note: 'First' is inferred from the designation dates in the table.
    • Sarsai Nawar Jheel in Etawah district became a Ramsar site on 19 September 2019. Wikipedia ↗
    • Sandi Bird Sanctuary in Hardoi district became a Ramsar site on 26 September 2019. Wikipedia ↗
    • Samaspur Bird Sanctuary in Rae Bareli district became a Ramsar site on 3 October 2019. Wikipedia ↗
    • Saman Bird Sanctuary in Mainpuri district became a Ramsar site on 2 December 2019. Wikipedia ↗
    • Nawabganj (Unnao) and Parvati Arga (Gonda) bird sanctuaries were designated Ramsar sites in 2019. vajiramandravi.com ↗ Note: Year from a coaching-site table; districts from Wikipedia's sanctuary list. Exact dates not opened.
    • Sur Sarovar (Keetham Lake) near Agra became a Ramsar site on 21 August 2020. Wikipedia ↗
    • Haiderpur Wetland became a Ramsar site on 13 April 2021. Wikipedia ↗ Note: District not stated on the opened page.
    • Bakhira Wildlife Sanctuary in Sant Kabir Nagar became a Ramsar site on 29 June 2021. Wikipedia ↗
    • Patna Bird Sanctuary in Etah district became a Ramsar site on 31 January 2026. Wikipedia ↗
    • Shekha Jheel Bird Sanctuary in Aligarh became India's 99th Ramsar site on 22 April 2026. Wikipedia ↗ Note: Date from Wikipedia; '99th' from a Drishti IAS note and a PIB release title.
    • Surha Tal (Jai Prakash Narayan Bird Sanctuary) in Ballia became India's 100th Ramsar site in June 2026. as of June 2026 PIB ↗
    • Surha Tal, an oxbow lake of the Ganga, was Uttar Pradesh's 13th Ramsar site. as of June 2026 drishtiias.com ↗
    • Sauj Jheel in Mainpuri district became a Ramsar site on 15 October 2026, Uttar Pradesh's 14th. as of 15 October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Sauj Jheel is a shallow floodplain lake that regularly hosts more than 30,000 waterbirds, including sarus cranes. as of 25 October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Bakhira Wildlife Sanctuary is described as the largest natural floodplain wetland of eastern Uttar Pradesh. as of 25 October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh notified 101 wetlands across 26 districts, covering about 2,750 hectares, under the Wetlands Rules, 2017. as of June 2026 freepressjournal.in ↗

    UP State symbols

    • Uttar Pradesh's State animal is the barasingha or swamp deer (Rucervus duvaucelii). Wikipedia ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's State bird is the sarus crane (Antigone antigone). Wikipedia ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's State tree is the Ashoka (Saraca asoca). Wikipedia ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's State flower is the palash (Butea monosperma). Wikipedia ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's State aquatic animal is the Gangetic dolphin, declared in October 2023. as of October 2023 dtnext.in ↗

    ISFR 2023: Uttar Pradesh

    • ISFR 2023 puts Uttar Pradesh's forest cover at 15,045.80 km², which is 6.24% of the State's area. as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • ISFR 2023 puts Uttar Pradesh's tree cover at 8,950.92 km², or 3.72% of its area. as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's total forest and tree cover in ISFR 2023 is 23,996.72 km², or 9.96% of its area. as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's forest cover comprises 2,688.73 km² very dense, 4,001.41 km² moderately dense and 8,355.66 km² open forest. as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Against ISFR 2021, Uttar Pradesh gained 118.43 km² of forest cover and 440.76 km² of tree cover. as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗ Note: Changes computed from the revised 2021 figures (forest cover 14,927.37 km², tree cover 8,510.16 km²).
    • Uttar Pradesh's 559.19 km² rise in forest and tree cover was second highest in India, after Chhattisgarh's 683.62 km². as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Sonbhadra has the highest share of area under forest cover among Uttar Pradesh districts, about 36.77%. as of ISFR 2023 gktoday.in ↗ Note: From a GK question page, not the FSI volume (ISFR Volume II PDF was too large to open).
    • Uttar Pradesh's geographical area is 2,40,928 km². nri.up.gov.in ↗

    UP Pollution Control Board

    • The UP Pollution Control Board was constituted on 3 February 1975 under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974. indiaenvironmentportal.org.in ↗
    • It was first called the UP Water Pollution Prevention and Control Board and was renamed on 13 July 1982. indiaenvironmentportal.org.in ↗
    • UNCONFIRMED The UP Pollution Control Board is headquartered in Lucknow. uppcb.com ↗ Note: Headquarters seen only in search snippets; the Board's site (source URL) could not be opened.

    UP State Action Plan on Climate Change

    • UNCONFIRMED Uttar Pradesh's State Action Plan on Climate Change 2.0 covers the period 2021-2030. napccindia.moef.gov.in ↗ Note: Seen only in a search snippet of the MoEFCC NAPCC portal; the page (source URL) and its PDF failed to open.

    UP Solar Energy Policy 2022

    • The UP Solar Energy Policy 2022 targets 22,000 MW of solar power projects by 2026-27. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • UPNEDA is the nodal agency for the UP Solar Energy Policy 2022. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • The policy aims to cover about 13.50 lakh residential houses with rooftop solar during the policy period. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • The solar policy plans a 4,000 MW solar evacuation corridor in Bundelkhand and training of 30,000 Surya Mitras. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • Ayodhya is the pilot model solar city under the policy, with 16 Nagar Nigam cities to follow. invest.up.gov.in ↗

    UP State Bio-Energy Policy 2022

    • Uttar Pradesh declared its State Bio-Energy Policy 2022 in September 2022, with UPNEDA as nodal agency. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • The policy promotes compressed biogas, bio-coal and biodiesel plants, with subsidies capped at Rs 20 crore per plant. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • Bioenergy units get government land on lease at Rs 1 per acre per year and full stamp duty exemption. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh targets 1,000 tonnes per day of compressed biogas; 48 CBG and nine biodiesel plants were commissioned. as of March 2026 agrospectrumindia.com ↗

    UP EV policy 2022

    • Under the UP EV Manufacturing and Mobility Policy 2022, EVs bought from 14 October 2022 to 13 October 2025 got full road-tax exemption. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • From 14 October 2025 to 13 October 2027 the full rebate applies to EVs manufactured, purchased and registered in Uttar Pradesh. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • The EV policy offers 30% capital subsidy, up to Rs 1,000 crore each, to the first two ultra-mega battery projects. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • Over 2,77,000 electric vehicles were registered in Uttar Pradesh in 2023. as of 2023 invest.up.gov.in ↗

    UP Green Hydrogen Policy 2024

    • The UP Green Hydrogen Policy 2024 targets one million tonnes a year of green hydrogen/ammonia capacity by 2028. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • The policy gives capital subsidy up to 30%, and up to 40% for the first five projects. invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh's hydrogen demand is about 0.9 million tonnes a year, mainly from fertiliser and refinery sectors. as of 2024 invest.up.gov.in ↗
    • The Green Hydrogen Policy plans four Centres of Excellence for research and innovation. invest.up.gov.in ↗

    UP Eco-Tourism Development Board

    • The UP cabinet approved the Uttar Pradesh Eco-Tourism Development Board on 16 August 2022. as of August 2022 drishtiias.com ↗
    • The Chief Minister chairs the Eco-Tourism Development Board, which is headquartered in Lucknow. as of August 2022 drishtiias.com ↗
    • The Uttar Pradesh Forest Corporation was established on 25 November 1974 under the UP Forest Corporation Act, 1974. ecotourism.up.gov.in ↗

    UP plantation drives

    • Uttar Pradesh planted 36.51 crore saplings in one day on 20 July 2024. as of July 2024 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • The 2024 drive was named 'Ped Lagao, Ped Bachao Jan Abhiyan-2024' and reached 36.80 crore saplings. as of 2024 theprint.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh planted a record 37.21 crore saplings in a single day on 9 July 2025. as of July 2025 ianslive.in ↗
    • On 12 July 2026 Uttar Pradesh planted 35.27 crore saplings in a day against a 35 crore target. as of July 2026 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • The 2026 drive, Paudharopan Mahayagya-2026, was launched from Gorakhpur under the 'Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam' campaign. as of July 2026 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh planted over 242 crore saplings in nine years and aims at 15% green cover by 2030. as of March 2026 ianslive.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh held an 'Ek Ped Guru Ke Naam' plantation drive on Teachers' Day, 5 September 2026. as of September 2026 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • The Pavitra Dhara scheme planted 3.72 crore saplings along the Ganga, Yamuna, Saryu, Hindon and Gomti. as of March 2025 theprint.in ↗

    UP heritage trees

    • Uttar Pradesh has 948 heritage trees of 28 species spread across all 75 districts. as of July 2025 theprint.in ↗
    • Varanasi has the most heritage trees (99), followed by Prayagraj (53) and Hardoi (37). as of July 2025 theprint.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh announced a 'Heritage Tree Adoption' scheme in July 2025 to protect century-old trees. as of July 2025 theprint.in ↗

    UP State Biodiversity Board / heritage sites

    • Ken Nala, Gulra in Bhinga Reserve Forest, Shravasti (80 hectares) was notified a Biodiversity Heritage Site on 4 June 2026. as of 4 June 2026 upsbdb.org ↗
    • Ken Nala was notified under Section 37 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and is Uttar Pradesh's second such site. as of June 2026 upsbdb.org ↗ Note: The first UP Biodiversity Heritage Site could not be identified: the 2016 gazette PDF on the Board's site is a scanned image.
    • The Uttar Pradesh State Biodiversity Board is based in Lucknow. upsbdb.org ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh records 2,932 plant species, about 6.45% of India's flora. upsbdb.org ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh records 2,387 animal species, including 358 birds, 152 fishes and 87 mammals. upsbdb.org ↗

    Air pollution in UP

    • IQAir's World Air Quality Report 2025 ranked Loni, Uttar Pradesh, the world's most polluted city, with PM2.5 of 112.5 µg/m³. as of March 2026 dtnext.in ↗
    • Ghaziabad was also among the world's ten most polluted cities in IQAir's 2025 report. as of March 2026 onmanorama.com ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh launched the World Bank-aided Rs 2,741 crore UP Clean Air Management Project on 5 June 2026. as of June 2026 egov.eletsonline.com ↗
    • UP CAMP is described as India's first airshed-based clean air initiative. as of June 2026 egov.eletsonline.com ↗

    Namami Gange in UP

    • Under Namami Gange, 74 sewage treatment projects are approved in Uttar Pradesh and 41 are complete. as of January 2026 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh has 152 operational sewage treatment plants. as of January 2026 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • A 55 MLD sewage treatment plant at Assi-BHU, Varanasi, costing Rs 308 crore, began operating in 2025-26. as of January 2026 freepressjournal.in ↗

    Ken-Betwa link / Bundelkhand water

    • The Ken-Betwa Link Project costs Rs 44,605 crore; its foundation stone was laid on 25 December 2024. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • The project builds the 96.7 m Daudhan Dam on the Ken in Panna and Chhatarpur districts of Madhya Pradesh. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • A 216.465 km Ken-Betwa link canal will end at Barua Sagar near Jhansi. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • In Uttar Pradesh the project benefits Banda, Mahoba, Jhansi and Lalitpur districts of Bundelkhand. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • Ken-Betwa will irrigate 10.62 lakh hectares, give drinking water to 62 lakh people and generate 103 MW hydropower. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • Ken-Betwa is the first river-interlinking project under the National Perspective Plan to reach implementation; completion is scheduled for 2030. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • Uttar Pradesh is one of seven States covered by Atal Bhujal Yojana, launched in April 2020. as of February 2025 theprint.in ↗

    Sarnath World Heritage Site

    • Sarnath near Varanasi was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List on 25 July 2026 as India's 45th site. as of July 2026 outlooktraveller.com ↗ Note: A cultural site, listed here for its Uttar Pradesh relevance.

    Recent Developments 2022–26

    Schemes, laws, conferences and counts newer than the book, or missing from it.

    Mission LiFE

    • Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment) was launched on 20 October 2022 at the Statue of Unity, Kevadia, Gujarat. freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Prime Minister Narendra Modi and UN Secretary-General António Guterres jointly launched Mission LiFE. freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Over six crore people joined 34 lakh Mission LiFE events and 4.96 crore pledges were taken. as of December 2025 PIB ↗

    Green Credit Programme

    • The Green Credit Programme was introduced in 2023 as a market-based mechanism for voluntary environmental actions. india.mongabay.com ↗
    • The tree-plantation methodology of February 2024 was replaced by a new one on 29 August 2025. as of August 2025 india.mongabay.com ↗
    • Green credits now require at least 40% canopy density after five years, with one credit per surviving tree. as of August 2025 india.mongabay.com ↗
    • Under the 2025 rules, tree-plantation green credits are non-tradable and non-transferable, except between holding and subsidiary companies. as of August 2025 india.mongabay.com ↗

    NDC / Panchamrit

    • India's updated NDC (2022) pledges a 45% cut in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 from 2005 levels. PIB ↗
    • The 2022 NDC also targets about 50% of installed electric capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030. PIB ↗
    • India cut emissions intensity by about 36% between 2005 and 2020 and crossed 50% non-fossil capacity in 2025. as of 2025 PIB ↗
    • India's Long-Term Low Emissions Development Strategy, submitted to the UNFCCC in 2022, charts a path to net zero by 2070. PIB ↗
    • The Cabinet in March 2026 approved India's NDC for 2031-35: 47% lower emissions intensity by 2035 from 2005 levels. as of March 2026 newsonair.gov.in ↗
    • The 2035 NDC also targets 60% of installed power capacity from non-fossil sources. as of March 2026 newsonair.gov.in ↗
    • India had 52.57% non-fossil power capacity by February 2026, meeting the 2030 target five years early. as of February 2026 newsonair.gov.in ↗
    • UNCONFIRMED The 2035 NDC is reported to include a carbon sink of 3.5-4 billion tonnes CO2-equivalent. as of March 2026 newsonair.gov.in ↗ Note: Sink figure seen only in search snippets (sources differ: 3.5-4 or 4 billion tonnes); not on the opened page.
    • India's non-fossil capacity reached 300.50 GW, over 54% of about 552 GW total, by 31 July 2026. as of 31 July 2026 PIB ↗

    MISHTI

    • MISHTI targets mangrove restoration over 540 km² in nine States and four Union Territories. as of October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Rs 88.44 crore has been released under MISHTI to restore 9,949.5 hectares of degraded mangroves. as of October 2026 PIB ↗
    • In 2025 MISHTI restored 4,536 hectares and identified 22,560 hectares of degraded mangroves across 13 States/UTs. as of 2025 PIB ↗

    Amrit Dharohar

    • Amrit Dharohar promotes Ramsar sites through species conservation, nature tourism, wetland livelihoods and wetland carbon assessment. as of October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Under Amrit Dharohar, flora and fauna of 75 Ramsar sites were inventoried and carbon stock of 39 sites assessed. as of October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Mission Sahbhagita's Save Wetlands Campaign began in Goa on 4 February 2023 and mapped over 1.7 lakh wetlands. as of October 2026 PIB ↗

    Project Dolphin

    • Project Dolphin was launched on 15 August 2020 to conserve marine and riverine dolphins. PIB ↗
    • India's first river dolphin estimation counted 6,327 dolphins across 28 rivers in eight States, surveying 8,507 km. as of March 2025 downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • After Uttar Pradesh (2,397), Bihar has 2,220 river dolphins, West Bengal 815 and Assam 635; Punjab has three. as of March 2025 downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • The second dolphin estimation covers the Ganga, Indus, Brahmaputra, Sundarbans and Odisha, including Irrawaddy dolphins. as of January 2026 PIB ↗

    Project Cheetah

    • Project Cheetah began on 17 September 2022 when eight Namibian cheetahs were released in Kuno National Park. PIB ↗
    • Twenty cheetahs came from Namibia and South Africa in 2022-23, the first intercontinental translocation of a large carnivore. PIB ↗
    • India had 30 cheetahs in December 2025, of which 19 were born in India. as of December 2025 PIB ↗
    • India had 52 cheetahs, 32 of them India-born, four years after the project began. as of September 2026 businesstoday.in ↗ Note: PIB reported 53 in May 2026 (release not opened); numbers change with births and deaths.
    • India aims for a metapopulation of 60-70 cheetahs across 17,000 km² by 2032; Gandhi Sagar sanctuary is the next site. as of December 2025 PIB ↗

    International Big Cat Alliance

    • India launched the International Big Cat Alliance in April 2023 to conserve seven big cat species. PIB ↗
    • IBCA covers tiger, lion, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma, and is headquartered in India. PIB ↗
    • IBCA's Framework Agreement entered into force on 23 January 2025; membership has grown to 18 countries. as of April 2026 PIB ↗

    Project Lion / lion estimate

    • The 16th lion estimation (2025) counted 891 Asiatic lions in Gujarat, up from 674 in 2020. as of May 2025 tribuneindia.com ↗
    • Barda Wildlife Sanctuary recorded 17 lions in 2025, its first recorded lion presence since 1879. as of May 2025 tribuneindia.com ↗
    • Project Lion focuses on landscape-based conservation, habitat restoration, community participation and disease management. as of March 2025 PIB ↗

    Jal Jeevan Mission

    • The Cabinet on 10 March 2026 extended Jal Jeevan Mission to December 2028 with an outlay of Rs 8.69 lakh crore. as of March 2026 theprint.in ↗
    • Rural tap-water coverage rose from 3.23 crore households (16.72%) in 2019 to over 15.86 crore (81.94%). as of June 2026 PIB ↗
    • JJM 2.0 aims to give tap connections to all 19.36 crore rural households by December 2028. as of March 2026 theprint.in ↗

    Atal Bhujal Yojana

    • Atal Bhujal Yojana, launched in April 2020, covers 8,774 gram panchayats in 80 districts of seven States. as of February 2025 theprint.in ↗ Note: Other official replies cite 8,203 gram panchayats; figure varies by source.
    • The seven Atal Bhujal States are Haryana, Gujarat, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. as of February 2025 theprint.in ↗
    • The Centre proposed extending Atal Bhujal Yojana to Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and Telangana. as of February 2025 theprint.in ↗

    PM Surya Ghar

    • PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana was launched in February 2024 with Rs 75,021 crore for one crore households. PIB ↗
    • By 12 August 2026, 51.58 lakh households had rooftop solar under PM Surya Ghar, totalling 14.8 GW. as of 12 August 2026 PIB ↗
    • PM Surya Ghar offers up to 300 free units a month and a subsidy of up to Rs 78,000. as of June 2026 PIB ↗

    National Green Hydrogen Mission

    • The National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in January 2023 with Rs 19,744 crore, targeting 5 MMT a year by 2030. PIB ↗
    • About 8,000 tonnes a year of green hydrogen capacity had been commissioned in India by February 2026. as of February 2026 PIB ↗
    • India's first indigenous hydrogen fuel-cell train began running on the Jind-Sonipat section in July 2026. as of July 2026 PIB ↗

    PM-KUSUM

    • PM-KUSUM promotes solarisation of agriculture and aimed to install 14 lakh standalone solar pumps by 31 March 2026. as of February 2026 PIB ↗

    Ethanol blending (E20)

    • India achieved 20% ethanol blending in petrol in 2025, five years ahead of the original 2030 target. as of July 2025 tribuneindia.com ↗
    • Ethanol blending in petrol stood at only 1.5% in 2014. as of July 2025 tribuneindia.com ↗

    Single-use plastic ban / PWM Rules

    • India banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022 under the Plastic Waste Management Amendment Rules, 2021. tribuneindia.com ↗
    • Plastic carry-bag thickness was raised from 50 to 75 microns on 30 September 2021 and to 120 microns on 31 December 2022. tribuneindia.com ↗
    • PWM amendment rules notified on 23 January 2025 require barcode or QR-code information on plastic packaging from 1 July 2025. legal500.com ↗
    • The number of waste recycling plants in India rose from 829 in 2019-20 to 3,036 in 2024-25. as of 2024-25 PIB ↗

    Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act 2022

    • The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Bill was passed by Lok Sabha on 2 August 2022 and Rajya Sabha on 8 December 2022. prsindia.org ↗
    • The 2022 amendment cut the Act's schedules from six to four and added a schedule for CITES-listed specimens. prsindia.org ↗
    • The amendment raised the general-violation fine from Rs 25,000 to Rs 1 lakh and empowered regulation of invasive alien species. prsindia.org ↗

    Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023

    • The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Bill was passed by Lok Sabha on 25 July 2023 and Rajya Sabha on 1 August 2023. prsindia.org ↗
    • The amendment exempts AYUSH practitioners and users of codified traditional knowledge from benefit sharing. prsindia.org ↗
    • It decriminalised offences, replacing imprisonment with penalties of Rs 1 lakh to Rs 50 lakh. prsindia.org ↗

    Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act 2023

    • The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Bill was passed by Lok Sabha on 26 July 2023 and Rajya Sabha on 2 August 2023. prsindia.org ↗
    • The amended Act exempts strategic linear projects within 100 km of international borders from forest clearance. prsindia.org ↗
    • It also exempts security infrastructure up to 10 hectares and permits zoos, safaris and eco-tourism facilities on forest land. prsindia.org ↗

    Loss and Damage Fund

    • At COP28, countries pledged roughly $700 million to the new loss and damage fund. as of December 2023 wri.org ↗
    • The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage is headquartered in Manila, Philippines. as of July 2026 eco-business.com ↗
    • Its first funding window, the Barbados Implementation Modalities, offers $250 million and drew 176 requests. as of July 2026 eco-business.com ↗

    Global Stocktake (COP28)

    • The first Global Stocktake at COP28, Dubai, called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems. as of December 2023 wri.org ↗
    • It also called for tripling global renewable energy capacity and doubling energy efficiency by 2030. as of December 2023 wri.org ↗

    COP29 Baku

    • COP29 in Baku set a new climate finance goal of at least $300 billion a year by 2035, led by developed countries. as of November 2024 c2es.org ↗
    • COP29 launched the Baku to Belém Roadmap to scale climate finance to $1.3 trillion. as of November 2024 c2es.org ↗
    • COP29 finalised Article 6 guidance, fully operationalising carbon markets under the Paris Agreement. as of November 2024 c2es.org ↗

    COP30 Belém

    • COP30 was held in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025 and adopted 56 consensus decisions. as of November 2025 cop30.br ↗
    • The Global Mutirão decision created a Global Implementation Accelerator and the Belém Mission to 1.5°C. as of November 2025 c2es.org ↗
    • COP30 called for efforts to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035 and adopted 59 Belém adaptation indicators. as of November 2025 c2es.org ↗
    • COP30 agreed to launch a just transition mechanism. as of November 2025 c2es.org ↗
    • India joined Brazil's Tropical Forests Forever Facility as an Observer at COP30. as of November 2025 PIB ↗

    COP31 venue

    • COP31 is being held in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026. as of November 2026 c2es.org ↗
    • Türkiye holds the COP31 presidency while Australia's Chris Bowen serves as President of Negotiations. as of November 2025 pm.gov.au ↗
    • COP32 is scheduled for Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, from 8 to 19 November 2027. c2es.org ↗

    Kunming-Montreal GBF / CBD COPs

    • At CBD COP16 in Cali, Colombia (2024), India launched its updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2024-2030. PIB ↗
    • CBD COP17 was held in Yerevan, Armenia, and ended on 31 October 2026 with the 'Yerevan Pathway'. as of October 2026 downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • COP17's global review found countries far from meeting the 2030 Kunming-Montreal targets; about $2 billion in new funding was pledged. as of October 2026 downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • CBD COP18 will be hosted by Ecuador in 2028. as of October 2026 downtoearth.org.in ↗

    High Seas (BBNJ) Treaty

    • The BBNJ (High Seas) Treaty crossed 60 ratifications in September 2025, triggering entry into force on 17 January 2026. as of September 2025 downtoearth.org.in ↗
    • The treaty covers high-seas marine protected areas, sharing of marine genetic resource benefits and environmental impact assessments. as of September 2025 downtoearth.org.in ↗

    ISFR 2023 national

    • ISFR 2023 puts India's forest and tree cover at 8,27,357 km², or 25.17% of its geographical area. as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • India's forest cover is 7,15,343 km² (21.76%) and tree cover 1,12,014 km² (3.41%). as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Forest and tree cover rose by 1,445 km² over 2021: forest cover by 156 km² and tree cover by 1,289 km². as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗
    • Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan recorded the largest increases in forest and tree cover. as of ISFR 2023 freepressjournal.in ↗

    Tiger estimate / tiger reserves

    • The All India Tiger Estimation 2022 put India's tigers at 3,682 (range 3,167-3,925), up from 2,967 in 2018. as of 2022 PIB ↗
    • India has 58 tiger reserves covering about 85,000 km²; the newest is Madhav in Madhya Pradesh (2025). as of April 2026 PIB ↗
    • The sixth cycle of the All India Tiger Estimation is under way; India has 32 identified tiger corridors. as of April 2026 PIB ↗

    Elephant estimate / elephant reserves

    • The first DNA-based elephant census (SAIEE 2021-25) estimates India's wild elephants at 22,446. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • India has 33 elephant reserves covering 80,777 km² in 14 States and 150 identified elephant corridors. as of August 2026 PIB ↗
    • India holds nearly 60% of the world's wild Asian elephants; West Bengal has the most corridors, 26. as of August 2026 PIB ↗

    Leopard / snow leopard estimates

    • India's leopard population was estimated at 13,874 in 2022, up from 12,852 in 2018. as of February 2024 theprint.in ↗
    • Madhya Pradesh has the most leopards (3,907), followed by Maharashtra (1,985) and Karnataka (1,879). as of February 2024 theprint.in ↗
    • India's first snow leopard assessment (2019-23) estimated 718 animals, with 477 in Ladakh and 124 in Uttarakhand. as of April 2026 PIB ↗

    Ramsar sites in India

    • India has 103 Ramsar sites covering over 13.87 lakh hectares, up from 26 in 2014. as of 15 October 2026 PIB ↗
    • The latest additions, on 15 October 2026, are Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) and Sauj Jheel (Uttar Pradesh). as of 15 October 2026 PIB ↗
    • India ranks first in Asia and third in the world by number of Ramsar sites. as of October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Eleven Ramsar sites were added in 2025 to reach 96; Glaw Lake (Arunachal Pradesh) became the 101st in August 2026. as of October 2026 PIB ↗
    • Chilika Lake and Keoladeo National Park became India's first Ramsar sites on 1 October 1981. PIB ↗
    • Sundarban Wetland (4,23,000 hectares) is India's largest Ramsar site, designated on 30 January 2019. PIB ↗
    • Indore and Udaipur became India's first Ramsar-accredited Wetland Cities in January 2025. PIB ↗
    • The Ramsar Convention has 172 Contracting Parties and over 2,536 sites; India joined on 1 February 1982. as of October 2026 PIB ↗

    Protected area and biosphere reserve counts

    • India's protected area network grew from 745 in 2014 to 1,134 in 2025. as of 2025 PIB ↗
    • India had 106 national parks, 573 wildlife sanctuaries, 115 conservation reserves and 220 community reserves. as of 27 November 2023 PIB ↗ Note: Category-wise break-up for the 2025 total of 1,134 was not on an opened page.
    • India has 18 biosphere reserves covering 91,425 km², of which 13 are in UNESCO's World Network. as of April 2026 PIB ↗
    • Cold Desert Biosphere Reserve, Himachal Pradesh, joined UNESCO's network in September 2025 as India's 13th. as of September 2025 PIB ↗
    • UNCONFIRMED No new Indian natural World Heritage Site since 2024 could be confirmed. as of November 2026 whc.unesco.org ↗ Note: UNESCO's India page (source URL) returned 403. The only post-2024 inscription verified was Sarnath (cultural, July 2026).

    Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam

    • 'Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam' was launched on World Environment Day, 5 June 2024. PIB ↗
    • A total of 262.4 crore saplings were planted under 'Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam' till 31 December 2025. as of 31 December 2025 PIB ↗

    National Clean Air Programme

    • The National Clean Air Programme, launched in January 2019, covers 130 cities. PIB ↗
    • NCAP's revised target is a 40% cut in particulate (PM10) levels by 2025-26 against the 2017 baseline. theweek.in ↗
    • In 2024-25, 103 of 130 NCAP cities improved PM10; 64 cut it by 20% and 25 by 40%. as of 2024-25 PIB ↗

    Other national facts

    • India has 18 Blue Flag certified beaches across seven coastal States and four Union Territories. as of 2025-26 PIB ↗
    • India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme now covers 490 obligated entities after new sector targets in January 2026. as of January 2026 PIB ↗

    UPPCS Mains

    Added content Not from the book. UPPCS Mains has been descriptive since 2018, so the book's objective "Mains" questions (2002–2017) do not show today's pattern. The questions below were collected in November 2026 from reproductions of the papers; the outlines are study aids built from these notes, not official model answers.

    Real Mains questions, 2018–2025

    34 Environment questions: 16 from GS Paper III and 18 from the UP-specific GS Paper VI (from 2023). Answers are short: 8 marks in about 125 words, or 12 marks in about 200 words. GS Paper V had no Environment question in 2023–2025. Disaster-management questions and GS Paper I were not collected.

    Answer outlines

    13 outlines covering 22 of the 34 questions. For 125 words use the opening, three or four points with two facts, and the close. For 200 words use all the points.

    1. Ramsar sites of Uttar Pradesh

    Asked

    • Identify the Ramsar sites of Uttar Pradesh and describe their features. 2024 GS-VI · 8 marks · 125 words

    Open with

    Define a Ramsar site (wetland of international importance under the 1971 Ramsar Convention) and state UP's count.

    Develop

    • Group the sites instead of listing blindly: river stretch (Upper Ganga, Brijghat to Narora), bird sanctuaries (Nawabganj, Samaspur, Sandi, Saman, Parvati Arga, Patna, Shekha Jheel, Surha Tal), lakes and jheels (Sarsai Nawar, Sur Sarovar, Haiderpur, Bakhira, Sauj Jheel).
    • Features: oxbow lakes and floodplain wetlands of the Ganga plain; wintering ground for migratory waterbirds; sarus crane habitat.
    • Services: flood buffering, groundwater recharge, water purification, livelihoods for fishers.
    • Threats: encroachment, siltation, sewage and farm run-off, invasive weeds.
    • Measures: Wetlands Rules 2017, Amrit Dharohar, State wetland notification.

    Facts to quote

    • UP has 14 Ramsar sites, second to Tamil Nadu's 20 (October 2026). When this question was asked in 2024 the count was 10.
    • First site: Upper Ganga River, 8 November 2005.
    • Six sites were added in 2019; Sur Sarovar 2020; Haiderpur and Bakhira 2021; Patna Bird Sanctuary, Shekha Jheel, Surha Tal and Sauj Jheel in 2026.
    • Surha Tal (Ballia) became India's 100th Ramsar site in June 2026.
    • Bakhira is the largest natural floodplain wetland of eastern UP.
    • UP notified 101 wetlands in 26 districts under the Wetlands Rules, 2017.

    Close with

    Link wetlands to water security and climate resilience of the Ganga plain.

    2. Wildlife sanctuaries of UP and the Tarai belt

    Asked

    • Explain the ecological importance of the Wildlife Sanctuaries in the Tarai region of Uttar Pradesh. 2023 GS-VI · 12 marks · 200 words
    • Describe the wildlife sanctuaries of Uttar Pradesh. Which of these sanctuaries are crucial for conservation of endangered species? 2024 GS-VI · 12 marks · 200 words

    Open with

    State the network: one national park (Dudhwa) plus the State's wildlife and bird sanctuaries, concentrated in the Tarai, the Vindhyan south and river corridors.

    Develop

    • Tarai group: Dudhwa National Park, Kishanpur, Katarniaghat, Pilibhit, Sohagi Barwa, Suhelwa.
    • Ecological value of the Tarai: sal forest, tall grassland and wetland mosaic; corridor with Nepal's forests; habitat of tiger, rhino, swamp deer, elephant.
    • River sanctuaries: National Chambal (gharial, dolphin), Katarniaghat's Girwa river (gharial, Gangetic dolphin), turtle sanctuary on the Ganga.
    • Vindhyan and Bundelkhand group: Chandra Prabha, Kaimur, Ranipur, Mahavir Swami.
    • Crucial for endangered species: Dudhwa (swamp deer, rhino, tiger), Katarniaghat and Chambal (gharial), Hastinapur and bird sanctuaries (sarus crane).

    Facts to quote

    • Dudhwa Tiger Reserve = Dudhwa National Park + Kishanpur + Katarniaghat.
    • Rhinos were reintroduced in Dudhwa in 1984-85.
    • UP's tigers rose from 173 (2018) to 205 (2022); Dudhwa Tiger Reserve from 82 to 135.
    • Terai Elephant Reserve approved in October 2022, in Lakhimpur Kheri and Pilibhit.
    • Ranipur (2022) is UP's newest tiger reserve and the first in Bundelkhand.
    • Hastinapur is the largest sanctuary; Chandra Prabha (1957) the oldest.
    • UP has 2,397 river dolphins, the most of any State (2025 estimate).

    Close with

    Stress landscape-level management across the India-Nepal Tarai and community participation.

    3. Wildlife conservation challenges and human-wildlife conflict

    Asked

    • Critically examine the challenges of conservation of wild life. 2020 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words
    • Wildlife-human conflicts are increasing in Uttar Pradesh. Discuss its main causes and suggest effective measure to reduce it. 2025 GS-VI · 8 marks · 125 words

    Open with

    Say that success in raising numbers has pushed animals into shrinking, fragmented habitats, so conflict and conservation are now one problem.

    Develop

    • Causes: habitat loss and fragmentation, sugarcane fields next to forests in the Tarai acting as cover for big cats, blocked corridors, linear projects, prey decline.
    • Other challenges: poaching and illegal trade, invasive species, pollution of rivers, forest fires, disease, weak staffing.
    • Legal frame: Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 and its 2022 amendment; Project Tiger, Project Elephant, Project Dolphin.
    • Measures: secure corridors, early-warning and rapid-response teams, quick compensation, crop and livestock insurance, fencing at hotspots, awareness, eco-tourism income for villages.

    Facts to quote

    • UP's tigers: 173 (2018) to 205 (2022).
    • Terai Elephant Reserve (2022) covers Dudhwa and Pilibhit landscapes.
    • The 2022 amendment cut the Act's schedules from six to four and raised penalties.
    • India: 3,682 tigers (2022), 58 tiger reserves, 33 elephant reserves, 150 elephant corridors.

    Close with

    End with coexistence: conservation that pays local people is the only durable model.

    4. UP Green Hydrogen Policy 2024

    Asked

    • What are the aims and objectives of Green Hydrogen Policy – 2024 of Uttar Pradesh Government ? Mention the governments incentives for Green Hydrogen Projects. 2025 GS-VI · 12 marks · 200 words

    Open with

    Define green hydrogen (made by electrolysis using renewable power) and place the State policy under the National Green Hydrogen Mission.

    Develop

    • Aims: build production capacity, cut industry emissions, create a hydrogen and ammonia ecosystem, attract investment, support research.
    • Demand base: fertiliser plants and refineries in the State.
    • Incentives: capital subsidy, extra support for early projects, Centres of Excellence.
    • Challenges: cost against grey hydrogen, renewable power and water availability, storage and transport.

    Facts to quote

    • Target: one million tonnes a year of green hydrogen or ammonia capacity by 2028.
    • Capital subsidy up to 30%, and up to 40% for the first five projects.
    • UP's hydrogen demand is about 0.9 million tonnes a year.
    • Four Centres of Excellence are planned.
    • National mission (January 2023): Rs 19,744 crore, 5 million tonnes a year by 2030.

    Close with

    Tie it to UP's solar push and the national net-zero 2070 goal.

    5. Bio-energy and biomass in Uttar Pradesh

    Asked

    • Critically analyse the current initiatives and future prospects for bio-energy development in Uttar Pradesh. 2023 GS-VI · 12 marks · 200 words
    • Biomass energy considered renewable and ecologically sensitive in Uttar Pradesh. Explain. 2025 GS-VI · 8 marks · 125 words

    Open with

    Biomass is renewable because crops and residues regrow; UP has a large base in sugarcane, paddy and wheat residues and cattle dung.

    Develop

    • Current initiatives: State Bio-Energy Policy 2022 promoting compressed biogas, bio-coal and biodiesel; UPNEDA as nodal agency.
    • Why 'ecologically sensitive': done badly it means residue burning, soil-nutrient loss, land diverted from food, and air pollution; done well it stops stubble burning and methane release.
    • Prospects: rural jobs, farmer income from residue, cleaner cooking and transport fuel, lower fuel imports.
    • Constraints: residue collection and storage chain, plant viability, gas grid access.

    Facts to quote

    • Policy declared September 2022; subsidies capped at Rs 20 crore per plant.
    • Land on lease at Rs 1 per acre per year and full stamp-duty exemption for bioenergy units.
    • Target of 1,000 tonnes a day of compressed biogas; 48 CBG and nine biodiesel plants commissioned (March 2026).
    • Biogas is mainly methane and carbon dioxide.
    • India reached 20% ethanol blending in petrol in 2025.

    Close with

    Present bio-energy as a waste-to-wealth route that also tackles stubble burning.

    6. Social forestry in Uttar Pradesh

    Asked

    • What are the key initiatives and strategies undertaken by the Government of Uttar Pradesh to promote social-forestry in the State ? 2023 GS-VI · 12 marks · 200 words

    Open with

    Define social forestry: raising trees outside traditional forests, on community, farm and roadside land, for fuelwood, fodder and environmental benefit.

    Develop

    • Why it matters in UP: low natural forest cover in a densely farmed plain.
    • Strategies: mass plantation drives with public participation, agroforestry on farms, plantations along rivers, roads and canals, heritage-tree protection.
    • Institutions: Forest Department, UP Forest Corporation, Central Agroforestry Research Institute at Jhansi.
    • Gaps: sapling survival, monoculture, monitoring.

    Facts to quote

    • ISFR 2023: UP forest cover 6.24%, tree cover 3.72%, together 9.96% of the State.
    • UP's gain in forest and tree cover (559.19 km²) was the second highest in India after Chhattisgarh.
    • Single-day plantations: 36.51 crore saplings (20 July 2024), 37.21 crore (9 July 2025), 35.27 crore (12 July 2026).
    • Over 242 crore saplings in nine years; aim of 15% green cover by 2030.
    • Pavitra Dhara: 3.72 crore saplings along the Ganga, Yamuna, Saryu, Hindon and Gomti.
    • 948 heritage trees of 28 species; adoption scheme announced July 2025.

    Close with

    Argue for survival audits and farmer-led agroforestry over headline numbers.

    7. Groundwater problems in Uttar Pradesh

    Asked

    • Mention the major problems and challenges associated with the utilization of the groundwater in Uttar Pradesh. 2023 GS-VI · 8 marks · 125 words

    Open with

    UP's farming and drinking water depend heavily on groundwater, so falling levels and poor quality are both development issues.

    Develop

    • Quantity: over-extraction by tube wells for water-intensive crops, falling water tables in the west, hard-rock scarcity in Bundelkhand.
    • Quality: arsenic along the Ganga plain, fluoride and nitrate pockets, industrial and sewage contamination.
    • Governance: weak regulation of extraction, low recharge, loss of ponds and wetlands.
    • Responses: Atal Bhujal Yojana, rainwater harvesting, wetland notification, river-linking for Bundelkhand, crop diversification.

    Facts to quote

    • UP is one of seven States under Atal Bhujal Yojana (launched April 2020).
    • Arsenic-affected States in the notes include Uttar Pradesh.
    • Ken-Betwa link will benefit Banda, Mahoba, Jhansi and Lalitpur.
    • Bundelkhand is keyed by UPPSC as UP's most climate-vulnerable agro-climatic zone.
    • The Central Ground Water Board prepares the Annual Groundwater Quality Report.

    Close with

    Recommend demand management first: recharge alone cannot keep pace with extraction.

    8. Sustainable Development Goals and India

    Asked

    • Throw light on the 'Pursuit of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in India'. 2018 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words
    • What do you understand by "leaving no one behind" with reference to sustainable development goals? 2020 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words
    • What is Sustainable Development Goal-2030? Discuss the relevances of different agenda associated with it. 2021 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words
    • Describe the various efforts being made in India to achieve the 'Sustainable Development Goals'. 2023 GS-III · 12 marks · 200 words
    • How can inclusive and sustainable industrialization (SDG 9) drive economic growth (SDG 8), while ensuring environmental sustainability (SDG 12, 13) in India? 2025 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words

    Open with

    State what the SDGs are: 17 goals and 169 targets in the UN's 2030 Agenda, adopted in 2015.

    Develop

    • 'Leaving no one behind' is the Agenda's central pledge: reach the poorest and most excluded first.
    • India's machinery: NITI Aayog as nodal body, SDG India Index ranking States, State and district indicator frameworks.
    • Efforts by goal: tap water (SDG 6), clean energy (SDG 7), lifestyle change (SDG 12), climate targets (SDG 13).
    • Industry link (SDG 9, 8, 12, 13): green manufacturing, renewable power for industry, circular economy, green jobs.
    • Gaps: nutrition, gender, data quality, finance.

    Facts to quote

    • India ranked 109 in the global SDG Index (2024).
    • UP was the fastest-moving State in the SDG India Index between 2018 and 2023-24.
    • UP's SDG indicator-framework progress report is prepared by the Planning Department (UPPCS 2025 key).
    • Rural tap-water coverage rose from 16.72% (2019) to 81.94% (June 2026).
    • India holds about one-sixth of the world's people, so its progress decides global success.

    Close with

    Close on localisation: goals are met in districts and gram panchayats.

    9. Energy demand, renewables and solar viability

    Asked

    • Discuss the causes of energy crisis in India. 2019 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words
    • Examine the financial and technical viability of solar energy projects in India. Also discuss the Government Schemes launched to promote solar energy in the country. 2022 GS-III · 12 marks · 200 words
    • What steps are being taken to meet the continuously increasing demand of energy resources in India ? Discuss with special reference to renewable and sustainable energy resources. 2023 GS-III · 12 marks · 200 words

    Open with

    India's energy demand is rising with growth and urbanisation while coal and imported oil still dominate; renewables are the main response.

    Develop

    • Causes of the energy crisis: demand growth, import dependence, coal supply and distribution-company finances, transmission losses.
    • Steps: non-fossil capacity targets, rooftop solar, solar pumps for farms, green hydrogen, ethanol blending, International Solar Alliance.
    • Solar viability, financial: falling tariffs against high upfront cost, discom payment delays, need for storage.
    • Solar viability, technical: intermittency, grid integration, land, imported components.
    • UP angle: State Solar Energy Policy 2022.

    Facts to quote

    • Non-fossil capacity reached 300.50 GW, over 54% of installed power capacity (31 July 2026); the 2030 target of 50% was met in 2025.
    • PM Surya Ghar (February 2024): one crore households, Rs 75,021 crore, subsidy up to Rs 78,000.
    • National Green Hydrogen Mission: 5 million tonnes a year by 2030.
    • 20% ethanol blending achieved in 2025.
    • UP Solar Energy Policy 2022: 22,000 MW by 2026-27; Ayodhya as model solar city; 4,000 MW corridor in Bundelkhand.

    Close with

    Conclude that storage, grids and discom reform now matter more than adding panels.

    10. Economic development versus carbon emissions

    Asked

    • Write a note on "Problem of Equilibrium between Economic Development and Carbon Emission." 2018 GS-III · 12 marks · 200 words

    Open with

    Growth needs energy, and India's energy is still carbon-heavy; the task is to raise incomes while lowering emissions per unit of output.

    Develop

    • India's position: low per-person emissions, development needs, and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities.
    • Strategy: cut emissions intensity, not growth; shift power to non-fossil sources; efficiency; carbon market; lifestyle change.
    • Costs: transition finance, coal-region jobs, technology access.
    • Global side: climate finance from developed countries.

    Facts to quote

    • Updated NDC (2022): 45% cut in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 from 2005 levels; about 50% non-fossil power capacity.
    • NDC for 2031-35 (approved March 2026): 47% lower intensity and 60% non-fossil capacity.
    • Emissions intensity fell about 36% between 2005 and 2020.
    • Net zero by 2070, set out in the Long-Term Low Emissions Development Strategy (2022).
    • COP29 set a climate-finance goal of at least $300 billion a year by 2035.

    Close with

    Frame it as decoupling: India has already grown while cutting intensity.

    11. Biodiversity and why the tropics are rich

    Asked

    • Define Biodiversity. Why are tropical countries rich in biodiversity? Explain. 2019 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words

    Open with

    Define biodiversity as the variety of life at three levels: genes, species and ecosystems.

    Develop

    • Latitudinal gradient: species numbers rise from the poles to the Equator.
    • Reasons: stable, warm and wet climate all year; more solar energy and productivity; long undisturbed evolutionary time; many niches in layered rain forest.
    • Evidence: tropical rain forests and coral reefs hold the highest diversity.
    • India: a megadiverse country with four hotspots.

    Facts to quote

    • Tropical rain forests have the maximum biodiversity (asked in six UPPSC papers).
    • India's hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Sundaland.
    • Habitat destruction is the main cause of biodiversity loss.

    Close with

    Note that the richest regions are also losing habitat fastest.

    12. Ecologically sensitive areas and their protection

    Asked

    • What are the ecologically sensitive areas in India ? Mention the policies of the Government of India for their protection. 2024 GS-III · 12 marks · 200 words

    Open with

    Explain that eco-sensitive zones are notified around protected areas under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, as shock absorbers.

    Develop

    • Types to mention: eco-sensitive zones, the Western Ghats and Himalaya, wetlands and Ramsar sites, mangroves and coasts, biosphere reserves.
    • Regulation in an eco-sensitive zone: activities are prohibited, regulated or permitted; not everything is banned.
    • Policies: Environment (Protection) Act, Wild Life (Protection) Act, Forest (Conservation) Act, Wetlands Rules 2017, MISHTI for mangroves, biosphere reserve programme.
    • Issues: local livelihoods, weak enforcement, delays in notification.

    Facts to quote

    • Eco-sensitive zones come under the 1986 Environment Act, not the Wildlife Act.
    • India has 18 biosphere reserves, 13 in UNESCO's network.
    • 103 Ramsar sites (October 2026).
    • Protected-area network grew from 745 (2014) to 1,134 (2025).

    Close with

    Balance: zoning should restrict damaging industry, not local farming.

    13. Plastic waste management

    Asked

    • What are the major guidelines of Uttar Pradesh Government with reference to Plastic Waste Management ? 2023 GS-VI · 8 marks · 125 words

    Open with

    Plastic is non-biodegradable; rules now target single-use items, thin carry bags and producer responsibility.

    Develop

    • National rules: ban on identified single-use plastic items, minimum carry-bag thickness, extended producer responsibility, labelling.
    • State role: enforcement by urban bodies and the pollution control board, collection and recycling, awareness.
    • Gaps: enforcement at source, alternatives for small traders, informal recyclers.

    Facts to quote

    • Single-use plastic items banned from 1 July 2022.
    • Carry-bag thickness raised to 75 microns (30 September 2021) and 120 microns (31 December 2022).
    • Barcode or QR information on plastic packaging from 1 July 2025.
    • Recycling plants rose from 829 (2019-20) to 3,036 (2024-25).
    • The notes do not hold UP's own guidelines; add them from the State's notification.

    Close with

    Stress reduction and reuse ahead of recycling.

    Asked, but not covered in these notes

    These real questions need material the notes do not hold yet, mostly UP government documents. Prepare them from the State's own sources.

    • Describe the targets of energy generation through renewable energy sources in accordance with National Energy Policy 2017 drafted by NITI Aayog. 2018 GS-III · 8 marks · 125 words
